```ts
console.log(leaf.parent?.value, cacheEntry.deref()?.children.length);
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::mem::size_of;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

// A recursive type has no finite size; Box breaks the recursion with an 8-byte pointer
#[derive(Debug)]
enum List {
    Cons(i32, Box<List>),
    Nil,
}

impl List {
    fn sum(&self) -> i32 {
        match self {
            List::Cons(value, rest) => value + rest.sum(),
            List::Nil => 0,
        }
    }
}

// Parent links are Weak so the parent <-> child cycle doesn't keep both alive forever
struct TreeNode {
    value: i32,
    parent: RefCell<Weak<TreeNode>>,
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<TreeNode>>>,
}

fn main() {
    let list = List::Cons(1, Box::new(List::Cons(2, Box::new(List::Nil))));
    println!("{list:?} sums to {}", list.sum());

    // Thin pointers are 8 bytes; unsized targets (str, dyn Trait) add a length or vtable word
    println!("Box<i32>={}B Option<Box<i32>>={}B Box<str>={}B Rc<i32>={}B",
        size_of::<Box<i32>>(), size_of::<Option<Box<i32>>>(), size_of::<Box<str>>(), size_of::<Rc<i32>>());

    let leaf = Rc::new(TreeNode { value: 3, parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()), children: RefCell::new(vec![]) });
    let branch = Rc::new(TreeNode { value: 5, parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()), children: RefCell::new(vec![Rc::clone(&leaf)]) });
    *leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&branch);

    let parent_value = leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade().map(|p| p.value);
    println!("leaf {} has parent {:?}; branch has {} child", leaf.value, parent_value, branch.children.borrow().len());
    println!("branch strong={} weak={}", Rc::strong_count(&branch), Rc::weak_count(&branch));
    println!("leaf   strong={} weak={}", Rc::strong_count(&leaf), Rc::weak_count(&leaf));

    // Arc: same layout as Rc, but the counters are atomics so clones can cross threads
    let shared = Arc::new(vec![10, 20, 30]);
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..3)
        .map(|i| {
            let shared = Arc::clone(&shared);
            thread::spawn(move || shared[i] * 2)
        })
        .collect();
    let doubled: Vec<i32> = handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect();
    println!("{doubled:?}, strong count after threads exit = {}", Arc::strong_count(&shared));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Use `Box` for recursive types, trait objects (`Box<dyn Error>`) and moving large values without copying them on the stack. For shared read-only data across Tokio tasks, `Arc<T>` is the default and cheap enough to clone per request; `Arc<str>` and `Arc<[T]>` save an allocation and a pointer hop over `Arc<String>` and `Arc<Vec<T>>`.
- **Footgun:** An `Rc<RefCell<T>>` cycle (parent and child holding strong references to each other) leaks silently: neither count reaches zero, no Drop runs, and nothing warns you. Make back-references `Weak` and call `upgrade()`, which returns `None` once the target is gone.
- **Architecture note:** Prefer ownership trees and indices over pointer graphs: a `Vec<Node>` plus `usize` ids (an arena) gives you parent links without Rc, RefCell or Weak and keeps nodes contiguous in memory. `Rc<RefCell<T>>` is the closest thing to a JS object reference, and reaching for it everywhere is usually a sign the design is fighting the borrow checker.

Go deeper: [Appendix 1: Borrow Checker Mastery](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/borrow-checker), [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

### Chapter 11: Interior Mutability: Cell, RefCell, Mutex & RwLock

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/interior_mutability

In JavaScript, `const` only freezes the binding: any code holding a reference can mutate the object. Rust's default is the opposite: `&T` means read-only. Interior mutability types are the explicit, typed exceptions: `Cell` and `RefCell` within one thread, and `Mutex`, `RwLock` and atomics when threads share the data.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Each tool moves the borrow check somewhere else. `Cell<T>` has zero overhead (same size as `T`) because it never hands out references, only copies values in and out. `RefCell<T>` adds an isize borrow flag (positive = number of readers, -1 = one writer), so `RefCell<u32>` is 16 bytes and a conflicting borrow panics at runtime instead of failing to compile. `Mutex<T>` owns the data and only exposes it through a guard; on Linux it is a 4-byte futex word plus a poison flag, so `Mutex<u64>` is 16 bytes (the playground prints 16, macOS prints 24). Atomics compile to single instructions (`lock xadd` on x86) and need no lock at all. JavaScript needs none of this on the main thread because only one piece of code runs at a time; between worker_threads the only shared memory is a SharedArrayBuffer, and `Atomics` is the only safe way to touch it.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// const freezes the binding, not the object: anyone holding a reference can mutate it
const stats = { hits: 0, log: [] as string[] };

function record(target: typeof stats, path: string): void {
  target.hits++;
  target.log.push(path);
}

record(stats, '/health');
record(stats, '/users');

// Between worker_threads, only a SharedArrayBuffer is truly shared, and Atomics is the
// only safe way to mutate it. There is no Mutex<T> that owns the data.
const shared = new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4));
Atomics.add(shared, 0, 1);

console.log(stats.hits, stats.log, Atomics.load(shared, 0));
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};
use std::mem::size_of;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex, RwLock};
use std::thread;

// Single-threaded: mutate through &self, checked at zero cost (Cell) or at runtime (RefCell)
struct RequestStats {
    hits: Cell<u32>,
    log: RefCell<Vec<String>>,
}

impl RequestStats {
    fn record(&self, path: &str) {
        self.hits.set(self.hits.get() + 1);
        self.log.borrow_mut().push(path.to_string());
    }
}

fn main() {
    let stats = RequestStats { hits: Cell::new(0), log: RefCell::new(Vec::new()) };
    stats.record("/health");
    stats.record("/users");
    println!("hits={} log={:?}", stats.hits.get(), stats.log.borrow());

    // RefCell enforces the borrow rules at runtime: borrow_mut() here would panic
    let reader = stats.log.borrow();
    println!("try_borrow_mut while a reader is alive fails: {}", stats.log.try_borrow_mut().is_err());
    drop(reader);

    // Multi-threaded: the Mutex owns the counter, the atomic needs no lock at all
    let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64));
    let hits = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..4)
        .map(|_| {
            let (counter, hits) = (Arc::clone(&counter), Arc::clone(&hits));
            thread::spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..1_000 {
                    *counter.lock().unwrap() += 1; // guard drops at the end of this statement
                    hits.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for handle in handles {
        handle.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("mutex={} atomic={}", *counter.lock().unwrap(), hits.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    // RwLock: many readers at once, or one writer
    let cache = RwLock::new(String::from("v1"));
    {
        let (r1, r2) = (cache.read().unwrap(), cache.read().unwrap());
        println!("two concurrent readers: {r1} {r2}");
    }
    *cache.write().unwrap() = String::from("v2");
    println!("after write: {}", cache.read().unwrap());

    println!("Cell<u32>={}B RefCell<u32>={}B Mutex<u64>={}B AtomicU64={}B",
        size_of::<Cell<u32>>(), size_of::<RefCell<u32>>(), size_of::<Mutex<u64>>(), size_of::<AtomicU64>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Keep critical sections short: `*counter.lock().unwrap() += 1;` drops the guard at the end of the statement. For a single counter or flag, an `AtomicU64` or `AtomicBool` beats a Mutex. Use `RwLock` only when reads vastly outnumber writes and take long enough to matter; for tiny reads a Mutex is often faster.
- **Footgun:** Holding a `std::sync::MutexGuard` across `.await` makes the future `!Send`, so `tokio::spawn` refuses to compile it, and where it does compile (`spawn_local`, `block_on`) another task locking on the same thread deadlocks it. Tokio's guidance: use `std::sync::Mutex` for short critical sections without awaits, and `tokio::sync::Mutex` only when the guard must live across one. Also, a thread that panics while holding a std Mutex poisons it, and every later `lock()` returns `Err`.
- **Architecture note:** Because a Rust Mutex wraps the data (`Mutex<T>`), there is no way to reach the counter without taking the lock, unlike Java's `synchronized` or a C mutex sitting next to the data it is meant to protect. `Send` and `Sync` finish the job: `RefCell` is `Send` but not `Sync`, so the compiler rejects sharing it between threads and you have to upgrade to `Mutex` or `RwLock`.

Go deeper: [Appendix 1: Borrow Checker Mastery](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/borrow-checker), [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

### Chapter 12: Struct Memory Layout, Alignment & Padding

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/memory_alignment

V8 decides how JavaScript objects are laid out (hidden classes, tagged slots, boxed doubles) and you can't change it. Rust structs are plain bytes with a size and alignment you can print: by default rustc reorders fields to minimize padding, `#[repr(C)]` keeps declaration order for FFI, `packed` removes padding, and `align(64)` pads to a cache line.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Every type has an alignment (u8: 1, u32: 4, u64: 8) and each field must sit at an offset that is a multiple of it. With `#[repr(C)]`, `{ a: u8, b: u64, c: u8 }` needs 7 padding bytes after `a` and 7 trailing bytes so arrays stay aligned: 24 bytes for 10 bytes of data. The default `repr(Rust)` puts `b` first and packs `a` and `c` behind it for 16 bytes, though that order is not a stable guarantee. `packed` gets it to 10 bytes but forbids references to misaligned fields. `Option<&u64>` and `Option<NonZeroU64>` stay 8 bytes by using the impossible zero value as `None` (a niche), while `Option<u64>` needs a separate tag and grows to 16. In Node (x64 builds ship without V8 pointer compression), `{ a: 1, b: 2.5, c: 3 }` is a 48-byte object: a 24-byte header (map, properties, elements) plus three 8-byte tagged slots, and 2.5 lives in a separate HeapNumber because it isn't a Smi.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// A JS object's layout is chosen by V8, not by you. On x64 Node (no pointer compression)
// it starts with a 24-byte header (map, properties, elements), then 8-byte field slots.
const point = { a: 1, b: 2.5, c: 3 }; // 2.5 is not a Smi, so V8 may box it as a HeapNumber

// For an exact byte layout you place bytes by hand, like #[repr(C, packed)]:
const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(10);
const view = new DataView(buffer);
view.setUint8(0, point.a);
view.setBigUint64(1, 42n, true); // unaligned 8-byte write at offset 1: DataView allows it
view.setUint8(9, point.c);

// Typed arrays, unlike DataView, require alignment:
// new Float64Array(buffer, 1) -> RangeError: start offset of Float64Array should be a multiple of 8
console.log(buffer.byteLength, view.getBigUint64(1, true));
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::mem::{align_of, offset_of, size_of};
use std::num::NonZeroU64;

// repr(C): declaration order is kept, so padding lands where you put it
#[allow(dead_code)]
#[repr(C)]
struct DeclaredOrder {
    a: u8,  // offset 0, then 7 padding bytes so b is 8-aligned
    b: u64, // offset 8
    c: u8,  // offset 16, then 7 trailing bytes so size is a multiple of align
}

// Default repr(Rust): rustc may reorder fields (it puts b first here); the order is not a stable guarantee
#[allow(dead_code)]
struct CompilerOrder {
    a: u8,
    b: u64,
    c: u8,
}

// packed: no padding, align 1. Taking &wire.b is a compile error (E0793), reading by value is fine
#[allow(dead_code)]
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct WireHeader {
    a: u8,
    b: u64,
    c: u8,
}

// One counter per 64-byte cache line so two threads updating neighbours don't false-share
#[allow(dead_code)]
#[repr(align(64))]
struct PaddedCounter {
    hits: u64,
}

fn report<T>(name: &str) {
    println!("{name:<22} size={:>2} align={:>2}", size_of::<T>(), align_of::<T>());
}

fn main() {
    report::<DeclaredOrder>("repr(C) a,b,c");
    report::<CompilerOrder>("repr(Rust) a,b,c");
    report::<WireHeader>("repr(C, packed)");
    report::<PaddedCounter>("repr(align(64))");

    println!("repr(C) offsets:    a={} b={} c={}", offset_of!(DeclaredOrder, a), offset_of!(DeclaredOrder, b), offset_of!(DeclaredOrder, c));
    println!("repr(Rust) offsets: a={} b={} c={}", offset_of!(CompilerOrder, a), offset_of!(CompilerOrder, b), offset_of!(CompilerOrder, c));

    // Niche optimisation: Option reuses an impossible bit pattern instead of adding a tag
    report::<Option<&u64>>("Option<&u64>");
    report::<Option<NonZeroU64>>("Option<NonZeroU64>");
    report::<Option<u64>>("Option<u64>");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Print it, don't guess: `size_of`, `align_of` and `std::mem::offset_of!` (stable since 1.77) answer layout questions, and an `assert_eq!(size_of::<T>(), 16)` test catches regressions. For large arrays of structs, removing padding (or switching to a struct of arrays) directly cuts cache misses.
- **Footgun:** A `#[repr(packed)]` struct can't hand out `&wire.b` (error E0793) because a misaligned reference is undefined behavior; read the field by value (`let b = wire.b;`) instead. And never transmute bytes into a default-repr struct: its field order may change between compiler versions. Use `#[repr(C)]` plus a crate like `zerocopy` or `bytemuck` for wire formats.
- **Architecture note:** `#[repr(align(64))]` gives each hot counter its own cache line so two cores incrementing neighbouring counters don't keep stealing the line from each other (false sharing). crossbeam's `CachePadded<T>` does the same, and uses 128 bytes on x86_64 and aarch64 because Intel prefetches cache lines in pairs and Apple M-series chips use 128-byte lines.

Go deeper: [Appendix 8: Senior Rust Interview Q&A](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/interviews), [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting)

## Part 3: Databases & SQL

### Chapter 13: Prisma / TypeORM vs SQLx Compile-Time SQL

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/sqlx_compile_time

Prisma and TypeORM generate SQL at runtime, and their types come from `schema.prisma` (Prisma) or decorated entity classes (TypeORM), not from the database. SQLx's `query!` and `query_as!` macros send your raw SQL to a real database at compile time, so a misspelled column, a wrong type, or a nullable column mapped to a non-Option field fails `cargo build`.

**Why Rust does it this way:** At build time the macro reads DATABASE_URL, asks Postgres to prepare the statement, and gets back the parameter types plus each result column's type and nullability. It then generates the row-decoding code: `int8` becomes `i64` and a nullable `text` becomes `Option<String>`. The playground has no database, so this snippet simulates that described-columns table and the `fetch_optional` contract (zero rows is `Ok(None)`, not an error). At runtime nothing is built: the SQL string is sent as-is and each connection caches the prepared statement. Prisma's types come from `schema.prisma` via `prisma generate`; if the live database drifts from that file, the code still type-checks and fails in production. `$queryRaw` is typed only by the generic you assert (Prisma's TypedSQL is its closer equivalent to SQLx).

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

const prisma = new PrismaClient();

// Typed against schema.prisma by `prisma generate`, not against the live database:
// if a migration drifted, this compiles and fails at runtime
const users = await prisma.user.findMany({
  where: { isActive: true },
  select: { id: true, email: true, displayName: true },
});

// Raw SQL escapes the type system entirely: the row type is whatever you claim it is
const rows = await prisma.$queryRaw<{ id: bigint; email: string }[]>`
  SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ${1}
`;

console.log(users.length, rows[0]?.email);
```

Rust:

```rust
// Real SQLx (needs DATABASE_URL at build time, or a committed .sqlx/ cache):
//
//     let user = sqlx::query_as!(
//         UserRow,
//         "SELECT id, email, display_name, is_active FROM users WHERE id = $1",
//         user_id
//     )
//     .fetch_optional(&pool)
//     .await?;
//
// At compile time the macro sends the SQL to Postgres as a prepared statement, reads back
// the parameter and column types plus nullability, and emits code that fails to build if
// UserRow doesn't match. The playground has no database, so this file SIMULATES that step.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct UserRow {
    id: i64,                      // int8 NOT NULL -> i64
    email: String,                // text NOT NULL -> String
    display_name: Option<String>, // text NULL     -> Option<String>
    is_active: bool,              // bool NOT NULL -> bool
}

// What Postgres reports when the macro describes the query
struct DescribedColumn {
    name: &'static str,
    pg_type: &'static str,
    nullable: bool,
}

const DESCRIBED: [DescribedColumn; 4] = [
    DescribedColumn { name: "id", pg_type: "int8", nullable: false },
    DescribedColumn { name: "email", pg_type: "text", nullable: false },
    DescribedColumn { name: "display_name", pg_type: "text", nullable: true },
    DescribedColumn { name: "is_active", pg_type: "bool", nullable: false },
];

fn rust_type_for(column: &DescribedColumn) -> String {
    let base = match column.pg_type {
        "int4" => "i32",
        "int8" => "i64",
        "text" | "varchar" => "String",
        "bool" => "bool",
        other => panic!("no mapping for {other}"),
    };
    if column.nullable { format!("Option<{base}>") } else { base.to_string() }
}

// Stand-in for .fetch_optional(&pool): zero rows is Ok(None), not an error
fn fetch_optional(table: &[UserRow], id: i64) -> Result<Option<&UserRow>, String> {
    Ok(table.iter().find(|row| row.id == id))
}

fn main() {
    println!("Types the macro would derive from the database:");
    for column in &DESCRIBED {
        println!("  {:<13} {:<5} -> {}", column.name, column.pg_type, rust_type_for(column));
    }

    let users = vec![
        UserRow { id: 1, email: "ada@example.com".into(), display_name: None, is_active: true },
        UserRow { id: 2, email: "linus@example.com".into(), display_name: Some("Linus".into()), is_active: false },
    ];

    for id in [2, 99] {
        match fetch_optional(&users, id) {
            Ok(Some(user)) => println!("id {id}: {} active={} name={:?}", user.email, user.is_active, user.display_name),
            Ok(None) => println!("id {id}: no row"),
            Err(e) => eprintln!("database error: {e}"),
        }
    }
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Run `cargo sqlx prepare` and commit the generated `.sqlx/` directory: with it present (or `SQLX_OFFLINE=true`), CI and Docker builds compile without a database. `cargo sqlx prepare --check` in CI fails when queries changed but the cache wasn't regenerated.
- **Footgun:** Nullability inference is conservative for expressions and outer joins: a `LEFT JOIN` column or `count(*)` can come back as `Option<T>`. Override per column with an alias: `SELECT count(*) AS "total!"` forces non-null and `"name?"` forces Option. The macros check against whatever schema DATABASE_URL points at, so run migrations before building.
- **Architecture note:** SQLx is not an ORM: there is no query builder in the hot path and no generated client, just your SQL, compile-time-generated decode code and the Postgres wire protocol. For dynamic SQL (optional filters, variable column lists) use `sqlx::QueryBuilder` or the unchecked `sqlx::query_as::<_, T>()` with `#[derive(FromRow)]`, and accept that those are only checked at runtime.

Go deeper: [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice), [Appendix 6: Testing & Mocking in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/testing)

### Chapter 14: Connection Pools: pg.Pool vs sqlx::Pool

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/db_pool

`pg.Pool` hands out clients on a single-threaded event loop. `sqlx::Pool` is shared by every Tokio worker thread at once: it's an `Arc` internally so cloning is cheap, an async semaphore caps open connections, and a checked-out `PoolConnection` returns to the pool when it drops.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Both pools solve the same problem: each Postgres connection is a separate backend process on the server costing a few MB of RAM, so you open a handful and reuse them. pg.Pool defaults to `max: 10`, `idleTimeoutMillis: 10000` and `connectionTimeoutMillis: 0`, which means a request waits forever when the pool is exhausted. SQLx's `PgPoolOptions` defaults to `max_connections(10)`, `min_connections(0)`, a 30-second `acquire_timeout`, a 10-minute `idle_timeout`, a 30-minute `max_lifetime` and `test_before_acquire(true)`; an exhausted pool returns `Error::PoolTimedOut`. The real difference is ownership: `pool.connect()` in Node returns a client you must `release()`, while a Rust `PoolConnection` returns itself on Drop, including on early return, `?` and panic unwinding. This snippet models that with std threads, a Mutex and a Condvar; the real SQLx pool uses an async semaphore so waiting tasks don't block worker threads.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import pg from 'pg';

const pool = new pg.Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max: 10, // the default
  idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000, // the default
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000, // default is 0: wait forever for a free client
});

// pool.query() checks a client out, runs one statement and releases it for you
const { rows } = await pool.query<{ id: number; email: string }>(
  'SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = $1',
  [42],
);

// pool.connect() hands you the client: forget release() and that connection leaks
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('SELECT 1');
} finally {
  client.release();
}

console.log(rows[0]?.email, pool.totalCount, pool.idleCount, pool.waitingCount);
```

Rust:

```rust
// A std-only model of how sqlx::Pool behaves (the real one is async and uses a semaphore,
// not a Condvar): bounded connections, an acquire timeout, and RAII return-to-pool on Drop.
use std::sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

struct Connection {
    id: u32,
}

struct PoolInner {
    idle: Mutex<Vec<Connection>>,
    returned: Condvar,
}

// Like sqlx::Pool, cloning is cheap: every clone points at the same Arc'd pool
#[derive(Clone)]
struct Pool(Arc<PoolInner>);

struct PooledConnection {
    conn: Option<Connection>,
    pool: Pool,
}

impl PooledConnection {
    fn id(&self) -> u32 {
        self.conn.as_ref().map_or(0, |c| c.id)
    }
}

// Same idea as sqlx's PoolConnection: dropping the handle gives the connection back
impl Drop for PooledConnection {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(conn) = self.conn.take() {
            self.pool.0.idle.lock().unwrap().push(conn);
            self.pool.0.returned.notify_one();
        }
    }
}

impl Pool {
    fn new(max_connections: u32) -> Self {
        let idle = (1..=max_connections).map(|id| Connection { id }).collect();
        Pool(Arc::new(PoolInner { idle: Mutex::new(idle), returned: Condvar::new() }))
    }

    fn acquire(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Result<PooledConnection, &'static str> {
        let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
        let mut idle = self.0.idle.lock().unwrap();
        loop {
            if let Some(conn) = idle.pop() {
                return Ok(PooledConnection { conn: Some(conn), pool: self.clone() });
            }
            let remaining = deadline.saturating_duration_since(Instant::now());
            if remaining.is_zero() {
                return Err("PoolTimedOut"); // sqlx::Error::PoolTimedOut
            }
            idle = self.0.returned.wait_timeout(idle, remaining).unwrap().0;
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let pool = Pool::new(2);

    let first = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let second = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    println!("checked out #{} and #{}", first.id(), second.id());
    println!("third acquire while both are busy: {:?}", pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(50)).err());

    drop(first); // back to the pool, no release() call to forget
    let reused = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    println!("reused connection #{}", reused.id());
    drop((second, reused));

    // 6 worker threads share 2 connections; each waits its turn instead of opening a new socket
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..6)
        .map(|worker| {
            let pool = pool.clone();
            thread::spawn(move || {
                let conn = pool.acquire(Duration::from_secs(2)).expect("pool starved");
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)); // pretend to run a query
                (worker, conn.id())
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for handle in handles {
        let (worker, conn_id) = handle.join().unwrap();
        println!("worker {worker} ran on connection #{conn_id}");
    }
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Size the pool from the database side, not the CPU count: the sum of `max_connections` across all app replicas must stay under Postgres's `max_connections` (100 by default) minus headroom for migrations and admin sessions. Put PgBouncer in front if you run many replicas, and set a short `acquire_timeout` (a few seconds) so overload fails fast instead of queueing requests.
- **Footgun:** Holding a `PoolConnection` (or an open `Transaction`) across a slow `.await` such as an HTTP call pins that connection for the whole call: with 10 connections and a 2-second upstream, throughput caps at 5 requests per second. Pass `&pool` to queries (`.fetch_one(&pool)`) so each statement checks out a connection only while it runs.
- **Architecture note:** Prisma's Rust query engine ran its own pool (`connection_limit` defaulted to physical CPUs x 2 + 1, `pool_timeout` to 10s); with driver adapters the pool is the underlying driver's, such as pg.Pool. In Rust you put one `PgPool` in Axum `State`; because it's `Clone + Send + Sync`, every handler on every worker thread shares the same set of sockets.

Go deeper: [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

### Chapter 15: Transactions & RAII Rollback

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/db_transactions

In Node.js you write `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` by hand around try/catch/finally, or use Prisma's `$transaction` callback. In SQLx, `pool.begin()` returns a `Transaction` value: `commit()` consumes it, and if it is dropped without a commit (early return, `?`, panic) it rolls back.

**Why Rust does it this way:** The danger in the Node version is the cleanup path. If an error skips `ROLLBACK` and the client is released, the session stays in an aborted transaction and the next borrower's queries fail with "current transaction is aborted". If a non-error early return skips `COMMIT`, the next borrower silently runs inside your open transaction. SQLx ties the transaction's lifetime to a value: `commit(self)` takes ownership, so the type system stops you from using a transaction after committing it. Drop can't run async code, so SQLx queues the `ROLLBACK` on the connection and it is sent before that connection is reused. This snippet simulates the behavior in memory: writes are staged, `commit()` applies them, and the `?` on the unknown account returns early and discards the staged debit. Beginning a transaction on an open one (`tx.begin()`) issues a SAVEPOINT, which gives you nested transactions.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import pg from 'pg';

const pool = new pg.Pool();

async function transfer(from: number, to: number, amount: number): Promise<void> {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    await client.query('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2', [amount, from]);
    await client.query('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2', [amount, to]);
    await client.query('COMMIT');
  } catch (err) {
    // Skip this and the client goes back to the pool inside an aborted transaction:
    // the next borrower gets "current transaction is aborted" on every query
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

await transfer(1, 2, 30);
```

Rust:

```rust
// Simulates sqlx::Transaction semantics with an in-memory table: writes are staged,
// commit() applies them, and dropping the transaction without commit discards them.
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Database {
    balances: BTreeMap<&'static str, i64>,
}

struct Transaction<'db> {
    db: &'db mut Database,
    staged: BTreeMap<&'static str, i64>,
    committed: bool,
}

impl Database {
    fn begin(&mut self) -> Transaction<'_> {
        println!("  BEGIN");
        Transaction { db: self, staged: BTreeMap::new(), committed: false }
    }
}

impl Transaction<'_> {
    fn balance(&self, account: &'static str) -> Result<i64, String> {
        self.staged.get(account).or_else(|| self.db.balances.get(account)).copied().ok_or(format!("no account {account}"))
    }

    fn set_balance(&mut self, account: &'static str, amount: i64) {
        self.staged.insert(account, amount);
    }

    // Takes self by value: after commit the transaction can't be used again
    fn commit(mut self) {
        self.db.balances.append(&mut self.staged);
        self.committed = true;
        println!("  COMMIT");
    }
}

impl Drop for Transaction<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if !self.committed {
            println!("  ROLLBACK (dropped without commit, {} staged write(s) discarded)", self.staged.len());
        }
    }
}

fn transfer(db: &mut Database, from: &'static str, to: &'static str, amount: i64) -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut tx = db.begin();
    let from_balance = tx.balance(from)?;
    if from_balance < amount {
        return Err(format!("{from} has {from_balance}, needs {amount}")); // tx drops here -> ROLLBACK
    }
    tx.set_balance(from, from_balance - amount);
    let to_balance = tx.balance(to)?; // unknown account: `?` returns early, the debit above is rolled back
    tx.set_balance(to, to_balance + amount);
    tx.commit();
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    let mut db = Database::default();
    db.balances.insert("alice", 100);
    db.balances.insert("bob", 50);

    for (from, to, amount) in [("alice", "bob", 30), ("alice", "carol", 10), ("bob", "alice", 500)] {
        println!("transfer {amount} {from} -> {to}");
        if let Err(e) = transfer(&mut db, from, to, amount) {
            println!("  error: {e}");
        }
    }
    println!("final balances: {:?}", db.balances);
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Write transactional helpers against `&mut PgConnection` and pass `&mut *tx`, so the same function runs inside or outside a transaction and tests can wrap it in one that never commits. For SERIALIZABLE isolation, run `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE` as the first statement and retry on SQLSTATE 40001.
- **Footgun:** With `panic = "abort"` in Cargo.toml a panic never runs Drop, so SQLx sends no ROLLBACK. The data is still safe, because the process dies, the socket closes and Postgres aborts the transaction, but any cleanup of your own in Drop never runs. Keep transactions short: row locks are held until commit, and a session left "idle in transaction" stops VACUUM from cleaning up dead rows.
- **Architecture note:** This is RAII applied to a protocol, the same pattern as `MutexGuard` and `PoolConnection`: "a transaction is open on this connection" is state held by a value, and every exit path ends it. JavaScript is gaining a similar tool, `await using` with `Symbol.asyncDispose` (Node 24+), but it's opt-in per resource, whereas Drop always runs during unwinding.

Go deeper: [Appendix 6: Testing & Mocking in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/testing), [Appendix 14: Rust Developer Roadmap (roadmap.sh)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/roadmap)

### Chapter 16: Redis Caching & Cache Stampede Protection

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/redis_caching

Node.js uses `ioredis`; Rust uses `redis-rs`, whose `MultiplexedConnection` is a cheap-to-clone handle that pipelines commands from many tasks over one TCP socket. Redis stores the value, but it doesn't stop a stampede: when a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses at once. Single-flight loading fixes that.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Both clients multiplex: ioredis sends every caller's commands down one connection and matches replies in FIFO order, and redis-rs's `MultiplexedConnection` does the same through a background task, so plain GET/SET traffic doesn't need a connection pool. The stampede problem lives in your app, not in Redis: 1,000 requests miss `user:10` in the same millisecond and run the same slow query 1,000 times. The Node fix keeps a `Map<string, Promise>` of in-flight loads. The Rust snippet does the same across threads with a `OnceLock` per key: the first caller computes, concurrent callers block until the value is ready, and eight misses cause one database load. The playground has no Redis, so the snippet keeps values in memory with a TTL as a stand-in for SETEX; in a Tokio service you'd use `tokio::sync::OnceCell` or the `moka` crate's `get_with`, which coalesces concurrent loads for you.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL ?? 'redis://127.0.0.1:6379');
const inFlight = new Map<string, Promise<string>>();

async function loadUserFromDb(id: number): Promise<string> {
  return JSON.stringify({ id, name: 'Ada' }); // stand-in for a slow query
}

async function getUser(id: number): Promise<string> {
  const key = `user:${id}`;
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) return cached;

  // Single-flight: concurrent misses in THIS process share one database load
  let pending = inFlight.get(key);
  if (!pending) {
    pending = loadUserFromDb(id)
      .then(async (json) => {
        await redis.set(key, json, 'EX', 60);
        return json;
      })
      .finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
    inFlight.set(key, pending);
  }
  return pending;
}

const burst = await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 8 }, () => getUser(10)));
console.log(burst.length);
```

Rust:

```rust
// Real redis-rs (tokio feature), not runnable on the playground:
//
//     let client = redis::Client::open("redis://127.0.0.1/")?;
//     let mut con = client.get_multiplexed_async_connection().await?; // cheap to clone, one TCP socket
//     let cached: Option<String> = con.get("user:10").await?;
//     let _: () = con.set_ex("user:10", &json, 60).await?;
//
// This file SIMULATES the cache in memory to show the part Redis doesn't solve for you:
// when a hot key expires, N concurrent requests must trigger ONE database load, not N.
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex, OnceLock};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

struct Slot {
    value: OnceLock<String>,
    created: Instant,
}

struct SingleFlightCache {
    slots: Mutex<HashMap<String, Arc<Slot>>>,
    ttl: Duration,
}

impl SingleFlightCache {
    fn get_or_compute(&self, key: &str, compute: impl FnOnce() -> String) -> String {
        let slot = {
            let mut slots = self.slots.lock().unwrap();
            match slots.get(key).filter(|slot| slot.created.elapsed() < self.ttl) {
                Some(fresh) => Arc::clone(fresh),
                None => {
                    let slot = Arc::new(Slot { value: OnceLock::new(), created: Instant::now() });
                    slots.insert(key.to_string(), Arc::clone(&slot));
                    slot
                }
            }
        }; // map lock released here, so slow loads for other keys aren't blocked

        // First caller runs compute; concurrent callers for the same slot block until it finishes
        slot.value.get_or_init(compute).clone()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let cache = SingleFlightCache { slots: Mutex::new(HashMap::new()), ttl: Duration::from_millis(300) };
    let db_loads = AtomicUsize::new(0);

    let load_user = || {
        db_loads.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)); // slow query
        String::from(r#"{"id":10,"name":"Ada"}"#)
    };

    let request_burst = || {
        thread::scope(|s| {
            for _ in 0..8 {
                s.spawn(|| cache.get_or_compute("user:10", load_user));
            }
        });
    };

    request_burst();
    println!("8 concurrent misses -> {} database load(s)", db_loads.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    request_burst();
    println!("8 hits within TTL   -> {} database load(s) total", db_loads.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(350));
    request_burst();
    println!("after TTL expiry    -> {} database load(s) total", db_loads.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Add jitter to TTLs (say 60s plus or minus 10%) so keys written together don't expire together. For protection across replicas, take a short Redis lock with `SET lock:user:10 <token> NX PX 5000` and have the losers wait briefly and re-read, or serve stale data while one worker refreshes.
- **Footgun:** A multiplexed connection is shared, so connection-scoped commands interfere with other callers: `SELECT`, `WATCH`/`MULTI` and blocking pops like `BLPOP` change state for, or stall, every task using that handle. Use a dedicated connection (or a `bb8`/`deadpool` pool) for those. And version your keys (`user:v2:10`) so a deploy that changes the struct doesn't fail to deserialize old cache entries.
- **Architecture note:** The single-flight slot is an `Arc<Slot>` cloned out of the map before the slow load runs, so the map lock is released and a slow load for one key never blocks lookups of other keys; only callers of the same key wait. `OnceLock::get_or_init` runs the closure at most once per slot even when eight threads race, the same contract the in-flight Promise map gives you on one JS thread.

Go deeper: [Appendix 14: Rust Developer Roadmap (roadmap.sh)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/roadmap)

### Chapter 17: SeaORM & ActiveModel vs TypeORM

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/seaorm_patterns

If you want an ORM rather than raw SQLx, SeaORM gives you entities, relations, migrations and an ActiveModel that tracks which columns changed. Unlike TypeORM's runtime decorators, entities are plain Rust types generated by derive macros, and queries are built with the SeaQuery builder and executed through SQLx.

**Why Rust does it this way:** TypeORM reads entity metadata at runtime from decorators (via `reflect-metadata` and `emitDecoratorMetadata`), and `repository.save(entity)` SELECTs the row by primary key to work out what changed before it can UPDATE. SeaORM puts change tracking in the type: every ActiveModel field is an `ActiveValue`, either `Set(v)` (write it), `Unchanged(v)` (loaded, skip it) or `NotSet` (omit it so the database default applies). Converting a loaded `Model` into an ActiveModel marks every field Unchanged, so setting one field produces `UPDATE users SET email = $1 WHERE id = $2` with no extra round trip, and an insert with `id: NotSet` lets SERIAL generate the key. The snippet re-implements that ActiveValue logic in plain Rust because the playground doesn't ship sea-orm. The honest trade-off: column names and types are checked by the compiler against your entity structs, but the SQL is built at runtime, so it isn't verified against the live schema the way `sqlx::query!` is.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { Column, DataSource, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';

// Decorators record column metadata at runtime via reflect-metadata
// (tsconfig: experimentalDecorators + emitDecoratorMetadata)
@Entity({ name: 'users' })
class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
  id!: number;

  @Column()
  username!: string;

  @Column()
  email!: string;
}

const db = new DataSource({ type: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL, entities: [User] });
await db.initialize();

const repo = db.getRepository(User);
const user = await repo.findOneByOrFail({ id: 7 });
user.email = 'new@example.com';
// save() first SELECTs the row by primary key to diff it, then UPDATEs the changed columns
await repo.save(user);
```

Rust:

```rust
// Mirrors SeaORM's ActiveModel / ActiveValue so it runs on the playground (no sea-orm crate there).
// Real SeaORM builds the SQL at runtime with SeaQuery and executes it through SQLx.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum ActiveValue<T> {
    Set(T),       // changed: written by INSERT / UPDATE
    Unchanged(T), // loaded from the database: skipped by UPDATE
    NotSet,       // unknown: omitted so the database default applies
}
use ActiveValue::{NotSet, Set, Unchanged};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct UserModel {
    id: i32,
    username: String,
    email: String,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct UserActiveModel {
    id: ActiveValue<i32>,
    username: ActiveValue<String>,
    email: ActiveValue<String>,
}

// Like SeaORM's IntoActiveModel: a freshly loaded row starts fully Unchanged
impl From<UserModel> for UserActiveModel {
    fn from(m: UserModel) -> Self {
        Self { id: Unchanged(m.id), username: Unchanged(m.username), email: Unchanged(m.email) }
    }
}

impl UserActiveModel {
    fn set_columns(&self) -> Vec<(&'static str, String)> {
        let mut columns = Vec::new();
        if let Set(v) = &self.id { columns.push(("id", v.to_string())); }
        if let Set(v) = &self.username { columns.push(("username", v.clone())); }
        if let Set(v) = &self.email { columns.push(("email", v.clone())); }
        columns
    }

    fn insert_sql(&self) -> (String, Vec<String>) {
        let columns = self.set_columns();
        let names: Vec<&str> = columns.iter().map(|(name, _)| *name).collect();
        let placeholders: Vec<String> = (1..=columns.len()).map(|i| format!("${i}")).collect();
        let sql = format!("INSERT INTO users ({}) VALUES ({}) RETURNING id", names.join(", "), placeholders.join(", "));
        (sql, columns.into_iter().map(|(_, value)| value).collect())
    }

    fn update_sql(&self) -> Result<(String, Vec<String>), &'static str> {
        let id = match &self.id {
            Set(id) | Unchanged(id) => *id,
            NotSet => return Err("update needs a primary key"),
        };
        let changed: Vec<_> = self.set_columns().into_iter().filter(|(name, _)| *name != "id").collect();
        if changed.is_empty() {
            return Err("nothing changed");
        }
        let assignments: Vec<String> = changed.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, (name, _))| format!("{name} = ${}", i + 1)).collect();
        let sql = format!("UPDATE users SET {} WHERE id = ${}", assignments.join(", "), changed.len() + 1);
        let mut params: Vec<String> = changed.into_iter().map(|(_, value)| value).collect();
        params.push(id.to_string());
        Ok((sql, params))
    }
}

fn main() {
    // id is NotSet, so it's left out and the SERIAL default generates it
    let new_user = UserActiveModel { id: NotSet, username: Set("rustacean".into()), email: Set("r@example.com".into()) };
    println!("{:?}", new_user.insert_sql());

    let loaded = UserModel { id: 7, username: "rustacean".into(), email: "r@example.com".into() };
    let mut active: UserActiveModel = loaded.into();
    println!("{:?}", active.update_sql()); // nothing is Set yet

    active.email = Set("new@example.com".into());
    println!("{:?}", active.update_sql()); // only the changed column, no reload needed
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Generate entities from an existing database with `sea-orm-cli generate entity -u $DATABASE_URL -o src/entity`, and keep schema changes in `sea-orm-migration` so entities and migrations stay in sync. For a hot query, drop down to SQLx: you can build the SeaORM connection from an existing `sqlx::PgPool`, so both share one pool.
- **Footgun:** Building an ActiveModel by hand with every field `Set` and calling `update()` writes every column, overwriting concurrent changes to fields you never meant to touch. Start from a loaded model (`model.into_active_model()`) and `Set` only what changed. The opposite trap: a required column left `NotSet` on insert fails at the database, not at compile time.
- **Architecture note:** Underneath, SeaORM is SeaQuery (a SQL AST builder) plus a SQLx driver, so you get SQLx's pool, TLS and Postgres wire protocol. Relations are declared once with `#[derive(DeriveRelation)]` and loaded with `find_with_related` (one JOIN) or the loader API, which batches related rows in one query instead of TypeORM-style lazy N+1 loading.

Go deeper: [Appendix 14: Rust Developer Roadmap (roadmap.sh)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/roadmap)

### Chapter 18: MongoDB: Mongoose vs official mongodb crate

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/mongodb_driver

Mongoose layers schemas, casting, hooks and change-tracked Documents over the MongoDB Node driver. The official Rust `mongodb` crate is closer to the bare driver: a `Collection<T>` is typed by your Serde struct, so the struct is the schema and every decode checks it.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Mongoose hydrates each result into a Document with internal state for change tracking, getters, setters and casting, which is why `.lean()` (plain objects straight from the driver) is the standard fix for read-heavy endpoints. The Rust driver decodes BSON directly into your struct through Serde, so a read is just the decode. An ObjectId is exactly 12 bytes: a 4-byte big-endian Unix timestamp, a 5-byte random value unique to the process, and a 3-byte counter, which is why ids sort roughly by creation time. Numbers are where Node and Rust disagree: the Node driver stores an integer JS number as Int32 when it fits in 32 bits and as Double otherwise, while Serde maps `i32`, `i64` and `f64` to distinct BSON types. A count written from Node as 3,000,000,000 is a Double, and a Rust `i64` field rejects it. The playground has neither MongoDB nor the bson crate, so this snippet simulates the ObjectId layout and that decode rule in plain Rust.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import mongoose, { Schema, Types } from 'mongoose';

interface User {
  email: string;
  loginCount: number;
}

const userSchema = new Schema<User>({
  email: { type: String, required: true, lowercase: true },
  loginCount: { type: Number, default: 0 },
});
userSchema.pre('save', function () {
  // document middleware: runs on doc.save(), not on updateOne()
});
const UserModel = mongoose.model<User>('User', userSchema);

await mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URL ?? 'mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/app');

// Hydrated Document: change tracking, getters/setters, casting, save() and hooks
const doc = await UserModel.findOne({ email: 'ada@example.com' });
// lean(): the plain object the driver decoded, with no Mongoose wrapper
const plain = await UserModel.findOne({ email: 'ada@example.com' }).lean();

console.log(doc?._id instanceof Types.ObjectId, plain?.loginCount);
```

Rust:

```rust
// Real driver (mongodb 3.x + serde), not runnable on the playground:
//
//     #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
//     struct User { #[serde(rename = "_id")] id: ObjectId, email: String, login_count: i64 }
//     let users: Collection<User> = client.database("app").collection("users");
//     let user: Option<User> = users.find_one(doc! { "email": "ada@example.com" }).await?;
//
// This file SIMULATES the two parts that surprise Node developers: the 12-byte ObjectId
// and strict numeric types when decoding BSON into a Rust struct.
use std::fmt;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};
use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

// 4-byte big-endian timestamp | 5-byte per-process random | 3-byte counter
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct ObjectId([u8; 12]);

static COUNTER: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0x00ab_cdef); // real drivers start at a random value

impl ObjectId {
    fn new(process_random: [u8; 5]) -> Self {
        let secs = SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_secs() as u32;
        let counter = COUNTER.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) & 0x00ff_ffff;
        let mut bytes = [0u8; 12];
        bytes[0..4].copy_from_slice(&secs.to_be_bytes());
        bytes[4..9].copy_from_slice(&process_random);
        bytes[9..12].copy_from_slice(&counter.to_be_bytes()[1..]);
        ObjectId(bytes)
    }

    fn timestamp_secs(&self) -> u32 {
        u32::from_be_bytes([self.0[0], self.0[1], self.0[2], self.0[3]])
    }
}

impl fmt::Debug for ObjectId {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        let hex: String = self.0.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect();
        write!(f, "ObjectId(\"{hex}\")")
    }
}

// A slice of the BSON type system: numbers carry their wire type
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Bson {
    Int32(i32),
    Int64(i64),
    Double(f64),
    String(String),
}

struct User {
    id: ObjectId,
    email: String,
    login_count: i64,
}

fn field<'d>(doc: &'d [(&str, Bson)], name: &str) -> Result<&'d Bson, String> {
    doc.iter().find(|(key, _)| *key == name).map(|(_, value)| value).ok_or(format!("missing field `{name}`"))
}

fn decode_user(id: ObjectId, doc: &[(&str, Bson)]) -> Result<User, String> {
    let email = match field(doc, "email")? {
        Bson::String(s) => s.clone(),
        other => return Err(format!("email: expected string, found {other:?}")),
    };
    let login_count = match field(doc, "login_count")? {
        Bson::Int32(n) => i64::from(*n), // widening is lossless
        Bson::Int64(n) => *n,
        Bson::Double(d) => return Err(format!("login_count: invalid type double {d}, expected i64")),
        Bson::String(_) => return Err("login_count: invalid type string, expected i64".to_string()),
    };
    Ok(User { id, email, login_count })
}

fn show(result: Result<User, String>) {
    match result {
        Ok(user) => println!("Ok: {} logins={} _id={:?}", user.email, user.login_count, user.id),
        Err(e) => println!("Err: {e}"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let id = ObjectId::new([0x5a, 0x1f, 0x09, 0xc3, 0x77]);
    println!("{id:?} created at unix {} ({} bytes)", id.timestamp_secs(), std::mem::size_of::<ObjectId>());

    // The Node driver stores integer JS numbers that fit in 32 bits as Int32 ...
    let small = [("email", Bson::String("ada@example.com".into())), ("login_count", Bson::Int32(42))];
    show(decode_user(id, &small));

    // ... and larger ones as Double, which a strict i64 field rejects
    let large = [("email", Bson::String("bot@example.com".into())), ("login_count", Bson::Double(3_000_000_000.0))];
    show(decode_user(ObjectId::new([0x5a, 0x1f, 0x09, 0xc3, 0x77]), &large));

    // Writing it as Int64 (Long / BigInt on the Node side) decodes cleanly
    let explicit = [("email", Bson::String("ops@example.com".into())), ("login_count", Bson::Int64(3_000_000_000))];
    show(decode_user(ObjectId::new([0x5a, 0x1f, 0x09, 0xc3, 0x77]), &explicit));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Map the id explicitly: `#[serde(rename = "_id", skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] id: Option<ObjectId>` lets the server generate ids on insert. Build filters with `doc! { "email": email }`, and keep `Collection<Document>` for genuinely schemaless data.
- **Footgun:** Mongoose features don't exist in the Rust driver: `default: 0`, `lowercase: true` and `pre('save')` logic must move into your constructors or service layer, or into a server-side `$jsonSchema` validator so every client, Node or Rust, is held to the same rules during a migration. Without that, a Node service and a Rust service writing the same collection drift apart.
- **Architecture note:** The driver is async on Tokio. The 3.x API takes the filter directly (`find_one(doc! { .. }).await`) and sets options through builder methods. It keeps a connection pool per server, and `max_pool_size` defaults to 10 in the Rust driver versus `maxPoolSize` 100 in the Node driver, so a service ported one-to-one can hit pool waits under load that the Node version never saw.

Go deeper: [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

## Part 4: Queues & Workers

### Chapter 19: BullMQ vs Redis Streams in Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/redis_queues

BullMQ runs job queues on Redis using lists, sorted sets and Lua scripts, and every handler in a Node process shares one JS thread. The usual Rust equivalent is Redis Streams with consumer groups (`XADD`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XAUTOCLAIM`) through the `redis` crate, or a framework like `apalis` that wraps them, with workers running as Tokio tasks across all cores.

**Why Rust does it this way:** A Redis Stream is an append-only log. A consumer group keeps one cursor for the whole group plus a Pending Entries List (PEL) that records, for each delivered entry, the owning consumer, the delivery time and a delivery count. `XREADGROUP ... >` hands out only never-delivered entries and adds them to the PEL; `XACK` removes them. If a worker crashes, its entries stay pending until another consumer reclaims them with `XAUTOCLAIM` (Redis 6.2+) after a minimum idle time, which bumps the delivery count you can use to dead-letter poison jobs. That is at-least-once delivery, the same guarantee BullMQ gets from lock renewal and its stalled-job check. The model above runs in memory so it works in the playground; a production worker needs the `redis` crate (with the `streams` and `tokio-comp` features) and a Redis server. The throughput gap comes from the runtime: BullMQ's `concurrency: 50` means 50 promises interleaved on one thread, so CPU-heavy jobs run one after another, while 50 Tokio tasks reading the same group run on every core.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Worker, type Job } from 'bullmq';

interface EmailJob { to: string; subject: string }
declare function sendEmail(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void>;

// BullMQ keeps jobs in Redis lists, sorted sets and hashes, and moves them
// between "wait", "active", "delayed", "completed" and "failed" with Lua scripts.
const worker = new Worker<EmailJob>(
  'emails',
  async (job: Job<EmailJob>) => {
    await sendEmail(job.data.to, job.data.subject);
    return { deliveredAt: Date.now() };
  },
  {
    connection: { host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379 },
    concurrency: 50, // 50 jobs in flight, but all their JS still runs on one thread
  },
);

// A job whose lock isn't renewed (crashed or event-loop-blocked worker) is "stalled"
// and moved back to wait: at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent.
worker.on('stalled', (jobId) => console.warn(`job ${jobId} stalled, will be retried`));
worker.on('failed', (job, err) => console.error(job?.id, err.message));
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

// In-memory model of a Redis Stream consumer group, so the XADD / XREADGROUP /
// XACK / XAUTOCLAIM lifecycle runs here without a Redis server.
struct Entry {
    id: u64,
    payload: &'static str,
}

struct Pending {
    consumer: &'static str,
    delivered_at_ms: u64,
    deliveries: u32,
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct ConsumerGroup {
    stream: Vec<Entry>,              // append-only log
    next_undelivered: usize,         // the group's cursor (">" in XREADGROUP)
    pending: BTreeMap<u64, Pending>, // Pending Entries List (PEL): delivered, not yet acked
}

impl ConsumerGroup {
    // XADD jobs * payload ...
    fn xadd(&mut self, payload: &'static str) -> u64 {
        let id = self.stream.len() as u64 + 1;
        self.stream.push(Entry { id, payload });
        id
    }

    // XREADGROUP GROUP workers <consumer> COUNT <count> STREAMS jobs >
    fn xreadgroup(&mut self, consumer: &'static str, count: usize, now_ms: u64) -> Vec<(u64, &'static str)> {
        let end = (self.next_undelivered + count).min(self.stream.len());
        let batch: Vec<(u64, &'static str)> = self.stream[self.next_undelivered..end]
            .iter()
            .map(|entry| (entry.id, entry.payload))
            .collect();
        for (id, _) in &batch {
            self.pending.insert(*id, Pending { consumer, delivered_at_ms: now_ms, deliveries: 1 });
        }
        self.next_undelivered = end;
        batch
    }

    // XACK jobs workers <id>
    fn xack(&mut self, id: u64) -> bool {
        self.pending.remove(&id).is_some()
    }

    // XAUTOCLAIM jobs workers <consumer> <min-idle-ms> 0
    fn xautoclaim(&mut self, consumer: &'static str, min_idle_ms: u64, now_ms: u64) -> Vec<u64> {
        let mut claimed = Vec::new();
        for (id, entry) in self.pending.iter_mut() {
            if now_ms - entry.delivered_at_ms >= min_idle_ms {
                entry.consumer = consumer;
                entry.delivered_at_ms = now_ms;
                entry.deliveries += 1;
                claimed.push(*id);
            }
        }
        claimed
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut group = ConsumerGroup::default();
    for job in ["welcome-email", "invoice-pdf", "resize-avatar", "sync-crm"] {
        group.xadd(job);
    }

    // t=0: worker-a takes two jobs, acks one, then crashes before acking the other
    for (id, job) in group.xreadgroup("worker-a", 2, 0) {
        println!("worker-a got #{id} {job}");
        if id == 1 {
            group.xack(id);
        }
    }
    println!("worker-a crashed; PEL holds {} unacked entry", group.pending.len());

    // t=10ms: worker-b reads only NEW entries; #2 is not redelivered automatically
    for (id, job) in group.xreadgroup("worker-b", 10, 10) {
        println!("worker-b got #{id} {job}");
        group.xack(id);
    }

    // t=60s: a reaper claims anything idle for more than 30s
    for id in group.xautoclaim("worker-b", 30_000, 60_000) {
        let entry = &group.pending[&id];
        println!("worker-b reclaimed #{id} from crashed consumer (delivery #{}, now owned by {})", entry.deliveries, entry.consumer);
        group.xack(id);
    }
    println!("PEL empty: {} -> every job processed at least once", group.pending.is_empty());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Read in batches with `XREADGROUP GROUP workers <consumer> COUNT 32 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS jobs >` so one round trip fetches up to 32 jobs, and run a periodic `XAUTOCLAIM jobs workers <consumer> 60000 0` reaper. `apalis` packages this pattern, plus retries and monitoring, if you'd rather not hand-roll it.
- **Footgun:** A missing `XACK` doesn't cause redelivery on its own: the entry just sits in the PEL, invisible to `>` reads, and the PEL grows until memory or `XPENDING` alerts catch it. Pair every consumer group with a reclaim loop, and dead-letter entries whose delivery count passes a threshold so one poison job can't loop forever.
- **Architecture note:** Acked entries are not deleted, so cap the stream with `XADD jobs MAXLEN ~ 1000000 * ...` (the `~` lets Redis trim whole internal nodes cheaply). Trimming ignores the PEL, so size the cap well above your worst-case backlog or pending jobs get trimmed away. `BLOCK` holds its connection for the whole wait, so give blocking `XREADGROUP` calls a dedicated connection and send `XACK` and other short commands over a shared `redis::aio::MultiplexedConnection`.

Go deeper: [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio)

### Chapter 20: Exponential Backoff & Dead-Letter Queues

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/job_retries

BullMQ retries a failed job using `attempts` and a `backoff` strategy. In Rust you write the retry policy yourself, or use a crate like `backon` or `tokio-retry`: classify errors as transient or permanent, wait an exponentially growing, randomly jittered delay between attempts, and move exhausted jobs to a dead-letter queue (DLQ).

**Why Rust does it this way:** BullMQ's exponential strategy waits `delay * 2^(attemptsMade - 1)`, so 1s, 2s, 4s and 8s for the config above. Without its `jitter` option, every job that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, so when a payment provider recovers, every queued retry hits it on the same tick. Full jitter (a random delay between 0 and the exponential ceiling, the variant AWS's backoff analysis recommends) spreads that herd out; BullMQ applies it with `backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000, jitter: 1 }`. The Rust version also puts retryability in the type: `JobError::Permanent` goes straight to the DLQ, the role `UnrecoverableError` plays in BullMQ, which has no separate DLQ and keeps exhausted jobs in its failed set. `checked_shl` and `saturating_mul` keep the arithmetic safe at high attempt counts, where a plain `1 << attempt` panics in debug builds once `attempt` reaches 64 and silently masks the shift amount in release.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Queue, Worker, UnrecoverableError } from 'bullmq';

const connection = { host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379 };
const payments = new Queue('payments', { connection });

await payments.add('charge', { orderId: 'ord_42', amountCents: 10_000 }, {
  attempts: 5,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 }, // waits 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s between attempts
  removeOnFail: false, // exhausted jobs stay in the "failed" set: BullMQ's de facto DLQ
});

new Worker('payments', async (job) => {
  const res = await fetch('https://psp.example.com/charge', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': job.data.orderId }, // retries must not double-charge
    body: JSON.stringify(job.data),
  });
  if (res.status === 422) throw new UnrecoverableError('card declined'); // skip remaining attempts
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`PSP responded ${res.status}`); // retried with backoff
}, { connection });
```

Rust:

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
enum JobError {
    Transient(&'static str), // timeouts, 503s: worth retrying
    Permanent(&'static str), // validation, 4xx: retrying can't help
}

// Capped exponential backoff: base * 2^attempt, never above cap_ms.
fn exponential_ms(attempt: u32, base_ms: u64, cap_ms: u64) -> u64 {
    let factor = 1u64.checked_shl(attempt).unwrap_or(u64::MAX);
    base_ms.saturating_mul(factor).min(cap_ms)
}

// Tiny deterministic PRNG so the playground output is stable (use the `rand` crate in production).
struct XorShift(u64);
impl XorShift {
    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
        let mut x = self.0;
        x ^= x << 13;
        x ^= x >> 7;
        x ^= x << 17;
        self.0 = x;
        x
    }
}

// "Full jitter": sleep a random duration in [0, ceiling], so a fleet of
// workers that failed together spreads out instead of retrying in lockstep.
fn full_jitter_ms(ceiling_ms: u64, rng: &mut XorShift) -> u64 {
    rng.next() % (ceiling_ms + 1)
}

fn run_with_retries(
    job: &str,
    max_attempts: u32,
    rng: &mut XorShift,
    mut attempt_fn: impl FnMut(u32) -> Result<(), JobError>,
) -> Result<u32, JobError> {
    let mut attempt = 0;
    loop {
        match attempt_fn(attempt) {
            Ok(()) => return Ok(attempt + 1),
            Err(JobError::Permanent(reason)) => return Err(JobError::Permanent(reason)),
            Err(err) if attempt + 1 >= max_attempts => return Err(err),
            Err(JobError::Transient(reason)) => {
                let ceiling = exponential_ms(attempt, 1_000, 30_000);
                let delay = full_jitter_ms(ceiling, rng);
                // In Tokio: tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(delay)).await
                println!("  {job}: attempt {} failed ({reason}); retry in {delay}ms (ceiling {ceiling}ms)", attempt + 1);
                attempt += 1;
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng = XorShift(0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15);
    let mut dead_letters: Vec<(&str, JobError)> = Vec::new();

    let jobs: [(&str, fn(u32) -> Result<(), JobError>); 3] = [
        ("charge ord_1", |attempt| if attempt < 3 { Err(JobError::Transient("PSP 503")) } else { Ok(()) }),
        ("charge ord_2", |_| Err(JobError::Permanent("card declined (422)"))),
        ("charge ord_3", |_| Err(JobError::Transient("socket timeout"))),
    ];

    for (name, attempt_fn) in jobs {
        match run_with_retries(name, 5, &mut rng, attempt_fn) {
            Ok(attempts) => println!("{name}: succeeded after {attempts} attempts"),
            Err(err) => {
                println!("{name}: giving up -> dead-letter queue ({err:?})");
                dead_letters.push((name, err));
            }
        }
    }
    println!("DLQ size: {} (inspect, fix, replay by hand)", dead_letters.len());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Retry only what is idempotent: send a stable `Idempotency-Key` (the job id or order id) so the downstream service can de-duplicate a charge that succeeded but whose response was lost. Cap both the per-attempt delay and the number of attempts, and log the attempt number with every failure.
- **Footgun:** A retry loop in async code that calls `std::thread::sleep` blocks a Tokio worker thread for the whole backoff, stalling every task on that thread; use `tokio::time::sleep`. And retrying 4xx validation errors burns attempts and delays the DLQ alert a human actually needs to see.
- **Architecture note:** Keep the policy a pure function of the attempt number, like `exponential_ms`, so you can unit test it without waiting on real time. Make the DLQ a real destination (a separate stream or table, or BullMQ's failed set with `removeOnFail: false`) that stores everything needed to replay: payload, last error, attempt count and timestamps.

Go deeper: [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

## Part 5: Async & Tokio

### Chapter 21: Promise.all vs tokio::join! & tokio::spawn

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/tokio_spawn

`Promise.all` waits for promises that are already running on Node's single JS thread. Rust futures are lazy and do nothing until polled. `tokio::join!` polls several futures concurrently inside one task, while `tokio::spawn` hands a future to Tokio's multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler so independent tasks can run in parallel on every core.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `join!` gives concurrency without parallelism: it polls each child future in turn whenever it is woken, all inside the task that awaited it, so the two sleeps overlap and the total is about 300ms, not 500ms. `spawn` creates a new task: Tokio makes one heap allocation holding a task header plus the future's state machine (sized by the largest set of locals alive across any `.await`) and puts it on a run queue. Tasks spawned from `main` land in a shared injection queue that any free worker pulls from, and idle workers also steal from busy ones, so the shards report different thread ids. Because a task can move between threads, `spawn` requires the future to be `Send + 'static`, so it can't borrow from the caller's stack. A Node promise is a V8 heap object whose continuations run from the microtask queue on the one main thread. For CPU parallelism Node needs a `worker_threads` Worker: a separate V8 isolate with its own heap and event loop, where every message is structured-cloned across the boundary.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

const fetchUsers = async () => ['Alice', 'Bob'];
const fetchPosts = async () => [{ title: 'Intro to Rust' }];

// Promises are eager: both functions are already running before Promise.all sees them.
// Promise.all only waits; every callback still runs on the one JS thread.
const [users, posts] = await Promise.all([fetchUsers(), fetchPosts()]);

// CPU parallelism needs a worker: a separate V8 isolate with its own heap,
// and data crossing the boundary is structured-cloned (copied).
const sum = await new Promise<number>((resolve, reject) => {
  const worker = new Worker(
    'const { parentPort } = require("node:worker_threads"); let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 5e6; i++) s += i; parentPort.postMessage(s);',
    { eval: true },
  );
  worker.once('message', resolve).once('error', reject);
});
console.log({ users, posts, sum });
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
use tokio::task::JoinSet;
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn fetch_users() -> Vec<&'static str> {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(200)).await;
    vec!["Alice", "Bob"]
}

async fn fetch_posts() -> usize {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(300)).await;
    42
}

#[tokio::main(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 4)]
async fn main() {
    // 1. join!: both futures are polled concurrently inside THIS task.
    //    Total time is the max (~300ms), not the sum, but there is no parallelism.
    let started = Instant::now();
    let (users, posts) = tokio::join!(fetch_users(), fetch_posts());
    println!("join!     -> {users:?} + {posts} posts in ~{}ms", started.elapsed().as_millis());

    // 2. try_join!: the Promise.all equivalent, returns the first Err and drops the rest
    let result = tokio::try_join!(
        async { Ok::<u8, String>(1) },
        async { Err::<u8, String>("db down".to_string()) },
    );
    println!("try_join! -> {result:?}");

    // 3. spawn: independent tasks; the work-stealing scheduler may run each on any worker thread
    let started = Instant::now();
    let mut tasks = JoinSet::new();
    for shard in 0..4u64 {
        tasks.spawn(async move {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
            (shard, format!("{:?}", std::thread::current().id()))
        });
    }
    while let Some(joined) = tasks.join_next().await {
        let (shard, thread) = joined.expect("task panicked");
        println!("spawn     -> shard {shard} finished on {thread}");
    }
    println!("4 spawned tasks in ~{}ms", started.elapsed().as_millis());

    // 4. spawn_blocking: CPU-bound work goes to a separate pool so async workers keep polling
    let sum = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| (0..5_000_000u64).sum::<u64>())
        .await
        .expect("blocking task panicked");
    println!("spawn_blocking -> {sum}");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Use `JoinSet` when you spawn a dynamic number of tasks: `join_next()` yields results as they finish, and dropping the set aborts every task still running. Use `try_join!` instead of `join!` when one error should fail the whole batch, like `Promise.all` rejecting.
- **Footgun:** Dropping a `JoinHandle` does not cancel the task: it detaches and keeps running, like an un-awaited promise. Call `handle.abort()` or keep tasks in a `JoinSet`. And a CPU-heavy loop or `std::thread::sleep` inside async code blocks its worker thread; move the work to `spawn_blocking` or use `tokio::time::sleep`.
- **Architecture note:** `#[tokio::main]` starts one worker thread per CPU core by default, plus a separate blocking pool (up to 512 threads by default) for `spawn_blocking`. Scheduling is cooperative: a task runs until it returns `Pending` at an `.await`, and Tokio adds a per-task operation budget so a loop over always-ready channels still yields to other tasks.

Go deeper: [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio), [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

### Chapter 22: Promise.race vs tokio::select!

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/select_race

`Promise.race()` settles with the first promise to finish but leaves the losers running. `tokio::select!` polls several futures, channel receives and timers, runs the branch that completes first, and drops every other branch. In Rust, dropping a future cancels it at its current `.await` point, so the losers stop immediately.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Every Rust future can be cancelled: it is a state machine, and once it is dropped instead of polled again, its locals' destructors run (that is what makes `CancelProbe` print) and the work stops. That makes timeouts real: `timeout(d, fut)` is a `select!` against a `Sleep`. Node has no equivalent, because a promise can't be cancelled from outside; `AbortController` works only when every function on the path accepts and forwards a signal, which is why `slowQuery()` logs long after it lost. The price in Rust is cancellation safety, because a losing branch can be dropped halfway. Tokio documents `mpsc::Receiver::recv`, `broadcast::Receiver::recv`, `TcpListener::accept` and `AsyncReadExt::read` as cancel-safe (nothing is lost if they lose the race). `read_exact`, `read_to_end` and `write_all` are not: dropped midway, bytes already read are gone, or a message is half-written. In a `loop { select! { .. } }`, create such futures once outside the loop, `tokio::pin!` them and poll `&mut fut` instead of recreating them on every iteration.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

async function slowQuery(signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<string> {
  await sleep(500, undefined, { signal });
  console.log('slowQuery finished anyway: nobody cancelled it');
  return 'rows';
}

// Promise.race settles with the winner but cancels nothing: the loser keeps running
const winner = await Promise.race([slowQuery(), sleep(100, 'timeout')]);
console.log(winner); // 'timeout', and ~400ms later the log above still prints

// Cancellation is opt-in: pass a signal and every layer must forward it
try {
  await slowQuery(AbortSignal.timeout(100));
} catch (err) {
  console.log('aborted:', (err as Error).name);
}
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio::time::{sleep, timeout};

// Prints when a future is dropped before finishing, i.e. cancelled.
struct CancelProbe {
    name: &'static str,
    finished: bool,
}

impl Drop for CancelProbe {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if !self.finished {
            println!("  [drop] {} was cancelled at its .await point", self.name);
        }
    }
}

async fn slow_query(ms: u64) -> &'static str {
    let mut probe = CancelProbe { name: "slow_query", finished: false };
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    probe.finished = true;
    "rows"
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Race a query against a timer: the losing branch is dropped, which cancels it
    tokio::select! {
        rows = slow_query(500) => println!("query won: {rows}"),
        _ = sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)) => println!("timer won after 100ms"),
    }

    // 2. timeout() is the same race, packaged
    match timeout(Duration::from_millis(300), slow_query(50)).await {
        Ok(rows) => println!("timeout(): finished in time with {rows}"),
        Err(_) => println!("timeout(): elapsed"),
    }

    // 3. select! in a loop: mpsc recv() is cancel-safe, so a losing poll never loses a message
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(8);
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        for job in 1..=3 {
            tx.send(job).await.expect("receiver alive");
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(30)).await;
        }
    });
    let mut heartbeat = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_millis(40));
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            biased; // poll top to bottom instead of randomly: messages before heartbeats
            maybe_job = rx.recv() => match maybe_job {
                Some(job) => println!("job {job}"),
                None => {
                    println!("all senders dropped, leaving loop");
                    break;
                }
            },
            _ = heartbeat.tick() => println!("heartbeat"),
        }
    }
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Add `biased;` as the first line of `select!` to poll branches top to bottom instead of in random order, and put shutdown or high-priority channels first. Without it, Tokio randomizes the order on each poll so one always-ready branch can't starve the others.
- **Footgun:** A future that isn't cancel-safe inside a looping `select!` loses data without any error: a `read_exact` that loses to a timer drops the bytes it already consumed, so the next read starts in the middle of a frame. Keep partial state in a buffer that outlives the loop (`read_buf` into a `BytesMut`), or let `tokio_util::codec::FramedRead` handle framing.
- **Architecture note:** `select!` expands into one future that polls every branch, so it runs inside the current task and spawns nothing. A branch whose pattern doesn't match (like `Some(x) = rx.recv()` once the channel closes) is disabled; when every branch is disabled the `else` branch runs, and without an `else` the macro panics.

Go deeper: [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio), [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

### Chapter 23: AbortController vs CancellationToken

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/cancellation_tokens

Node.js cancels work through `AbortController`, passing its `AbortSignal` into every API that supports one. Tokio has two mechanisms: dropping a future cancels it where it is suspended, and `tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken` signals tasks cooperatively so each one can stop where it chooses and clean up. `child_token()` builds a cancellation tree, which `AbortSignal.any()` approximates in Node.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Drop-based cancellation is abrupt: the future stops being polled and only `Drop` impls run, so there is no chance to flush a buffer or commit an offset. A `CancellationToken` makes shutdown cooperative: tasks `select!` on `token.cancelled()` next to their real work and decide what to finish first. Each token is an `Arc` pointing at a node in a parent/child tree. `cancel()` takes a short mutex, marks that node and all its descendants cancelled, and wakes every waiter through `tokio::sync::Notify`, with no OS signals or extra threads involved. Cancelling a child never affects its parent or siblings, the shape `AbortSignal.any([root.signal, own.signal])` reproduces in Node 20.3+. Two differences remain. An `AbortSignal` dispatches its `abort` event synchronously to its listeners, while a cancelled token only wakes tasks that the scheduler then polls. And CPU-bound code (a `spawn_blocking` closure or a tight loop) has no `.await` where it could be cancelled, so it must check `is_cancelled()` itself, just as JS code must check `signal.aborted`.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

async function pollQueue(name: string, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<number> {
  let batches = 0;
  try {
    while (true) {
      await sleep(25, undefined, { signal });
      batches++;
    }
  } catch (err) {
    if (!signal.aborted) throw err;
    console.log(`${name}: aborted after ${batches} batches`);
    return batches;
  }
}

const root = new AbortController();
const reports = new AbortController();
// AbortSignal.any (Node 20.3+) builds a child signal: aborted when ANY input aborts
const ingestSignal = AbortSignal.any([root.signal]);
const reportsSignal = AbortSignal.any([root.signal, reports.signal]);

const workers = [pollQueue('ingest', ingestSignal), pollQueue('reports', reportsSignal)];
await sleep(60);
reports.abort(); // stops only the reports worker
await sleep(60);
root.abort(); // stops everything derived from root
console.log(await Promise.all(workers));
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::task::JoinSet;
```
