```rust
use tokio::time::sleep;
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;

async fn poll_queue(name: &'static str, token: CancellationToken) -> u32 {
    let mut batches = 0;
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            // Cooperative: the task picks where it stops, so it can finish cleanup
            _ = token.cancelled() => {
                println!("{name}: cancelled after {batches} batches, flushing state");
                return batches;
            }
            _ = sleep(Duration::from_millis(25)) => batches += 1,
        }
    }
}

fn crunch(token: &CancellationToken) -> u64 {
    // CPU-bound loops have no .await to be cancelled at: check the token yourself
    let mut checksum = 0u64;
    for i in 0..u64::MAX {
        if i % 100_000 == 0 && token.is_cancelled() {
            break;
        }
        checksum = checksum.wrapping_add(i);
    }
    checksum
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let root = CancellationToken::new(); // like a top-level AbortController
    let ingest = root.child_token(); // cancelled when root is, but not vice versa
    let reports = root.child_token();

    let mut workers = JoinSet::new();
    workers.spawn(poll_queue("ingest", ingest.clone()));
    workers.spawn(poll_queue("reports", reports.clone()));

    sleep(Duration::from_millis(60)).await;
    reports.cancel(); // cancelling a child leaves its siblings and parent running
    println!("root cancelled? {} | ingest cancelled? {}", root.is_cancelled(), ingest.is_cancelled());

    sleep(Duration::from_millis(60)).await;
    root.cancel(); // cascades to every child token
    while let Some(done) = workers.join_next().await {
        done.expect("worker panicked");
    }

    let cpu_token = CancellationToken::new();
    let cpu_job = tokio::task::spawn_blocking({
        let token = cpu_token.clone();
        move || crunch(&token)
    });
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
    cpu_token.cancel();
    println!("cpu job stopped early: checksum {}", cpu_job.await.unwrap());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Give each subsystem a `child_token()` so it can be shut down on its own, and cancel the root on SIGTERM. Pair the tokens with `tokio_util::task::TaskTracker` or a `JoinSet` so after cancelling you can await every task's cleanup before the process exits.
- **Footgun:** A token only helps where it is checked. A loop that awaits an I/O call without racing it against `token.cancelled()` in `select!` won't notice cancellation until that call returns, which may be never. In CPU loops, check `is_cancelled()` every few thousand iterations, as `crunch` does.
- **Architecture note:** Cancellation is sticky: `cancelled()` on an already-cancelled token completes immediately, so a task that starts late can't miss the signal. `token.drop_guard()` returns a guard that cancels the token when it is dropped, tying cancellation to a scope like a `finally { ac.abort() }` that also runs during a panic.

Go deeper: [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio), [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

### Chapter 24: Error Architecture: anyhow vs thiserror

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/error_anyhow_thiserror

In Node.js anything can be thrown, and `catch (err: unknown)` can't know what it got. Rust splits errors into two roles: libraries return typed enums derived with `thiserror`, which implement `std::error::Error` so callers can `match` on variants, and applications wrap any error in `anyhow::Error`, adding `.context()` messages and an optional backtrace on the way up.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `thiserror` is a derive macro, not a runtime. It writes the `Display`, `std::error::Error` (including `source()` for `#[source]` and `#[from]` fields) and `From` impls you would otherwise write by hand, and it doesn't appear in your public API. The enum stays an inline value, 16 bytes here, so returning `Err` allocates nothing. `anyhow::Error` makes the opposite trade: it is a single pointer (8 bytes, and `Result<(), anyhow::Error>` is also 8 thanks to the non-null niche) to a heap block holding a vtable pointer, the original error and an optional `std::backtrace::Backtrace`, captured only when `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`, or `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` without `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`. Each `.context()` adds one more block that wraps the previous one. That allocation happens only on the error path. Context wraps the error rather than replacing it, so `err.chain()` walks every `source()` and `downcast_ref::<RepoError>()` still finds the typed error to choose an HTTP status. In V8, every `new Error()` eagerly captures a stack trace (up to `Error.stackTraceLimit`, 10 frames by default), and ES2022's `{ cause }` is the closest thing to `.context()`.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
class NotFoundError extends Error {
  override name = 'NotFoundError';
  constructor(readonly userId: number) {
    super(`user ${userId} not found`); // V8 captures the stack trace here, on every throw
  }
}

declare const db: { findUser(id: number): Promise<string | undefined> };

async function getUser(id: number): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const user = await db.findUser(id);
    if (!user) throw new NotFoundError(id);
    return user;
  } catch (err) {
    // ES2022 `cause` chaining is the closest thing to anyhow's .context()
    throw new Error(`GET /users/${id} failed`, { cause: err });
  }
}

try {
  await getUser(4);
} catch (err: unknown) { // the signature can't say what may be thrown
  const cause = err instanceof Error ? err.cause : undefined;
  console.log(cause instanceof NotFoundError ? 404 : 500);
}
```

Rust:

```rust
mod repo {
    use thiserror::Error;

    // Library layer: a closed set of failures callers can match on.
    // thiserror only generates Display, std::error::Error (with source()) and From impls.
    #[derive(Debug, Error)]
    pub enum RepoError {
        #[error("user {0} not found")]
        NotFound(u64),
        #[error("connection lost after {retries} retries")]
        ConnectionLost {
            retries: u32,
            #[source]
            source: std::io::Error,
        },
        #[error("corrupt row")]
        CorruptRow(#[from] std::num::ParseIntError),
    }

    pub fn find_user(id: u64) -> Result<String, RepoError> {
        match id {
            1 => Ok("alice".to_string()),
            2 => Err(RepoError::ConnectionLost {
                retries: 3,
                source: std::io::Error::new(std::io::ErrorKind::TimedOut, "socket read timed out"),
            }),
            3 => {
                let age: u32 = "forty".parse()?; // ParseIntError -> RepoError via #[from]
                Ok(format!("age {age}"))
            }
            _ => Err(RepoError::NotFound(id)),
        }
    }
}

use anyhow::{bail, Context};
use repo::RepoError;

// Application layer: any error type, plus human-readable context.
fn handle_get_user(id: u64) -> anyhow::Result<String> {
    if id == 0 {
        bail!("id must be positive");
    }
    let user = repo::find_user(id).with_context(|| format!("GET /users/{id} failed"))?;
    Ok(user)
}

fn http_status(err: &anyhow::Error) -> u16 {
    // The typed error survives inside anyhow: downcast to map it to a status code
    match err.downcast_ref::<RepoError>() {
        Some(RepoError::NotFound(_)) => 404,
        Some(_) => 503,
        None => 400,
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::mem::size_of;
    println!("anyhow::Error: {} bytes (one pointer to a heap block)", size_of::<anyhow::Error>());
    println!("Result<(), anyhow::Error>: {} bytes (null-pointer niche)", size_of::<Result<(), anyhow::Error>>());
    println!("RepoError: {} bytes (inline enum, no allocation)", size_of::<RepoError>());

    for id in [1, 2, 3, 4, 0] {
        match handle_get_user(id) {
            Ok(user) => println!("200 {user}"),
            Err(err) => {
                println!("{} {err}", http_status(&err)); // {err:#} would print the whole chain on one line
                for cause in err.chain().skip(1) {
                    println!("    caused by: {cause}");
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Add context that says what you were doing, not what failed: `.with_context(|| format!("loading config from {path}"))?`. Print with `{:#}` for a one-line chain (`loading config from app.toml: No such file or directory`) or `{:?}` for the multi-line report with the backtrace.
- **Footgun:** Returning `anyhow::Error` from a library's public API forces callers to guess which types to downcast to. And `#[from]` on two variants with the same source type won't compile, because it generates two conflicting `From` impls. Keep `thiserror` enums at crate boundaries and convert to `anyhow` only in binaries and request handlers.
- **Architecture note:** Neither crate changes how errors travel: `?` calls `From::from` on the error and returns early, a plain branch with no unwinding. Panics are Rust's only unwinding path and are meant for bugs, not expected failures like a missing user, whereas JS uses `throw` for both.

Go deeper: [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls), [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

### Chapter 25: Channels: mpsc, broadcast, watch & oneshot

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/channels_sync

Node.js passes messages with `EventEmitter` (synchronous callbacks on one thread) or `postMessage` between workers (a structured-cloned copy). Tokio has four typed channels: `mpsc` (many producers, one consumer, bounded for backpressure), `oneshot` (exactly one reply), `broadcast` (every subscriber sees every message) and `watch` (only the latest value). Sending moves ownership, so even a large buffer crosses threads without being copied.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Sending a `Vec<u8>` through a channel moves its 24-byte header (pointer, capacity, length); the heap buffer stays where it is and now belongs to the receiver. `postMessage` structured-clones the payload unless you list its `ArrayBuffer` as transferable, and `EventEmitter.emit` isn't a queue at all, just a synchronous loop over listeners, so a slow listener stalls whoever emitted. Inside, the four channels differ. Tokio's `mpsc` is a lock-free linked list of fixed-size slot blocks with a semaphore enforcing the bound, so `send().await` parks the producer while the buffer is full (backpressure). `broadcast` is a fixed ring buffer (capacity rounded up to a power of two); a subscriber that falls more than the capacity behind gets `RecvError::Lagged(n)` and skips ahead. `watch` is one value behind an `RwLock` plus a version counter, and `oneshot` is a single slot plus an atomic state word. The blocking `std::sync::mpsc` has used crossbeam-channel's design since Rust 1.67: a bounded channel is an array ring buffer whose slots carry sequence stamps, and an unbounded one is a linked list of blocks.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';
import { MessageChannel } from 'node:worker_threads';

// EventEmitter: emit() calls every listener synchronously, on this thread, with no buffer
const bus = new EventEmitter();
bus.on('frame', (frame: Uint8Array) => console.log('listener got', frame.length, 'bytes'));
bus.emit('frame', new Uint8Array(1024)); // returns only after all listeners ran

// MessagePort (what worker_threads use): an unbounded queue; messages are structured-cloned
const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel();
const frame = new Uint8Array(1024);
port1.postMessage(frame); // serializes and copies the 1 KiB
port1.postMessage(frame, [frame.buffer]); // transfers instead: `frame` is now detached
port2.once('message', (received: Uint8Array) => {
  console.log('port got', received.length, 'bytes; sender view now', frame.length); // 1024, 0
  port1.close();
});
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::{broadcast, mpsc, oneshot, watch};

enum Command {
    Get { key: String, reply: oneshot::Sender<Option<u64>> },
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // mpsc, bounded: send().await waits while both slots are full -> backpressure
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Vec<u8>>(2);
    let producer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for i in 0..4u8 {
            let frame = vec![i; 1024]; // 1 KiB on the heap
            // Moves the 24-byte Vec header into the channel; the KiB itself is never copied
            tx.send(frame).await.expect("receiver alive");
            println!("mpsc: queued frame {i}, free slots {}", tx.capacity());
        }
    }); // tx dropped here, which ends the receive loop below
    while let Some(frame) = rx.recv().await {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await; // slow consumer
        println!("mpsc: consumed frame {} ({} bytes)", frame[0], frame.len());
    }
    producer.await.unwrap();

    // oneshot: request/response to an actor task, like resolving a single Promise
    let (cmd_tx, mut cmd_rx) = mpsc::channel::<Command>(8);
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        while let Some(Command::Get { key, reply }) = cmd_rx.recv().await {
            let _ = reply.send(if key == "visits" { Some(42) } else { None });
        }
    });
    let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = oneshot::channel();
    cmd_tx.send(Command::Get { key: "visits".into(), reply: reply_tx }).await.unwrap();
    println!("oneshot: visits = {:?}", reply_rx.await.unwrap());

    // broadcast: every subscriber sees every message from a fixed ring; slow ones lag
    let (events, mut fast) = broadcast::channel::<u32>(4);
    let mut slow = events.subscribe();
    for n in 1..=6 {
        events.send(n).unwrap();
        fast.recv().await.unwrap(); // keeps up
    }
    match slow.recv().await {
        Err(broadcast::error::RecvError::Lagged(missed)) => println!("broadcast: slow subscriber lagged, {missed} messages overwritten"),
        other => println!("broadcast: {other:?}"),
    }
    println!("broadcast: slow subscriber resumes at {}", slow.recv().await.unwrap());

    // watch: one slot holding the latest value; intermediate values are never queued
    let (config_tx, mut config_rx) = watch::channel("v1");
    config_tx.send("v2").unwrap();
    config_tx.send("v3").unwrap();
    config_rx.changed().await.unwrap();
    println!("watch: saw {} (v2 was overwritten)", *config_rx.borrow_and_update());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Model shared state as an actor: one task owns the data and receives `enum Command` messages over `mpsc`, each carrying a `oneshot::Sender` for the reply, as above. There is no `Mutex`, no lock held across `.await`, and the bounded queue gives you backpressure for free.
- **Footgun:** A receive loop ends only when every `Sender` clone has been dropped. One forgotten clone, often captured by a task you no longer need, keeps `rx.recv()` pending forever. And `unbounded_channel()` has no backpressure: a producer faster than its consumer grows memory without limit.
- **Architecture note:** Use `std::sync::mpsc` or crossbeam between plain threads and Tokio channels between async tasks, because Tokio's `send().await` yields instead of blocking a worker thread. To cross between the two worlds, Tokio channels provide `blocking_send` and `blocking_recv` for code running outside the runtime, such as inside `spawn_blocking`.

Go deeper: [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio), [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy)

### Chapter 26: Graceful Shutdown & OS Signal Handling

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/graceful_shutdown

In Node.js you register `process.on('SIGTERM')`, call `server.close()` and wait for in-flight requests. In Rust, `tokio::signal` turns SIGTERM and Ctrl+C into futures, Axum's `axum::serve(..).with_graceful_shutdown(signal)` stops accepting and drains open connections, and a `CancellationToken` plus a task tracker stops background workers, all under a hard deadline that ends before the orchestrator sends SIGKILL.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Both runtimes handle signals the same way underneath. The real signal handler is tiny and async-signal-safe: it only writes to a pipe that wakes the event loop. libuv then calls your JS listener on the main thread; Tokio registers through `signal-hook-registry` and wakes the task awaiting `signal(SignalKind::terminate())`. In both, registering a handler replaces the default terminate-the-process action, so once you listen for SIGTERM, exiting is your job. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (30s by default) and then sends SIGKILL, so the drain needs its own, shorter deadline: the example stops accepting, lets requests 1 and 2 finish, then aborts request 3, which hangs. The playground can't deliver real signals, so a timer stands in for `shutdown_signal()`, the production function you would pass to Axum.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import http from 'node:http';
import { once } from 'node:events';

declare const db: { end(): Promise<void> };

const server = http.createServer((_req, res) => {
  setTimeout(() => res.end('ok'), 200);
});
server.listen(8080);

// libuv catches the signal and wakes the event loop; this listener then runs on the
// main thread. Registering it replaces Node's default "exit on SIGTERM".
process.once('SIGTERM', async () => {
  server.close(); // stop accepting; since Node 19 this also closes idle keep-alive sockets
  const deadline = setTimeout(() => {
    server.closeAllConnections(); // drop stragglers before Kubernetes sends SIGKILL
    process.exit(1);
  }, 25_000).unref();
  await once(server, 'close'); // fires after the last in-flight request finished
  clearTimeout(deadline);
  await db.end(); // then close pools and flush logs
  process.exit(0);
});
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::task::JoinSet;
use tokio::time::{sleep, timeout, Instant};
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;

// Production signal source. The playground can't deliver SIGTERM, so main() simulates it.
#[allow(dead_code)]
async fn shutdown_signal() {
    let ctrl_c = async { tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await.expect("install Ctrl+C handler") };
    #[cfg(unix)]
    let terminate = async {
        tokio::signal::unix::signal(tokio::signal::unix::SignalKind::terminate())
            .expect("install SIGTERM handler")
            .recv()
            .await;
    };
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    let terminate = std::future::pending::<()>();
    tokio::select! {
        _ = ctrl_c => {},
        _ = terminate => {},
    }
}

async fn handle_request(id: u32, cost_ms: u64) {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(cost_ms)).await;
    println!("  request {id} finished ({cost_ms}ms)");
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let shutdown = CancellationToken::new();
    let mut in_flight = JoinSet::new();

    // Stand-in for shutdown_signal(): "SIGTERM" arrives after 120ms
    let trigger = shutdown.clone();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        sleep(Duration::from_millis(120)).await;
        println!("SIGTERM: stop accepting new requests");
        trigger.cancel();
    });

    // Accept loop: one request every 50ms until shutdown begins
    let mut next_id = 0;
    let mut accept = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_millis(50));
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            _ = shutdown.cancelled() => break,
            _ = accept.tick() => {
                next_id += 1;
                let cost_ms = if next_id == 3 { 5_000 } else { 200 }; // request 3 hangs
                println!("accepted request {next_id}");
                in_flight.spawn(handle_request(next_id, cost_ms));
            }
        }
    }

    // Drain with a deadline shorter than Kubernetes' terminationGracePeriodSeconds
    let started = Instant::now();
    let drain = async { while in_flight.join_next().await.is_some() {} };
    if timeout(Duration::from_millis(500), drain).await.is_err() {
        println!("deadline hit, aborting {} stuck request(s)", in_flight.len());
        in_flight.shutdown().await;
    }
    println!("drained in {}ms; now close pools, flush logs, exit 0", started.elapsed().as_millis());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** With Axum, `axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal()).await?` stops accepting when the signal fires and then waits for open connections with no time limit. Add your own deadline after the signal, like the `timeout` around the drain above, so one stuck connection can't hold the pod until SIGKILL.
- **Footgun:** The kernel applies no default signal actions to PID 1 inside a container. If your binary (Node or Rust) runs as PID 1 and never registers a SIGTERM handler, SIGTERM is ignored and every rollout waits the full grace period for SIGKILL. Register the handler, or run under an init such as `tini` (`docker run --init`).
- **Architecture note:** Order matters: fail the readiness probe so the load balancer stops routing to you, stop accepting, drain in-flight requests, cancel background workers through the token and await them, then flush telemetry and close database pools. Dropping a Tokio runtime does not let tasks finish (they are dropped at their next `.await`), so call `pool.close().await` and await your workers explicitly.

Go deeper: [Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

## Part 6: Systems Internals

### Chapter 27: SIMD Vectorization & Zero-Cost Abstractions

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/simd_optimization

JavaScript has no SIMD API, and V8's JIT compilers don't auto-vectorize ordinary JS loops; in Node, SIMD means WebAssembly SIMD128 (fixed 128-bit vectors) or a native addon. Rust compiles through LLVM, which auto-vectorizes simple loops, and you can go further with explicit `std::arch` intrinsics behind `#[target_feature]` and runtime CPU detection. Portable `std::simd` exists but is still nightly-only.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Auto-vectorization is LLVM rewriting a loop to process a whole register of lanes at once, and it only does so when the result is provably identical. An integer sum qualifies; an `f32` sum does not, because float addition isn't associative and reordering changes the rounding. The output shows it: the strict left-to-right `f32` sum is off by about 159,000, while 8 independent accumulators land next to the exact answer. `sum_lanes` writes that reordering into the source, and in `--release` LLVM maps the 8 accumulators onto vector registers. The default `x86_64` target only assumes SSE2 (128-bit, 4 x f32); AVX2's 256-bit registers (8 x f32) are used only inside functions marked `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")]` or when building with `-C target-feature=+avx2` or `-C target-cpu=...`. Calling such a function on a CPU without AVX2 is undefined behavior, hence `is_x86_feature_detected!` and `unsafe`. The playground's Run button builds in debug mode, with no optimization and so no auto-vectorization, but the AVX2 path still executes vector instructions because intrinsics are explicit. WebAssembly SIMD128 gives Wasm modules running in Node a fixed 4 x f32 width whatever the CPU offers, and Rust can target it too with `-C target-feature=+simd128`.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

// JS has no SIMD API (SIMD.js was withdrawn), and V8's JITs don't auto-vectorize
// this loop: one add per iteration, with each f32 widened to a float64.
const xs = new Float32Array(1_000_003).map((_, i) => (i % 100) * 0.5);
let total = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) total += xs[i];

// SIMD in Node means WebAssembly SIMD128: fixed 128-bit vectors (4 x f32), e.g. Rust built with
// RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+simd128" cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release
const wasm = await WebAssembly.instantiate(await readFile('./sum_simd.wasm'));
console.log({ total, wasmExports: Object.keys(wasm.instance.exports) });
```

Rust:

```rust
// f32 addition is not associative, so LLVM must keep this reduction in
// strict left-to-right order and will NOT vectorize it, even in --release.
// (An integer sum like u32 does vectorize, because integer + is associative.)
fn sum_scalar(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    xs.iter().sum()
}

// Eight independent accumulators make the reordering explicit in the source,
// so in --release LLVM can keep them in SIMD registers (2 x SSE or 1 x AVX).
fn sum_lanes(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let mut acc = [0.0f32; 8];
    let chunks = xs.chunks_exact(8);
    let tail = chunks.remainder();
    for chunk in chunks {
        for lane in 0..8 {
            acc[lane] += chunk[lane];
        }
    }
    acc.iter().sum::<f32>() + tail.iter().sum::<f32>()
}

// Explicit intrinsics, compiled for AVX2 even though the default x86_64 baseline is SSE2.
// Calling it on a CPU without AVX2 is undefined behavior, hence `unsafe` + runtime detection.
#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")]
unsafe fn sum_avx2(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    use std::arch::x86_64::{_mm256_add_ps, _mm256_loadu_ps, _mm256_setzero_ps, _mm256_storeu_ps};
    let mut acc = _mm256_setzero_ps(); // one 256-bit register = 8 x f32
    let chunks = xs.chunks_exact(8);
    let tail = chunks.remainder();
    for chunk in chunks {
        // loadu = unaligned load; a Vec<f32> is only guaranteed 4-byte aligned
        acc = _mm256_add_ps(acc, _mm256_loadu_ps(chunk.as_ptr()));
    }
    let mut lanes = [0.0f32; 8];
    _mm256_storeu_ps(lanes.as_mut_ptr(), acc);
    lanes.iter().sum::<f32>() + tail.iter().sum::<f32>()
}

fn main() {
    let xs: Vec<f32> = (0..1_000_003).map(|i| (i % 100) as f32 * 0.5).collect();
    let exact: f64 = xs.iter().map(|&x| x as f64).sum();

    println!("exact (f64)      = {exact}");
    println!("scalar f32       = {}", sum_scalar(&xs));
    println!("8-lane f32       = {}", sum_lanes(&xs));

    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    {
        if is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") {
            // SAFETY: we just checked the CPU supports AVX2
            println!("AVX2 intrinsics  = {}", unsafe { sum_avx2(&xs) });
        } else {
            println!("AVX2 not available on this CPU: use the 8-lane fallback");
        }
    }
    println!("Different results are expected: reordering float adds changes the rounding.");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Check what LLVM emitted before hand-writing intrinsics: `cargo asm` (from cargo-show-asm) or `cargo rustc --release -- --emit asm`, then look for packed instructions such as `vaddps` or `paddd` on `xmm`/`ymm` registers. Slice iterators (`chunks_exact`, `zip`) vectorize more readily than index loops because they remove bounds checks.
- **Footgun:** `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"` tunes the binary for the build machine. Ship it to an older CPU or a different cloud instance family and it dies with SIGILL. For distributed binaries, keep the baseline target and dispatch at runtime with `is_x86_feature_detected!`, as above.
- **Architecture note:** Portable SIMD (`std::simd`, e.g. `f32x8`) still requires `#![feature(portable_simd)]` on nightly; on stable, the `wide` and `pulp` crates offer portable vector types. On AArch64 (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton), NEON is part of the baseline target, so 128-bit vectorization is always available there.

Go deeper: [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting), [Appendix 3: Cargo vs npm Architecture Guide](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cargo-vs-npm)

### Chapter 28: NAPI-RS: Accelerating Node.js with Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/napi_rs

Instead of rewriting a Node.js service, you can move one CPU-heavy function into Rust and ship it as a native addon with `napi-rs`. It builds on Node-API, Node's ABI-stable C interface, generates the JS loader and TypeScript types, and can run work on the libuv threadpool so the event loop stays free. The addon itself can't be built in the playground: it needs the `napi` and `napi-derive` crates, `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` and the `napi build` CLI.

**Why Rust does it this way:** A `#[napi]` function is compiled into a shared library (`.node`) that Node loads with `dlopen`. Each JS call goes through Node-API, which converts arguments: numbers are copied, strings are transcoded into a new UTF-8 buffer, and a `Buffer` arrives as a pointer and length into its existing backing store, so Rust reads the bytes without copying. That conversion is paid on every call, so the boundary pays off for coarse work (hash a 4 MiB upload once) and loses for fine-grained work (one Rust call per array element). A synchronous call blocks the event loop exactly as a slow JS function would. An `AsyncTask` runs `compute()` on a libuv threadpool thread and resolves a Promise from the main thread in `resolve()`, which is why the async version owns a copy of the bytes instead of borrowing memory the GC could reclaim. Because Node-API is ABI-stable, one binary per platform, architecture and libc works across Node major versions, unlike older nan/V8-API addons that needed a rebuild per Node release. `napi build --platform --release` produces `index.<platform>-<arch>[-<abi>].node` (e.g. `index.linux-x64-gnu.node`), and the napi CLI publishes one npm package per platform that the main package lists as `optionalDependencies`, so `npm install` downloads a single prebuilt binary and needs no Rust toolchain. ESM can't `import` a `.node` file without the experimental `--experimental-addon-modules` flag, so the generated loader `require`s it.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// `napi build --platform --release` emits index.<platform>-<arch>.node plus an index.js
// loader that picks the right binary and an index.d.ts with the generated types.
// (ESM can't import a .node file directly; the loader uses require under the hood.)
import { hashBuffer, hashBufferAsync } from '@acme/fast-hash';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const payload = await readFile('./upload.bin');
console.log(hashBuffer(payload)); // sync: the event loop is blocked while Rust runs
console.log(await hashBufferAsync(payload)); // AsyncTask: runs on the libuv threadpool
```

Rust:

```rust
// The playground can't build a Node addon (that needs crate-type = ["cdylib"],
// the napi + napi-derive crates and `napi build`), so this runs the pure core.
// The production wrapper, napi-rs v2/v3 style:
//
// use napi::bindgen_prelude::*;
// use napi_derive::napi;
//
// #[napi] // exported to JS as hashBuffer(input: Buffer): string
// pub fn hash_buffer(input: Buffer) -> String {
//     format!("{:016x}", fnv1a64(&input)) // &input borrows the Buffer's bytes: no copy
// }
//
// pub struct HashTask(Vec<u8>);
// impl Task for HashTask {
//     type Output = u64;
//     type JsValue = String;
//     fn compute(&mut self) -> Result<u64> { Ok(fnv1a64(&self.0)) } // libuv threadpool
//     fn resolve(&mut self, _env: Env, hash: u64) -> Result<String> { Ok(format!("{hash:016x}")) } // main thread
// }
//
// #[napi] // exported as hashBufferAsync(input: Buffer): Promise<string>
// pub fn hash_buffer_async(input: Buffer) -> AsyncTask<HashTask> {
//     AsyncTask::new(HashTask(input.to_vec())) // own a copy: the worker thread outlives this call
// }

/// FNV-1a, 64-bit: a tight byte loop that V8 runs far slower than native code.
fn fnv1a64(bytes: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    let mut hash: u64 = 0xcbf2_9ce4_8422_2325;
    for &byte in bytes {
        hash ^= byte as u64;
        hash = hash.wrapping_mul(0x0000_0100_0000_01b3);
    }
    hash
}

fn main() {
    // A JS Buffer arrives as a pointer + length into its ArrayBuffer backing store:
    // napi-rs hands Rust a &[u8] view of those bytes, no copy and no serialization.
    let payload: Vec<u8> = (0..4 * 1024 * 1024).map(|i| (i % 251) as u8).collect();
    let started = std::time::Instant::now();
    let hash = fnv1a64(&payload);
    println!("hashBuffer(4 MiB) = {hash:016x} in {:?} (debug build: time it with --release)",started.elapsed());
    println!("u64 results above 2^53 can't be JS numbers: return a String or BigInt");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Start from `napi new` (from `@napi-rs/cli`): it scaffolds the crate, a GitHub Actions matrix that cross-compiles every platform, and the npm packaging. For bulk data, accept `Buffer` or `Uint8Array` rather than strings or arrays of numbers, since those cross the boundary without per-element conversion.
- **Footgun:** Async tasks run on libuv's threadpool, which has only 4 threads by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`) and is shared with `fs`, `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2` and zlib. Long Rust jobs there can starve file I/O for the whole process; raise the pool size at startup or run your own Rust thread pool and report back through a threadsafe function.
- **Architecture note:** The addon shares the process with V8: a segfault from buggy `unsafe` code takes down the whole Node process, not one request. Keep it a thin layer of pure functions over plain data. JS values passed in are only valid during the call, so anything kept longer must be copied into Rust-owned memory, as `input.to_vec()` does above.

Go deeper: [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting)

### Chapter 29: Unsafe Rust: When & How to Use It

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/unsafe_rust

Rust is memory-safe by default. An `unsafe` block or function doesn't disable the borrow checker or type checking; it unlocks exactly five extra operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling `unsafe` functions (including FFI), accessing or modifying a `static mut`, implementing an `unsafe` trait (such as `Send` or `Sync`), and reading fields of a `union`. In exchange you promise to uphold the invariants the compiler can no longer check.

**Why Rust does it this way:** The skill is building a safe API over a small unsafe core, as `split_halves_mut` does: the borrow checker can't prove that two `&mut` slices into one array are disjoint, but a two-line argument can, so the function is safe for every caller. Each `unsafe` block carries a `// SAFETY:` comment saying why it is sound. Raw pointers (`*const T`, `*mut T`) are plain addresses with no lifetime and may be null or dangling; they take 8 bytes, or 16 for a slice pointer that also carries a length. Dereferencing one must still respect alignment: a `u32` needs an address divisible by 4, and `*ptr` on a misaligned address is undefined behavior even on x86, where the CPU would tolerate it, because LLVM is allowed to assume alignment. `read_unaligned` is the right tool for parsing packed wire formats. Node draws the line differently: `Buffer.readUInt32LE` is always bounds-checked and works at any alignment, typed arrays refuse misaligned views with a `RangeError`, and the one "unsafe" knob is `Buffer.allocUnsafe`, which skips zero-filling.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Buffer } from 'node:buffer';

// allocUnsafe skips zero-filling: small sizes are sliced from a shared 8 KiB pool,
// so the bytes may hold stale data from earlier allocations.
const scratch = Buffer.allocUnsafe(64);
scratch.fill(0);

const packet = Buffer.from([0xaa, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xff]);
console.log(packet.readUInt32LE(1)); // 1: bounds-checked, works at any alignment

// Typed arrays enforce alignment instead of allowing a misaligned view
try {
  new Uint32Array(packet.buffer, packet.byteOffset + 1, 1);
} catch (err) {
  console.log((err as RangeError).message); // start offset should be a multiple of 4
}
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::mem::{align_of, size_of, MaybeUninit};

/// Safe API, unsafe inside: the same trick std uses for slice::split_at_mut.
fn split_halves_mut(xs: &mut [u32]) -> (&mut [u32], &mut [u32]) {
    let len = xs.len();
    let mid = len / 2;
    let ptr = xs.as_mut_ptr();
    // SAFETY: [0, mid) and [mid, len) don't overlap and both lie inside `xs`,
    // so two &mut slices are sound. The borrow checker can't prove that by itself.
    unsafe {
        (
            std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr, mid),
            std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr.add(mid), len - mid),
        )
    }
}

fn read_u32_le(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize) -> Option<u32> {
    let end = offset.checked_add(size_of::<u32>())?;
    if end > bytes.len() {
        return None; // this check is what makes the unsafe block below sound
    }
    // SAFETY: 4 bytes are in bounds (checked above). read_unaligned because
    // offset may not be a multiple of align_of::<u32>() == 4; a plain *ptr would be UB.
    let raw = unsafe { bytes.as_ptr().add(offset).cast::<u32>().read_unaligned() };
    Some(u32::from_le(raw))
}

fn main() {
    let mut data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
    let (left, right) = split_halves_mut(&mut data);
    left[0] = 100;
    right[0] = 400;
    println!("split_halves_mut -> {data:?}");

    // Force the buffer onto a 4-byte boundary so offset 1 is guaranteed misaligned
    #[repr(align(4))]
    struct Aligned([u8; 6]);
    let buffer = Aligned([0xAA, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xFF]);
    let packet = &buffer.0;
    let misaligned = packet.as_ptr().wrapping_add(1).cast::<u32>();
    println!("u32 at offset 1 = {:?} (address aligned for u32? {})", read_u32_le(packet, 1), misaligned.is_aligned());
    println!("u32 at offset 4 = {:?} (out of bounds)", read_u32_le(packet, 4));

    println!("u8 align {}, u32 align {}, u64 align {}", align_of::<u8>(), align_of::<u32>(), align_of::<u64>());
    println!("*const u32: {} bytes, *const [u32] (fat: ptr + len): {} bytes", size_of::<*const u32>(), size_of::<*const [u32]>());

    // MaybeUninit: memory you promise to initialize before reading it
    let mut slot = MaybeUninit::<[u8; 4]>::uninit();
    slot.write([1, 2, 3, 4]);
    // SAFETY: fully written on the line above
    let bytes = unsafe { slot.assume_init() };
    println!("MaybeUninit -> {bytes:?}");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Run tests under Miri (`cargo +nightly miri test`): it interprets your code and reports undefined behavior such as misaligned reads, out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic, use-after-free and `&mut` aliasing violations, though it can't execute most foreign C calls. Turn on the `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` lint (it warns by default in edition 2024) so every operation inside an `unsafe fn` still needs its own `unsafe {}` block and justification.
- **Footgun:** Undefined behavior is not a crash you can catch. The optimizer assumes it never happens, so a misaligned `*ptr`, a `&mut` that aliases another reference, or reading a `MaybeUninit` before writing it can appear to work in debug and miscompile in release. Never create a reference (`&*ptr`) to memory you aren't sure is initialized, aligned and unaliased; use raw-pointer methods like `read_unaligned` and `ptr::copy` instead.
- **Architecture note:** Most application code needs no `unsafe` at all; it concentrates in a few audited places such as std's `Vec` and `HashMap`, Tokio's internals and FFI bindings. Put `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in application crates to make that a compiler-enforced policy, and use `cargo geiger` to see how much unsafe your dependency tree carries.

Go deeper: [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting), [Appendix 8: Senior Rust Interview Q&A](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/interviews)

### Chapter 30: FFI: Calling C Libraries from Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/foreign_function_interface

Node.js calls C through compiled addons (node-gyp and Node-API), runtime FFI libraries like `koffi`, or, since Node 26.1, the experimental built-in `node:ffi` module. Rust speaks the C ABI natively: declare functions in an `extern "C"` block, lay out structs with `#[repr(C)]`, and each call compiles to the same instructions a C compiler would emit, with no runtime marshalling layer.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `extern "C"` tells rustc to use the platform's C calling convention, and the linker resolves `strlen`, `qsort` and `getenv` from libc, which every Rust binary on Linux and macOS already links, so this example runs in the playground unchanged. Nothing checks those declarations against the real C headers: a wrong signature is undefined behavior, which is why each call needs `unsafe` and why real projects generate declarations with `bindgen`. Data must follow C's rules. Strings need a trailing NUL (`CString` allocates a copy and appends one; `c"..."` literals are NUL-terminated at compile time), and C strings you borrow come back as `CStr`. Struct layout must match too: `#[repr(C)]` keeps declaration order and pads each field to its alignment, so `{u8, u64, u8}` is 24 bytes with `offset` at byte 8, while Rust's default layout reorders the same fields into 16 bytes. Callbacks work in both directions: `compare_i32` is an `extern "C" fn` that C's `qsort` calls back into. koffi does the same job at runtime: it parses the prototype string, then converts each JS argument on every call (a JS string becomes a fresh NUL-terminated buffer), which is flexible but adds per-call overhead that a compiled Rust call doesn't have. `node:ffi` is marked experimental in the Node docs and sits behind a flag, so check the docs for your exact version.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import koffi from 'koffi';

const libPath =
  process.platform === 'win32' ? 'msvcrt.dll'
  : process.platform === 'darwin' ? 'libSystem.B.dylib'
  : 'libc.so.6';
const libc = koffi.load(libPath);

// koffi parses the C prototype at runtime and converts every argument on every call
const strlen = libc.func('size_t strlen(const char *s)');
const getenv = libc.func('const char *getenv(const char *name)');

console.log(strlen('hello from Node')); // the JS string is copied into a NUL-terminated buffer
console.log(String(getenv('PATH')).slice(0, 20));
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, c_int, c_void, CStr, CString};
use std::mem::{align_of, offset_of, size_of};

// Declarations of symbols that already exist in libc, which every Rust binary links.
// The compiler trusts these signatures blindly: a wrong one is undefined behavior.
extern "C" {
    fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize;
    fn getenv(name: *const c_char) -> *mut c_char;
    fn qsort(
        base: *mut c_void,
        count: usize,
        size: usize,
        compare: extern "C" fn(*const c_void, *const c_void) -> c_int,
    );
}

// A Rust function with the C calling convention, passed to C as a callback.
extern "C" fn compare_i32(a: *const c_void, b: *const c_void) -> c_int {
    // SAFETY: qsort only hands us pointers into the i32 array we gave it
    let (a, b) = unsafe { (*a.cast::<i32>(), *b.cast::<i32>()) };
    a.cmp(&b) as c_int
}

#[allow(dead_code)] // only the layouts matter in this demo
#[repr(C)] // C rules: fields in declaration order, each padded to its alignment
struct CHeader {
    flag: u8,
    offset: u64,
    kind: u8,
}

#[allow(dead_code)]
struct RustHeader {
    // default repr: the compiler may reorder fields to cut padding
    flag: u8,
    offset: u64,
    kind: u8,
}

fn main() {
    let message = CString::new("hello from Rust").expect("no interior NUL"); // appends the '\0' C expects
    // SAFETY: `message` is a valid NUL-terminated string that outlives the call
    let len = unsafe { strlen(message.as_ptr()) };
    println!("strlen = {len}");

    let mut nums = [42, -7, 19, 0, 3];
    // SAFETY: base/count/size describe `nums` exactly; compare_i32 matches the expected type
    unsafe { qsort(nums.as_mut_ptr().cast(), nums.len(), size_of::<i32>(), compare_i32) };
    println!("qsort with a Rust callback = {nums:?}");

    // SAFETY: c"PATH" is a NUL-terminated literal; getenv returns NULL or a C string owned by libc
    let path = unsafe { getenv(c"PATH".as_ptr()) };
    if !path.is_null() {
        // Borrow it, don't free it: libc owns this memory
        let path = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(path) }.to_string_lossy();
        println!("getenv(PATH) starts with {:?}", &path[..path.len().min(20)]);
    }

    println!(
        "#[repr(C)] CHeader: {} bytes, align {}, `offset` field at byte {}",
        size_of::<CHeader>(),
        align_of::<CHeader>(),
        offset_of!(CHeader, offset)
    );
    println!("default repr RustHeader: {} bytes (fields reordered)", size_of::<RustHeader>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Generate bindings with `bindgen` (from C headers, usually in `build.rs`), and expose Rust to C with `cbindgen`. Put the raw `extern` declarations in a `-sys` crate (like `openssl-sys` or `libsqlite3-sys`) and wrap them in a safe crate, so the `unsafe` lives in one place.
- **Footgun:** Memory must be freed by the allocator that allocated it: a pointer from C's `malloc` goes back to `free`, and a `CString` handed to C with `into_raw()` must come back through `CString::from_raw` to be freed. And `let p = CString::new(s).unwrap().as_ptr();` leaves `p` dangling, because the temporary `CString` is dropped at the end of that statement; bind it to a variable first, as `message` is above.
- **Architecture note:** A panic must not unwind out of an `extern "C"` function into C; since Rust 1.81 that aborts the process instead of being undefined behavior. Use `extern "C-unwind"` only when both sides agree on unwinding; otherwise catch panics at the boundary with `std::panic::catch_unwind` and return an error code.

Go deeper: [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting), [Appendix 5: Production Distroless Rust Dockerfile](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/docker)

### Chapter 31: Custom Allocators: jemalloc & mimalloc

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/custom_allocators

V8 manages JS objects in its own garbage-collected heap, while Buffers and other native memory come from the C allocator. Rust has no GC: every `Box`, `Vec` and `String` goes through one global allocator, the system `malloc` by default. One `#[global_allocator]` line swaps it for jemalloc (the `tikv-jemallocator` crate) or `mimalloc`. Those crates compile C code, so they can't run in the playground; the counting allocator above uses the same hook.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `GlobalAlloc` is a small trait (`alloc` and `dealloc`, with optional `realloc` and `alloc_zeroed`) that receives a `Layout`: the size and alignment a type needs (8 and 8 for `u64`). Because Rust frees every value at a known point, allocator calls are deterministic and the counts above are exact: growing a `Vec` by pushing takes 9 allocator calls (one alloc for capacity 4, then 8 reallocs up to 1024, leaving 4,096 bytes live for 4,000 bytes of data), while `with_capacity(1000)` allocates once. The choice of allocator matters most for long-running multi-threaded servers. glibc malloc spreads threads over several arenas with a per-thread cache, but long-lived servers often see fragmentation and RSS that is never returned to the OS. jemalloc uses size-class slabs, thread caches and decay-based purging of unused pages; mimalloc shards its free lists per page. On musl targets (Alpine images, static binaries), the default musl malloc is notably slow under multi-threaded load, the most common reason Rust services switch. V8 works differently: allocation in the young generation is a pointer bump, and the GC later copies survivors, so allocating is cheap but reclaiming costs GC time.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import v8 from 'node:v8';

// JS objects live in V8's garbage-collected heap (young and old generations)
const { heap_size_limit, used_heap_size } = v8.getHeapStatistics();
// Buffers and ArrayBuffers are malloc'd outside that heap and reported separately
const { external, arrayBuffers, rss } = process.memoryUsage();
const mb = (bytes: number) => Math.round(bytes / 2 ** 20);
console.log({
  heapLimitMB: mb(heap_size_limit),
  heapUsedMB: mb(used_heap_size),
  externalMB: mb(external),
  arrayBuffersMB: mb(arrayBuffers),
  rssMB: mb(rss),
});
// JS can't swap Node's native allocator; the usual trick is to preload one:
// LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2 node server.js
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout, System};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering::Relaxed};

// The same hook jemalloc and mimalloc use, wrapped around the system allocator.
// Production swap (needs the crate, so it can't run here):
//   #[global_allocator]
//   static GLOBAL: tikv_jemallocator::Jemalloc = tikv_jemallocator::Jemalloc;
//   // or: static GLOBAL: mimalloc::MiMalloc = mimalloc::MiMalloc;
struct CountingAlloc;

static CALLS: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
static LIVE_BYTES: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for CountingAlloc {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        let ptr = System.alloc(layout);
        if !ptr.is_null() {
            CALLS.fetch_add(1, Relaxed); // Relaxed: a statistic, nothing is published through it
            LIVE_BYTES.fetch_add(layout.size(), Relaxed);
        }
        ptr
    }

    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        System.dealloc(ptr, layout);
        LIVE_BYTES.fetch_sub(layout.size(), Relaxed);
    }

    unsafe fn realloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout, new_size: usize) -> *mut u8 {
        let new_ptr = System.realloc(ptr, layout, new_size);
        if !new_ptr.is_null() {
            CALLS.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            LIVE_BYTES.fetch_add(new_size, Relaxed);
            LIVE_BYTES.fetch_sub(layout.size(), Relaxed);
        }
        new_ptr
    }
}

#[global_allocator] // every Box, Vec, String and HashMap in the program now goes through it
static GLOBAL: CountingAlloc = CountingAlloc;

fn measure<T>(label: &str, work: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> T {
    let (calls_before, bytes_before) = (CALLS.load(Relaxed), LIVE_BYTES.load(Relaxed));
    let result = work();
    let calls = CALLS.load(Relaxed) - calls_before;
    let bytes = LIVE_BYTES.load(Relaxed) as isize - bytes_before as isize;
    println!("{label:<34} {calls:>3} alloc/realloc calls, {bytes:>6} bytes still live");
    result
}

fn main() {
    let grown = measure("Vec::new + 1000 pushes", || {
        let mut v = Vec::new();
        for x in 0..1000u32 {
            v.push(x); // capacity doubles: 4, 8, 16, ... 1024
        }
        v
    });
    let sized = measure("Vec::with_capacity(1000) + pushes", || {
        let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(1000);
        v.extend(0..1000u32);
        v
    });
    let boxed = measure("Box::new(0u64)", || Box::new(0u64));
    measure("String via format! (dropped)", || {
        let _s = format!("user-{}", 42);
    });

    let layout = Layout::new::<u64>();
    println!("Layout of u64: size {}, align {}", layout.size(), layout.align());
    println!("kept alive: {} + {} u32s, box = {}", grown.len(), sized.len(), boxed);
}
```

- **Pro tip:** The swap is a dependency plus a few lines: `#[cfg(not(target_env = "msvc"))] #[global_allocator] static GLOBAL: tikv_jemallocator::Jemalloc = tikv_jemallocator::Jemalloc;`. The original `jemallocator` crate is unmaintained; `tikv-jemallocator` is the maintained fork and doesn't support MSVC Windows targets, hence the `cfg`. Measure RSS and p99 latency under realistic load before and after, because the winner depends on the workload.
- **Footgun:** Inside a `GlobalAlloc` implementation you must not allocate (no `println!`, `format!` or `Vec`), or you recurse into your own allocator. And memory must go back to the allocator that produced it: freeing a pointer from C's `malloc` through Rust's allocator, or the reverse, is undefined behavior with any allocator, and with jemalloc it usually crashes.
- **Architecture note:** jemalloc returns memory to the OS gradually (unused pages decay over about 10 seconds by default), and that purging runs during allocator calls unless you enable `background_thread:true`, so an idle process can keep its RSS after a spike. The `tikv-jemalloc-ctl` crate exposes live statistics (`stats.allocated`, `stats.resident`) for a metrics endpoint. For per-request scratch data, an arena (bump) allocator like `bumpalo` skips the global allocator entirely and frees everything at once, close to how V8's young generation allocates.

Go deeper: [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting), [Appendix 5: Production Distroless Rust Dockerfile](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/docker)

### Chapter 32: Atomics & Hardware Memory Ordering

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/atomics_memory_ordering

In Node.js, threads share memory only through a `SharedArrayBuffer`, and every `Atomics` operation is sequentially consistent. Rust's atomic types (`AtomicBool`, `AtomicUsize`, `AtomicU64`, ...) work on any shared value and make you choose an `Ordering` per operation: `Relaxed` (atomic, but orders nothing else), `Release`/`Acquire` (publish data to another thread) or `SeqCst` (one global order, what JS always uses).

**Why Rust does it this way:** An atomic has the same size and alignment as its plain integer (`AtomicUsize` is 8 bytes, aligned to 8), and the CPU reads and modifies it in one indivisible step: on x86-64, `fetch_add` is `lock xadd` and `compare_exchange` is `lock cmpxchg`; on AArch64 they are LSE instructions (`ldadd`, `cas`) or load-exclusive/store-exclusive (`ldxr`/`stxr`) retry loops. Ordering is about the other memory around the atomic. `Relaxed` only guarantees that no increment is lost, which is enough for counters. A `Release` store makes every earlier write visible to any thread whose `Acquire` load reads that value, which is how `READY` safely publishes `DATA`. x86-64's memory model (TSO) already orders ordinary loads and stores that way, so Acquire/Release cost nothing extra there, while on ARM they compile to `ldar`/`stlr`. `SeqCst` adds one total order across all SeqCst operations, needed when two threads each set their own flag and then check the other's; a SeqCst store on x86-64 becomes `xchg`, a full barrier. JS `Atomics` are all SeqCst, and plain typed-array reads of a `SharedArrayBuffer` are unordered. `Atomics.wait`/`notify` are futex-style blocking, which Rust offers through `std::thread::park` or the `atomic-wait` crate rather than on atomics directly. Finally, `#[repr(align(64))]` puts each counter on its own 64-byte cache line so cores don't fight over one line (false sharing); `crossbeam_utils::CachePadded` packages the trick and pads to 128 bytes on x86-64, because those CPUs prefetch cache lines in pairs.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Worker, isMainThread, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';

if (isMainThread) {
  // SharedArrayBuffer is the only memory workers share; everything else is copied
  const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(8);
  const view = new Int32Array(shared); // [0] = data, [1] = ready flag
  new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: shared });
  Atomics.wait(view, 1, 0); // sleeps until the flag changes (allowed on Node's main thread)
  console.log('published value:', Atomics.load(view, 0)); // 42
} else {
  const view = new Int32Array(workerData as SharedArrayBuffer);
  // Every Atomics operation is sequentially consistent: JS has no Relaxed/Acquire/Release
  Atomics.store(view, 0, 42);
  Atomics.store(view, 1, 1);
  Atomics.notify(view, 1);
}
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::mem::{align_of, size_of};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::thread;

// One counter per 64-byte cache line, so threads bumping neighbours
// don't keep invalidating each other's line (false sharing).
#[repr(align(64))]
struct PaddedCounter(AtomicU64);

static DATA: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);
static READY: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

fn main() {
    // 1. Relaxed: the increment is atomic, but it orders nothing else. Right for statistics.
    let shards: Vec<PaddedCounter> = (0..4).map(|_| PaddedCounter(AtomicU64::new(0))).collect();
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for shard in &shards {
            s.spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    shard.0.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            });
        }
    });
    let total: u64 = shards.iter().map(|shard| shard.0.load(Ordering::Relaxed)).sum();
    println!("Relaxed sharded counter: {total} (no increment lost)");

    // 2. Release/Acquire: publish data, then raise a flag. A thread that reads the flag
    //    with Acquire sees every write made before the matching Release store.
    let producer = thread::spawn(|| {
        DATA.store(42, Ordering::Relaxed);
        READY.store(true, Ordering::Release); // "everything above is published"
    });
    let consumer = thread::spawn(|| {
        while !READY.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
            std::hint::spin_loop();
        }
        DATA.load(Ordering::Relaxed) // guaranteed 42, never 0
    });
    producer.join().unwrap();
    println!("Acquire load saw published data: {}", consumer.join().unwrap());

    // 3. Compare-and-swap loop: a lock-free running maximum
    let peak = AtomicU64::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for latency_ms in [120u64, 340, 95, 410, 220] {
            let peak = &peak;
            s.spawn(move || {
                let mut current = peak.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
                while latency_ms > current {
                    match peak.compare_exchange_weak(current, latency_ms, Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed) {
                        Ok(_) => break,
                        Err(actual) => current = actual, // another thread won the race: retry
                    }
                }
            });
        }
    });
    println!("CAS peak latency: {}ms (fetch_max does this in one call)", peak.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    println!("AtomicUsize: {} bytes, align {} (same as usize)", size_of::<AtomicUsize>(), align_of::<AtomicUsize>());
    println!("PaddedCounter: {} bytes, align {}", size_of::<PaddedCounter>(), align_of::<PaddedCounter>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Pick the weakest ordering that matches a known pattern: `Relaxed` for counters and statistics, a `Release` store with an `Acquire` load for publishing data or flags, `AcqRel` for read-modify-write operations that do both (like a lock's CAS). Use `SeqCst` only when you can name the cross-variable ordering it buys. Mara Bos's *Rust Atomics and Locks*, free online, is the standard reference.
- **Footgun:** `Relaxed` on a flag that guards other data is a real bug, not a slowdown: the reader can see `READY == true` and still read the old `DATA`. It shows up mostly on ARM (Apple Silicon, Graviton) and rarely on x86 dev machines, whose TSO model hides the hardware reordering, although the compiler may still reorder `Relaxed` accesses on any target. Test lock-free code with `loom`, which explores thread interleavings and models many weak-memory reorderings.
- **Architecture note:** Atomics are the building blocks under `Arc` (a `Relaxed` `fetch_add` on clone, a `Release` `fetch_sub` plus an `Acquire` fence before freeing), `Mutex` (a futex word on Linux), channels and Tokio's scheduler. So an `Arc::clone` is a single atomic instruction. JS has nothing similar, because objects can't be shared across workers at all, only copied or transferred.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy), [Appendix 1: Borrow Checker Mastery](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/borrow-checker)

### Chapter 33: Macros: Declarative vs Procedural Macros

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/procedural_macros

TypeScript decorators are functions that run when a class is evaluated, and Babel or SWC plugins rewrite the JS syntax tree in a separate build step. Rust has two macro systems, both expanded inside the compiler: declarative `macro_rules!` (pattern matching on token trees) and procedural macros, which come in three kinds: derive (`#[derive(Serialize)]`), attribute (`#[tokio::main]`) and function-like (`sql!(...)`).

**Why Rust does it this way:** A procedural macro is a Rust function from `TokenStream` to `TokenStream` that lives in its own crate with `proc-macro = true` under `[lib]`. Cargo compiles that crate for the host, not the target (even when you cross-compile to wasm), as a dynamic library (`.so`, `.dylib` or `.dll`), and rustc loads it and calls it while expanding macros. It gets token trees (identifiers, literals, punctuation, delimited groups), not a typed AST: expansion runs before type checking (and before names inside function bodies are resolved), so a derive can't ask whether a field's type implements a trait. It generates code and lets the type checker report errors later. `syn` parses the tokens into a syntax tree and `quote!` turns the output back into tokens. The three kinds differ in what they may replace: a derive (`#[proc_macro_derive]`) can only append items after the struct or enum, an attribute macro (`#[proc_macro_attribute]`) receives the attribute's arguments plus the item and replaces the item, and a function-like macro (`#[proc_macro]`) replaces its invocation. `macro_rules!` needs no extra crate and is hygienic for local variables, which is why `sum_all!(1, 2, total)` prints 103. Proc macros default to `Span::call_site()`, which is unhygienic. In JS, a TypeScript decorator compiles to a function call that runs on every process start, and TypeORM-style legacy decorators store metadata that is read back by runtime reflection. A Babel or SWC plugin (SWC plugins are compiled to Wasm) is the closer analogue, but its output is still dynamically typed JavaScript. Rust has no runtime reflection, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` generates a plain impl per type that the optimizer can inline.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// TC39 decorators (TypeScript 5.0+, no experimentalDecorators flag).
// A decorator is a plain function, called at RUNTIME when the class definition is evaluated.
const columns: string[] = [];

function column<This, Value>(_target: undefined, context: ClassFieldDecoratorContext<This, Value>) {
  columns.push(String(context.name)); // runs on every process start, not at build time
}

function entity<Class extends abstract new (...args: never[]) => object>(
  _target: Class,
  context: ClassDecoratorContext<Class>,
) {
  console.log(`registering ${String(context.name)} with columns`, columns);
}

@entity
class User {
  @column id = 0;
  @column name = '';
}

// The output is still JavaScript; the type annotations above are gone before it runs.
// The real build-time analogue is a Babel or SWC plugin, which rewrites the JS AST:
//   export default () => ({ visitor: { Identifier(path) { /* rewrite nodes */ } } });
console.log(new User());
```

Rust:

```rust
// A real derive lives in its own crate, built for the host and loaded by rustc:
//
//   # describe_derive/Cargo.toml
//   [lib]
//   proc-macro = true
//
//   [dependencies]
//   syn = "2"
//   quote = "1"
//
//   // describe_derive/src/lib.rs
//   use proc_macro::TokenStream;
//   use quote::quote;
//   use syn::{parse_macro_input, Data, DeriveInput, Fields};
//
//   #[proc_macro_derive(Describe)]
//   pub fn derive_describe(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
//       let ast = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput); // tokens -> syntax tree, no types
//       let name = &ast.ident;
//       let Data::Struct(data) = &ast.data else {
//           return syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "Describe only supports structs")
//               .to_compile_error()
//               .into();
//       };
//       let fields = match &data.fields {
//           Fields::Named(named) => named.named.iter().map(|f| f.ident.clone().unwrap()).collect(),
//           _ => Vec::new(),
//       };
//       quote! {
//           impl Describe for #name {
//               const FIELDS: &'static [&'static str] = &[#(stringify!(#fields)),*];
//               fn type_name() -> &'static str { stringify!(#name) }
//           }
//       }
//       .into() // a derive can only ADD items; the struct itself is left untouched
//   }
//
// The playground can't build a second crate, so below macro_rules! generates the same impl.

trait Describe {
    const FIELDS: &'static [&'static str];
    fn type_name() -> &'static str;
}

// Declarative macro: matches token trees against patterns and substitutes them
macro_rules! describe {
    (struct $name:ident { $($field:ident : $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {
        #[derive(Debug)]
        struct $name { $($field: $ty),* }

        impl Describe for $name {
            const FIELDS: &'static [&'static str] = &[$(stringify!($field)),*];
            fn type_name() -> &'static str { stringify!($name) }
        }
    };
}

describe! {
    struct User { id: u64, name: String }
}

// Hygiene: the macro's own `total` is a different variable from the caller's `total`
macro_rules! sum_all {
    ($($x:expr),*) => {{
        let mut total = 0;
        $(total += $x;)*
        total
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let user = User { id: 1, name: "ada".into() };
    println!("{} has fields {:?}", User::type_name(), User::FIELDS);
    println!("{user:?} -> id {} is {}", user.id, user.name);

    let total = 100;
    println!("sum_all!(1, 2, total) = {}", sum_all!(1, 2, total)); // 103, not 6
    println!("caller's total is still {total}");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Run `cargo expand` (the cargo-expand subcommand) to see exactly what `#[derive(Serialize)]` or `#[tokio::main]` generated. Inside your own proc macro, return `syn::Error::new_spanned(tokens, msg).to_compile_error()` instead of panicking, so the error underlines the user's code instead of the derive attribute.
- **Footgun:** Proc macros are not hygienic by default: an identifier emitted with `Span::call_site()` resolves in the caller's scope. Emit absolute paths such as `::std::fmt::Debug` or `::my_crate::Trait`, or your generated code breaks when the caller has a local item with the same name. Also, `syn` with the `full` feature adds noticeable time to clean builds.
- **Architecture note:** A proc-macro crate is built for the host and loaded into the rustc process, so it runs arbitrary code with your user's permissions during `cargo build`, like `build.rs`. Treat macro dependencies as build-time supply chain. They also can't see types: all they get is tokens.

Go deeper: [Appendix 3: Cargo vs npm Architecture Guide](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cargo-vs-npm), [Appendix 6: Testing & Mocking in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/testing)

### Chapter 34: Compile-Time Computation with const fn

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/const_eval

In JavaScript every top-level `const` is computed at runtime, on every process start. Rust's `const fn` can run inside the compiler: in a const context (a `const` or `static` item, an array length, a const generic, a `const { }` block) the result is computed during the build and stored as bytes in the binary.

**Why Rust does it this way:** rustc evaluates a `const fn` in a const context with its compile-time interpreter (CTFE, the same engine Miri is built on), running the function's MIR inside the compiler. The resulting 1 KiB CRC table is emitted as a `static` into read-only data (`.rodata` on ELF, `__TEXT,__const` on Mach-O), so it costs zero instructions at startup: the OS maps those pages from the executable when they are first read. A `const` item is copied into every use site and has no fixed address, so large tables belong in a `static`. Errors move to build time too: integer overflow (`factorial(21)` in a u64), out-of-bounds indexing or a failed `assert!` during const evaluation is error E0080, so the program never compiles. Limits on stable: no heap allocation at all (`Vec::new()` and `String::new()` are const only because they don't allocate), no I/O, and no trait method calls, which rules out `for` loops (they call `Iterator::next`, error E0015), `?` and iterator adapters. A `const fn` called in a normal `let` is just a runtime call. V8 has no build step: module top-level code is parsed (inner functions lazily) and compiled to Ignition bytecode (Node 22.1+ can skip that with its on-disk compile cache), and it always runs again on every start, and hot code may tier up to Sparkplug, Maglev or TurboFan. Inline caches remember object shapes at property-access sites to speed up later accesses, but they only make code run faster, they never move work to build time. The closest Node tool is a startup snapshot (`node --build-snapshot`), which serializes a heap that still has to be deserialized on every start.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// Module top-level code executes on every process start (Node's compile cache can skip parsing, never execution)
function buildCrc32Table(): Uint32Array {
  const table = new Uint32Array(256);
  for (let i = 0; i < 256; i++) {
    let crc = i;
    for (let bit = 0; bit < 8; bit++) {
      crc = crc & 1 ? (crc >>> 1) ^ 0xedb88320 : crc >>> 1;
    }
    table[i] = crc; // Uint32Array stores the value modulo 2^32
  }
  return table;
}

const started = performance.now();
const CRC32_TABLE = buildCrc32Table();
console.log(`table built at startup in ${(performance.now() - started).toFixed(3)} ms`);

function crc32(bytes: Uint8Array): number {
  let crc = 0xffffffff;
  for (const byte of bytes) {
    crc = CRC32_TABLE[(crc ^ byte) & 0xff] ^ (crc >>> 8);
  }
  return (crc ^ 0xffffffff) >>> 0;
}

console.log(`table[1] = 0x${CRC32_TABLE[1].toString(16)}`);
console.log(`crc32("hello") = 0x${crc32(new TextEncoder().encode('hello')).toString(16)}`);
```

Rust:

```rust
// CRC-32 (IEEE) lookup table, computed by the compiler instead of at startup
const fn crc32_table() -> [u32; 256] {
    let mut table = [0u32; 256];
    let mut i = 0;
    // `for` desugars to Iterator::next, a trait call stable const fn can't make, so: `while`
    while i < 256 {
        let mut crc = i as u32;
        let mut bit = 0;
        while bit < 8 {
            crc = if crc & 1 != 0 { (crc >> 1) ^ 0xEDB8_8320 } else { crc >> 1 };
            bit += 1;
        }
        table[i] = crc;
        i += 1;
    }
    table
}

// `static`: one copy at one address, stored in the binary's read-only data
static CRC32_TABLE: [u32; 256] = crc32_table();

const fn factorial(n: u64) -> u64 {
    if n == 0 { 1 } else { n * factorial(n - 1) }
}

// `const`: the value is pasted into every use site. factorial(21) overflows u64,
// which here is a compile error (E0080), not a silent wrap.
const FACTORIAL_20: u64 = factorial(20);

// Compile-time assertion: the build fails if the table is wrong
const _: () = assert!(CRC32_TABLE[1] == 0x7707_3096);

fn crc32(bytes: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    let mut crc = !0u32;
    for &b in bytes {
        crc = CRC32_TABLE[((crc ^ b as u32) & 0xFF) as usize] ^ (crc >> 8);
    }
    !crc
}

fn main() {
    println!("20! = {FACTORIAL_20}");
    println!("table[1] = {:#010x}, {} bytes at {:p}", CRC32_TABLE[1], size_of_val(&CRC32_TABLE), &CRC32_TABLE);
    println!("crc32(\"hello\") = {:#010x}", crc32(b"hello"));

    // Called outside a const context, a const fn is just a normal runtime call
    let n = std::env::args().count() as u64 + 4;
    println!("factorial({n}) at runtime = {}", factorial(n));

    // Inline const block: array repeat of a non-Copy value needs a const expression
    let buckets: [Vec<u8>; 4] = [const { Vec::new() }; 4];
    println!("{} empty buckets, none allocated: capacity {}", buckets.len(), buckets[0].capacity());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Use `static` for big tables (one copy, one address) and `const` for small values. `const _: () = assert!(...);` turns an invariant into a build failure, and `[const { Vec::new() }; N]` initializes an array of non-Copy values without a loop.
- **Footgun:** Stable `const fn` can't call trait methods, so `for` loops (E0015), `?`, `.iter().map()` and `==` on non-primitive types don't compile there. Write `while` loops with manual indices. And a `const fn` is only guaranteed to run at compile time in a const context: `let x = f(10);` runs at runtime (LLVM may still fold it, but that is an optimization, not a promise).
- **Architecture note:** A `static` table lives in the read-only segment mapped from the executable, so processes running the same binary share those pages through the OS page cache, and writing to them faults. The const evaluator itself is deterministic (no clock, no I/O, no randomness), so it never makes a build non-reproducible. Macros like `env!` and `include_bytes!` can still bake build-machine state into consts.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy)

## Part 7: Rust Philosophy

### Chapter P1: Fearless Concurrency & Send / Sync

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_fearless_concurrency

Node.js gives each isolate one thread, so plain JS objects can't be touched by two threads at once, and worker_threads copy data instead of sharing it. Rust allows real shared-memory threads and uses two marker traits, `Send` and `Sync`, so the compiler rejects any safe program that could have a data race.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `Send` means a value can be moved to another thread; `Sync` means `&T` can be shared between threads (`T: Sync` exactly when `&T: Send`). Both are auto traits: the compiler implements them for a struct when all of its fields have them, and they are zero-sized markers that only exist in the type checker. `Rc<T>` is neither, because `Rc::clone` does a plain increment that two threads could race on; `Arc` uses an atomic `fetch_add` (a `lock`-prefixed add on x86-64, `ldadd` on ARMv8.1+) and is Send + Sync when `T` is. `RefCell<T>` is Send but not Sync, because its borrow counter isn't atomic, and a std `MutexGuard` is not Send because some platforms require the locking thread to unlock. `thread::spawn` requires `F: Send + 'static`, so you must move or `Arc` the data; `thread::scope` (Rust 1.63) joins every thread before returning, so threads may borrow locals. The guarantee is precise: safe Rust has no data races, meaning unsynchronized access to the same memory where at least one access is a write. It does not prevent deadlocks or race conditions in ordering (threads finish in any order, hence the `sort()`). In Node, `workerData` and `postMessage` use the structured clone algorithm, so each worker gets a copy (or a transferred ArrayBuffer, which is detached in the sender). Only a SharedArrayBuffer is truly shared, and nothing checks it: `counter[0]++` from four workers compiles fine and can silently lose updates (rarely at 1,000 increments per worker, constantly at 1,000,000), while `Atomics.add` always gives the exact total. Within one thread, async code can still interleave at every `await`.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { Worker, isMainThread, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';

type Job = { shared: SharedArrayBuffer; config: { retries: number } };

if (isMainThread) {
  const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(4);
  const config = { retries: 3 };
  const workers = Array.from({ length: 4 }, () => new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: { shared, config } }));
  await Promise.all(workers.map((worker) => new Promise((resolve) => worker.on('exit', resolve))));
  // 4000: every worker saw the same SharedArrayBuffer. retries stays 3: config was copied.
  console.log('counter =', Atomics.load(new Int32Array(shared), 0), 'retries =', config.retries);
} else {
  const { shared, config } = workerData as Job;
  config.retries = 99; // workerData is a structured clone, so this edits a private copy
  const counter = new Int32Array(shared);
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    Atomics.add(counter, 0, 1); // `counter[0]++` compiles too, but can silently lose updates under contention
  }
}
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

// These compile only if the type really is Send / Sync: a zero-cost compile-time proof
fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
fn assert_sync<T: Sync>() {}

fn main() {
    assert_send::<Arc<Mutex<Vec<u32>>>>();
    assert_sync::<AtomicU64>();
    assert_send::<RefCell<u32>>(); // Send: may MOVE to another thread...
    // assert_sync::<RefCell<u32>>(); // ...not Sync (E0277): its borrow counter isn't atomic
    // assert_send::<Rc<u32>>();      // E0277: Rc's reference count is a plain integer

    // Scoped threads may borrow locals: the scope joins every thread before it returns
    let words = ["fearless", "concurrency", "send", "sync"];
    let total_len = AtomicU64::new(0);
    let total = &total_len;
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for chunk in words.chunks(2) {
            s.spawn(move || {
                let len: usize = chunk.iter().map(|w| w.len()).sum();
                total.fetch_add(len as u64, Ordering::Relaxed);
            });
        }
    });
    println!("total letters = {}", total_len.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    // thread::spawn needs 'static data: Arc shares ownership, Mutex serializes writes
    let log = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..4)
        .map(|id| {
            let log = Arc::clone(&log);
            thread::spawn(move || log.lock().unwrap().push(id * 10))
        })
        .collect();
    for handle in handles {
        handle.join().unwrap();
    }
    let mut entries = log.lock().unwrap().clone();
    entries.sort(); // threads finish in any order: a race condition, but not a data race
    println!("log = {entries:?}");

    let rc = Rc::new(5);
    // thread::spawn(move || println!("{rc}")); // E0277: `Rc<i32>` cannot be sent between threads safely
    println!("Rc stays on the thread that created it: {rc}");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Reach for `std::thread::scope` when threads only need to borrow local data: no `'static` bound, so no `Arc` and no clones. For data parallelism, rayon's `par_iter()` uses the same Send/Sync bounds to split work safely across a thread pool.
- **Footgun:** "Fearless" covers data races, not deadlocks: two threads locking the same two Mutexes in opposite order compiles cleanly and hangs forever. Also, holding a std `MutexGuard` across an `.await` makes the future `!Send`, so `tokio::spawn` rejects it; drop the guard before awaiting or use `tokio::sync::Mutex`.
- **Architecture note:** Raw pointers are neither Send nor Sync, so a type wrapping one must opt in with `unsafe impl Send`, a promise the compiler can't check. That is where thread-safety bugs can still hide in Rust: inside `unsafe` code, never in safe code built on correct abstractions.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy), [Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio)

### Chapter P2: RAII & Deterministic Resource Management

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_raii_drop

JavaScript reclaims memory whenever the garbage collector decides to, and runs your cleanup only if you call it (or use the newer `using` declaration). Rust uses RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): when the owner of a value goes out of scope, its `Drop::drop` runs right there, every time, in a defined order.

**Why Rust does it this way:** When rustc lowers a function to MIR it inserts a drop at every exit of a value's scope: the closing brace, an early `return`, `?`, `break`, and the cleanup path taken when a panic unwinds. If a value may or may not have been moved away, drop elaboration adds a hidden boolean drop flag so it is dropped exactly once. The order is fixed: locals in reverse declaration order, then a struct's fields in declaration order after its own `Drop::drop`. A `MutexGuard` unlocks, a `File` closes its descriptor and a transaction type rolls back the moment their owner ends, and the only runtime cost is the call itself.
