V8's Orinoco collector works on reachability, not scope. The young generation is a semi-space collected by the parallel Scavenger, which copies survivors, so its cost scales with live objects; the old generation uses mark-sweep-compact with concurrent and incremental marking. Collections are triggered by allocation pressure, so their timing is not deterministic. WeakMap entries are ephemerons (the map keeps a value alive only while its key is reachable), so marking has to revisit the ephemeron tables until nothing new is marked. None of this runs your cleanup code: FinalizationRegistry callbacks may run late or never. JavaScript's real answer is explicit resource management: `using` (TypeScript 5.2, native in Node 24) calls `[Symbol.dispose]()` at block exit. It is opt-in per binding, while in Rust every value gets this behaviour by default.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
import { closeSync, openSync, writeSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';

class LogFile implements Disposable {
  readonly path: string;
  readonly fd: number;

  constructor(path: string) {
    this.path = path;
    this.fd = openSync(path, 'w');
  }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    closeSync(this.fd);
    console.log(`closed ${this.path}`);
  }
}

// Runs whenever the GC gets around to collecting the object, or never: no guarantee
const registry = new FinalizationRegistry((path: string) => console.log(`GC noticed ${path}`));

{
  // `using` (TypeScript 5.2+, native in Node 24): disposed when the block exits.
  // It is opt-in per binding: a plain `const` here would leak the fd until exit.
  using log = new LogFile(join(tmpdir(), 'access.log'));
  writeSync(log.fd, 'GET /\n');
  registry.register(log, log.path);
}
console.log('block exited');
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::panic;
use std::sync::Mutex;

struct Noisy(&'static str);

impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("    drop {}", self.0);
    }
}

struct Connection {
    _socket: Noisy,
    _tls: Noisy,
}

fn consume(n: Noisy) {
    println!("    consume got {}", n.0);
} // `n` is dropped here, in the callee that owns it

fn main() {
    println!("1. locals drop in reverse declaration order:");
    {
        let _a = Noisy("a");
        let _b = Noisy("b");
    }

    println!("2. struct fields drop in declaration order:");
    drop(Connection { _socket: Noisy("socket"), _tls: Noisy("tls") });

    println!("3. a moved value drops with its new owner, exactly once:");
    let moved = Noisy("moved");
    consume(moved);

    println!("4. `let _ =` drops at once, `let _kept` waits for the scope:");
    let _ = Noisy("underscore");
    let _kept = Noisy("kept until end of main");

    println!("5. panic unwinding still runs Drop:");
    panic::set_hook(Box::new(|_| {})); // silence the default panic message
    let result = panic::catch_unwind(|| {
        let _tx = Noisy("transaction rolled back");
        panic!("boom");
    });
    println!("    caught panic: {}", result.is_err());

    let counter = Mutex::new(0);
    {
        let mut guard = counter.lock().unwrap();
        *guard += 1;
    } // MutexGuard::drop unlocks here
    println!("6. lock released by Drop, value = {}", counter.lock().unwrap());
    println!("end of main");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Name RAII guards `_guard`, never `_`: `let _ = mutex.lock();` drops the guard (and unlocks) at the end of that statement. Call `drop(guard)` to release a lock before slow work instead of waiting for the end of the scope.
- **Footgun:** Drop is reliable but not guaranteed: `std::mem::forget` is safe, `Rc`/`Arc` cycles leak, and `panic = "abort"` or `std::process::exit` skip destructors. Drop also can't return errors, so `File` ignores errors on close; call `file.sync_all()?` yourself when durability matters.
- **Architecture note:** A type can't be both `Copy` and `Drop` (E0184): a bitwise copy would run the destructor twice. Because drops are fixed when the program is compiled, Rust has no collector to pause the program; freeing a large structure costs exactly the time spent dropping it, at a line you can point to.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy), [Appendix 8: Senior Rust Interview Q&A](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/interviews)

### Chapter P3: The Zero-Cost Abstraction Principle

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_zero_cost

Bjarne Stroustrup's rule for zero-cost abstractions has two halves: what you don't use, you don't pay for, and what you do use, you couldn't hand code any better. Rust applies it to iterators, closures, generics and futures, which typically compile to the same code you would write by hand.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Generics are monomorphized: `apply_static` is compiled once per concrete closure type, so the call is direct and can be inlined. Each closure is its own anonymous struct holding only its captures (0 bytes with none, 8 for one `u64` or one reference), not a heap object. After inlining, `iter().filter().map().sum()` becomes one loop, and because slice iterators carry no index there is no bounds check to remove. LLVM then unrolls the loop and, for element types the target's SIMD supports, auto-vectorizes it; Rust's `noalias` on `&mut` helps where a loop writes through one reference while reading another. This happens in release builds (`opt-level = 3`). Debug builds keep every adapter as a real call and can be many times slower, so never benchmark them. The cost moves to compile time and binary size: every instantiation is a separate copy of the code. Some costs are opt-in and visible in the type: `&dyn Fn` is a 16-byte fat pointer (data + vtable), and calls go through the vtable unless the optimizer can see the concrete type, so in general a `dyn` call can't be inlined. V8 reaches speed by speculating instead: `filter` and `map` each allocate a new array, callbacks are heap `JSFunction`s (plus a Context object when they capture variables), and TurboFan inlines them only while the type feedback collected in inline caches stays stable. Push a `0.5` into an array of small integers and its elements kind changes from `PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS` to `PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS`, so optimized code built for small integers deoptimizes back to the interpreter. In V8 performance depends on what the program does at runtime; in Rust it is fixed by the types at compile time.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
const data = Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => i + 1); // PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS

// filter and map each allocate a new array; every callback is a heap JSFunction
const viaChain = data
  .filter((x) => x % 2 === 0)
  .map((x) => x * x)
  .reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0);

let viaLoop = 0;
for (const x of data) {
  if (x % 2 === 0) viaLoop += x * x;
}

// TurboFan inlines these callbacks only while type feedback stays stable.
// Storing a double flips the array to PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS, and optimized code
// compiled for small integers deoptimizes back to the interpreter.
data.push(0.5);
console.log({ viaChain, viaLoop, length: data.length });
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::mem::{size_of, size_of_val};

fn sum_even_squares_iter(values: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    values.iter().filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0).map(|&x| x * x).sum()
}

fn sum_even_squares_loop(values: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    let mut total = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < values.len() {
        let x = values[i]; // bounds check LLVM must prove away; the iterator never has one
        if x % 2 == 0 {
            total += x * x;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    total
}

// Generic: compiled once per concrete F, so the call can be inlined
fn apply_static<F: Fn(u64) -> u64>(f: F, x: u64) -> u64 {
    f(x)
}

// Trait object: compiled once, called through a vtable pointer at runtime
fn apply_dyn(f: &dyn Fn(u64) -> u64, x: u64) -> u64 {
    f(x)
}

fn main() {
    let data: Vec<u64> = (1..=10).collect();
    println!("iterator = {}, hand loop = {}", sum_even_squares_iter(&data), sum_even_squares_loop(&data));

    // Each closure is its own struct type holding only what it captures
    let offset = 7u64;
    let no_capture = |x: u64| x + 1;
    let captures_u64 = move |x: u64| x + offset;
    let captures_ref = |x: u64| x + data.len() as u64;
    println!(
        "closure sizes: {}B, {}B, {}B",
        size_of_val(&no_capture),
        size_of_val(&captures_u64),
        size_of_val(&captures_ref)
    );

    let as_dyn: &dyn Fn(u64) -> u64 = &captures_u64;
    println!("&dyn Fn = {}B (data pointer + vtable pointer)", size_of_val(&as_dyn));
    println!("static = {}, dyn = {}, no_capture = {}", apply_static(captures_u64, 1), apply_dyn(as_dyn, 1), no_capture(1));
    println!("captures_ref(0) = {}", captures_ref(0));
    println!("Option<&u64> = {}B, same as &u64 = {}B", size_of::<Option<&u64>>(), size_of::<&u64>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Measure with `cargo build --release` or `cargo bench`, never debug builds. To confirm an iterator chain became a tight loop, check the assembly with `cargo asm` (cargo-show-asm) or Compiler Explorer.
- **Footgun:** `dyn Trait` is not zero-cost: unless the optimizer can devirtualize, calls go through a vtable and can't be inlined. The opposite trap is monomorphization bloat: a generic function used with 50 types is compiled 50 times. Keep a thin generic wrapper over a non-generic inner function (`fn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) { open_inner(p.as_ref()) }`), the pattern std itself uses.
- **Architecture note:** "Zero-cost" means no runtime overhead compared to the hand-written equivalent, not "free". The price is paid at compile time and in code size. Niche optimization is part of it too: `Option<&u64>` is 8 bytes, the same as `&u64`, because null can never be a valid reference.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy), [Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting)

### Chapter P4: Make Illegal States Unrepresentable

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_type_driven

In JavaScript an object can be in a half-valid state (`{ status: 'disconnected', socketId: 42 }`), and TypeScript only checks it until the data crosses a runtime boundary. In Rust you model each state as its own type, so invalid combinations can't be constructed, and `PhantomData` lets you tag values with types that cost zero bytes.

**Why Rust does it this way:** In the typestate pattern `send` only exists on `Connection<Connected>`, so calling it on a disconnected handle is error E0599, not a runtime check. Transitions take `self` by value, so after `close()` the old `live` handle has been moved and any further use is E0382. TypeScript can narrow a discriminated union just as well, but it can't stop you from keeping and using a stale reference to the old object. The states cost nothing at runtime: `Disconnected` is a zero-sized type, so `Connection<Disconnected>` is just its 24-byte `String`, and `Connection<Connected>` adds a 4-byte socket id plus padding (32 bytes); there is no tag to check. `PhantomData<T>` is also 0 bytes: `Id<User>` and `Id<Order>` are both a plain `u64` at runtime, but mixing them up is E0308. `PhantomData` also tells the compiler that the type acts as if it owns a `T`, which affects variance, auto traits like Send, and drop checking. A private field plus a single `parse` constructor ("parse, don't validate") means every `Email` that exists has already been checked. TypeScript's equivalents are discriminated unions and branded types, and both are erased: `JSON.parse(...) as Connected` is trusted blindly and `socketId` comes back `undefined`. With serde, a missing required field is an error at the boundary (`Option` fields default to `None`). For validated newtypes, don't derive `Deserialize` directly, since that bypasses `parse`; use `#[serde(try_from = "String")]` so `parse` stays the only way in.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// A discriminated union: TypeScript narrows on `status`, so socketId exists only when connected
type Connection =
  | { status: 'disconnected'; addr: string }
  | { status: 'connected'; addr: string; socketId: number };

type Connected = Extract<Connection, { status: 'connected' }>;

function connect(conn: Extract<Connection, { status: 'disconnected' }>, socketId: number): Connected {
  return { status: 'connected', addr: conn.addr, socketId };
}

function send(conn: Connected, msg: string): void {
  console.log(`socket ${conn.socketId} -> ${conn.addr}: ${msg}`);
}

const idle = { status: 'disconnected', addr: '10.0.0.1:5432' } as const;
const live = connect(idle, 9001);
send(live, 'SELECT 1');
// send(idle, 'hi'); // compile error, like Rust. But `idle` is still usable: nothing was moved.

// Branded type: TypeScript's closest thing to a newtype, erased at runtime
type UserId = number & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
const asUserId = (raw: number) => raw as UserId;

// Types vanish at runtime: data from JSON.parse is trusted on the word of `as`
const fromWire = JSON.parse('{"status":"connected","addr":"x"}') as Connected;
console.log(fromWire.socketId, asUserId(42)); // undefined 42
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;
use std::mem::size_of;

// 1. Typestate: each state is its own type and carries only the data valid in it
struct Disconnected;
struct Connected {
    socket_id: u32,
}

struct Connection<S> {
    addr: String,
    state: S,
}

impl Connection<Disconnected> {
    fn new(addr: &str) -> Self {
        Connection { addr: addr.to_string(), state: Disconnected }
    }

    // Takes `self` by value: the disconnected handle is moved and can't be reused
    fn connect(self, socket_id: u32) -> Connection<Connected> {
        Connection { addr: self.addr, state: Connected { socket_id } }
    }
}

impl Connection<Connected> {
    fn send(&self, msg: &str) {
        println!("socket {} -> {}: {msg}", self.state.socket_id, self.addr);
    }

    fn close(self) -> Connection<Disconnected> {
        Connection { addr: self.addr, state: Disconnected }
    }
}

// 2. PhantomData: tag a type with T without storing a T
struct Id<T> {
    raw: u64,
    _entity: PhantomData<T>,
}

impl<T> Id<T> {
    fn new(raw: u64) -> Self {
        Id { raw, _entity: PhantomData }
    }
}

struct User;
struct Order;

fn load_user(id: Id<User>) -> String {
    format!("user #{}", id.raw)
}

// 3. Parse, don't validate: the private field means parse() is the only constructor
mod email {
    pub struct Email(String);

    impl Email {
        pub fn parse(raw: &str) -> Result<Email, String> {
            match raw.split_once('@') {
                Some((user, domain)) if !user.is_empty() && domain.contains('.') => Ok(Email(raw.to_lowercase())),
                _ => Err(format!("invalid email: {raw:?}")),
            }
        }

        pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
            &self.0
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let conn = Connection::new("10.0.0.1:5432");
    // conn.send("hi"); // E0599: no method named `send` found for `Connection<Disconnected>`
    let live = conn.connect(9001);
    live.send("SELECT 1");
    let closed = live.close();
    // live.send("again"); // E0382: borrow of moved value: `live`
    println!("closed {}", closed.addr);

    let user_id: Id<User> = Id::new(42);
    let order_id: Id<Order> = Id::new(42);
    println!("{}", load_user(user_id));
    // load_user(order_id); // E0308: expected `Id<User>`, found `Id<Order>`
    println!("order raw = {}, Id<User> = {}B, PhantomData<User> = {}B", order_id.raw, size_of::<Id<User>>(), size_of::<PhantomData<User>>());
    println!(
        "Connection<Disconnected> = {}B, Connection<Connected> = {}B",
        size_of::<Connection<Disconnected>>(),
        size_of::<Connection<Connected>>()
    );

    for raw in ["Ada@Example.com", "not-an-email"] {
        match email::Email::parse(raw) {
            Ok(email) => println!("valid: {}", email.as_str()),
            Err(err) => println!("{err}"),
        }
    }
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Use typestate when the state is known along a code path (builders, protocol handshakes, payment flows). Use an `enum` when the state is decided at runtime, for example loaded from a database, and match it exhaustively so a new variant breaks the build everywhere it isn't handled.
- **Footgun:** `#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]` on `Id<T>` adds `T: Clone`, `T: Copy` and `T: PartialEq` bounds, so `Id<User>` isn't Copy unless `User` is. For phantom-tagged types, implement those traits by hand. `PhantomData<T>` also makes `Id<T>` inherit `T`'s Send/Sync; use `PhantomData<fn() -> T>` for pure tags.
- **Architecture note:** State markers and `PhantomData` disappear after type checking, so typestate adds no runtime cost: each state's methods are compiled separately and no state tag is stored or checked.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy)

### Chapter P5: Explicit Over Implicit

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_explicit_over_implicit

JavaScript converts types implicitly (`'8080' + 1` is `'80801'`), hides errors (any function may throw) and starts async work as soon as you call it. Rust makes conversions (`From`, `TryFrom`, `as`), failure (`Result` and `?`), heap copies (`.clone()`) and async execution (`.await`) show up in the code.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Rust has no implicit numeric conversion, not even lossless widening: `42_i32 + 0.5` is error E0277 and `"5" + 5` is E0369. `From` is implemented only where the conversion can't lose information (`f64::from(i32)` exists, `f32::from(i32)` doesn't), `TryFrom` returns a `Result` for conversions that can fail, and `as` is explicit but lossy: it truncates (`300 as u8` is 44), reinterprets bits (`-1i32 as u32` is 4294967295) and saturates floats (`1e10 as i32` is `i32::MAX`, and NaN becomes 0). A fallible function says so in its return type, and `?` is a visible early return that converts the error with `From::from`. `Copy` is implicit only for cheap bitwise types; every heap duplication is a `.clone()`. Futures are lazy: an `async` block does nothing until it is polled, while calling a JS async function runs its body synchronously up to the first `await`. Rust still has a few implicit steps: deref coercion (`&String` to `&str`), auto-referencing for method calls (`s.len()` borrows `s`), lifetime elision and drop calls. The types choose them at compile time, never the runtime value, though `Deref` and `Drop` impls are still user code that runs implicitly. JavaScript coercion follows the spec's ToPrimitive, ToNumber and ToString rules, and it can call your own code (`valueOf`, `toString`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`), which may even throw. TypeScript blocks some of it but still allows `string + number`.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
// TypeScript accepts string + number: it silently concatenates
const port = '8080';
console.log(port + 1); // '80801'

// Number() and parseInt() disagree on the same input, and neither throws
console.log(Number('8080abc'), parseInt('8080abc', 10)); // NaN 8080

// Bitwise operators silently truncate to 32-bit integers
console.log((2 ** 32 + 5) | 0); // 5

// Nothing in this signature says it can throw
function parsePort(raw: string): number {
  const n = Number(raw);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n < 0 || n > 65535) throw new RangeError(`bad port ${raw}`);
  return n;
}

try {
  parsePort('70000');
} catch (err) {
  console.log((err as Error).message);
}

// Calling an async function starts running it immediately, even if nobody awaits it
async function warmCache(): Promise<void> {
  console.log('warming cache');
}
warmCache(); // floating promise: if it rejected, Node would crash with an unhandled rejection
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::num::ParseIntError;

enum ConfigError {
    NotANumber(ParseIntError),
    OutOfRange(i64),
}

// `?` runs From::from on the error, so this conversion is written once, here
impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(err: ParseIntError) -> Self {
        ConfigError::NotANumber(err)
    }
}

// The signature says it can fail; callers can't forget that
fn parse_port(raw: &str) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    let wide: i64 = raw.trim().parse()?;
    u16::try_from(wide).map_err(|_| ConfigError::OutOfRange(wide))
}

fn main() {
    // let oops = "5" + 5;   // E0369: no implicit string + number
    // let mix = 42_i32 + 0.5; // E0277: not even lossless widening is implicit
    let count: i32 = 42;
    let ratio = f64::from(count) + 0.5; // From exists only where the conversion is lossless
    println!("ratio = {ratio}");

    // `as` is explicit but lossy: truncation, wrapping and saturation all hide behind it
    println!("300_i32 as u8   = {}", 300_i32 as u8);
    println!("-1_i32 as u32   = {}", -1_i32 as u32);
    println!("1e10_f64 as i32 = {}", 1e10_f64 as i32);
    println!("u8::try_from(300) = {:?}", u8::try_from(300_i32));

    // An exhaustive match: adding a ConfigError variant breaks this until it is handled
    for raw in ["8080", "70000", "http"] {
        match parse_port(raw) {
            Ok(port) => println!("{raw:?} -> port {port}"),
            Err(ConfigError::NotANumber(err)) => println!("{raw:?} -> not a number: {err}"),
            Err(ConfigError::OutOfRange(n)) => println!("{raw:?} -> {n} is outside 0..=65535"),
        }
    }

    // Copy is implicit only for cheap bitwise types; heap copies always say .clone()
    let name = String::from("explicit");
    let copy_of_name = name.clone();
    println!("{name} / {copy_of_name}");

    // Futures are lazy: creating one runs nothing until it is awaited or polled
    let never_polled = async { println!("this never prints") };
    drop(never_polled);
    println!("future dropped without running");
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Implement `From<T>` for your error types: the standard library's blanket impl gives you `Into` for free, and `?` uses it automatically. For values from outside (config, network, user input), write `u16::try_from(n)?` instead of `n as u16`.
- **Footgun:** `as` never fails: it silently truncates integers, wraps signed to unsigned and saturates floats (NaN becomes 0). Enable Clippy's pedantic `cast_possible_truncation` and `cast_sign_loss` lints to flag risky casts in code review.
- **Architecture note:** Exhaustive `match` is explicitness that scales: add a variant to `ConfigError` and every match that doesn't handle it stops compiling, which turns a refactor into a checklist the compiler hands you.

Go deeper: [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy), [Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls)

## Part 8: LeetCode in Rust

### Chapter LC1: Two Sum (#1) — Single-Pass HashMap

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_two_sum

Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`. One pass with a hash map from value to index solves it in O(n) time and O(n) space, in both languages.

**Why Rust does it this way:** The algorithm is the same; the memory layout is not. A `Vec<i32>` stores 4-byte integers back to back, 16 per 64-byte cache line on x86-64, so `iter().enumerate()` streams through memory the hardware prefetcher predicts easily. A V8 array of small integers (`PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS`) is also contiguous, but each element is an 8-byte tagged slot in Node's x64 builds (they ship without pointer compression). Rust's `HashMap` is a SwissTable (the hashbrown crate): open addressing with `(i32, usize)` pairs stored inline in one allocation (16 bytes each, with padding) and one control byte per slot, and a lookup compares 16 control bytes at once with SSE2 on x86-64 before touching any key. `with_capacity(nums.len())` makes the single allocation big enough for every element, so the table never rehashes while you insert. The default hasher is SipHash-1-3, which resists HashDoS attacks but is slower than needed for integer keys. V8's `Map` is a deterministic, insertion-ordered hash table whose entries hold tagged values. Checking before inserting is what makes `[3, 3]` with target 6 return `[0, 1]` without ever pairing an element with itself.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
function twoSum(nums: number[], target: number): number[] {
  // V8's Map is an insertion-ordered hash table holding tagged values
  const seen = new Map<number, number>();
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const j = seen.get(target - nums[i]); // one lookup instead of has() + get()
    if (j !== undefined) return [j, i];
    seen.set(nums[i], i);
  }
  return [];
}

console.log(twoSum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)); // [0, 1]
console.log(twoSum([3, 3], 6)); // [0, 1]
console.log(twoSum([3], 6)); // []
```

Rust:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

// LeetCode's signature: takes ownership of the Vec, returns indices as i32
fn two_sum(nums: Vec<i32>, target: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
    // One allocation sized for every element, so inserting never triggers a rehash
    let mut seen: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::with_capacity(nums.len());
    for (i, &num) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        // Constraints keep |target - num| <= 2e9 < i32::MAX; outside them use checked_sub
        let complement = target - num;
        if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&complement) {
            return vec![j as i32, i as i32];
        }
        // Insert after the lookup, so an element can never pair with itself
        seen.insert(num, i);
    }
    vec![]
}

// Idiomatic Rust: borrow a slice, and use Option instead of an empty-Vec sentinel
fn two_sum_indices(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    let mut seen = HashMap::with_capacity(nums.len());
    for (i, &num) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(target - num)) {
            return Some((j, i));
        }
        seen.insert(num, i);
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(vec![2, 7, 11, 15], 9));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(vec![3, 3], 6));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum_indices(&[3, 2, 4], 6));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum_indices(&[3], 6));
    println!("each (i32, usize) slot in the table = {} bytes", size_of::<(i32, usize)>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** `HashMap::with_capacity(n)` sizes the table once (SwissTable keeps the load factor at or below 7/8). Outside LeetCode, swap in a faster non-cryptographic hasher for integer keys, such as `rustc_hash::FxHashMap` or `ahash`, when the keys don't come from untrusted input.
- **Footgun:** `target - num` panics on overflow in debug builds and wraps in release builds. LeetCode's limits (|values| up to 10^9) keep it inside i32, but with arbitrary input use `checked_sub` or widen to i64. And always check before inserting, or `[3]` with target 6 pairs index 0 with itself.
- **Architecture note:** LeetCode's signature takes `Vec<i32>` by value and returns indices as `i32`. Idiomatic Rust borrows `&[i32]` and returns `Option<(usize, usize)>`, which makes "no answer" explicit instead of an empty `Vec` sentinel.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC20: Valid Parentheses (#20) — Vector Stack

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_valid_parentheses

Given a string `s` of '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', decide whether every bracket is closed by the matching type in the right order. A stack of expected closing brackets solves it in one O(n) pass.

**Why Rust does it this way:** A `Vec<u8>` stack stores 1 byte per entry in one contiguous buffer; `push` and `pop` only touch the end, so both are amortized O(1), and `pop()` on an empty stack returns `None` instead of crashing. A `Vec<char>` would spend 4 bytes per entry, because `char` is a full Unicode scalar value. Scanning bytes is safe because UTF-8 is self-synchronizing: ASCII bytes (0x00 to 0x7F) never appear inside a multi-byte character, whose bytes are all 0x80 or above. So matching `b'('` can never hit half of an `é`, and `s.bytes()` skips the decoding work `s.chars()` does. Two cheap early exits: an odd length can never balance, and a valid string never nests deeper than `len / 2`, which is the capacity reserved up front. In JavaScript, V8 stores a string as one-byte (Latin-1) or two-byte (UTF-16) internally, `for...of` walks code points and hands back 1-character strings, and the stack array holds 8-byte tagged pointers to them. `pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined`, which the `!==` comparison happens to treat as a mismatch.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
function isValid(s: string): boolean {
  if (s.length % 2 === 1) return false;
  const expected: string[] = []; // each slot is a tagged pointer to a 1-char string
  for (const c of s) {
    if (c === '(') expected.push(')');
    else if (c === '{') expected.push('}');
    else if (c === '[') expected.push(']');
    else if (expected.pop() !== c) return false; // pop() on an empty array is undefined
  }
  return expected.length === 0;
}

for (const input of ['()[]{}', '(]', '([)]', '{[]}', '((', '']) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(input), isValid(input));
}
```

Rust:

```rust
fn is_valid(s: &str) -> bool {
    // An odd length can never balance
    if s.len() % 2 == 1 {
        return false;
    }
    // Brackets are ASCII, and no byte inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character is below 0x80,
    // so matching on bytes is correct for any &str and skips char decoding.
    // A valid string never nests deeper than len / 2.
    let mut expected: Vec<u8> = Vec::with_capacity(s.len() / 2);
    for b in s.bytes() {
        match b {
            b'(' => expected.push(b')'),
            b'{' => expected.push(b'}'),
            b'[' => expected.push(b']'),
            b')' | b'}' | b']' => {
                // pop() on an empty Vec is None, never undefined or a crash
                if expected.pop() != Some(b) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            _ => return false, // not a bracket
        }
    }
    expected.is_empty()
}

fn main() {
    for input in ["()[]{}", "(]", "([)]", "{[]}", "((", "", "(é)"] {
        println!("{input:?} valid? {}", is_valid(input));
    }
    println!("stack entry: u8 = {} byte, char = {} bytes", size_of::<u8>(), size_of::<char>());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** Push the expected closing bracket instead of the opening one, so the check is a single `pop() != Some(b)` with no lookup table.
- **Footgun:** Use `.chars()` only when you need Unicode scalar values; for ASCII grammars (brackets, CSV, JSON punctuation) `.bytes()` is correct and faster. Never slice `&s[i..i + 1]` at arbitrary byte offsets: slicing in the middle of a multi-byte character panics.
- **Architecture note:** `Vec::pop` returns `Option<T>`, so an unbalanced closing bracket becomes a `None` comparison handled by the type system, not an out-of-bounds read or an `undefined` that leaks into later logic.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC21: Merge Two Sorted Lists (#21)

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_merge_lists

Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing their nodes together. In Rust each link is an `Option<Box<ListNode>>`, and merging means moving those boxes from the inputs into the result without copying or cloning a single node.

**Why Rust does it this way:** `Option<Box<ListNode>>` is 8 bytes because a Box can never be null, so null is free to mean `None` (the niche optimization). `ListNode` is 16 bytes: a 4-byte `i32`, 4 bytes of padding and the 8-byte link, and every node is its own heap allocation. The loop keeps `tail` as a `&mut Option<Box<ListNode>>` pointing at the empty slot to fill: `take()` detaches the head node from its list, `Option::insert` moves the Box into the slot and returns `&mut Box<ListNode>`, and the cursor steps to its `next`. Each step only copies 8-byte pointers; node payloads never move and nothing is cloned. Ownership makes it impossible for a node to end up in both lists. Walking a linked list is pointer chasing: each `next` load depends on the previous one, so the CPU can't prefetch ahead the way it can for a `Vec`. That is why merging two sorted arrays is usually much faster in practice. In Node, a `{ val, next }` literal takes about 40 bytes (a 24-byte header with map, properties and elements pointers, plus two 8-byte tagged fields), and the GC tracks every `next` reference. Nodes allocated one after another are bump-allocated next to each other in the young generation, which partly hides the pointer-chasing cost. The recursive JS version uses one stack frame per node; the loop uses O(1) extra space.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
interface ListNode {
  val: number;
  next: ListNode | null;
}

function mergeTwoLists(a: ListNode | null, b: ListNode | null): ListNode | null {
  const dummy: ListNode = { val: 0, next: null };
  let tail = dummy;
  while (a && b) {
    if (a.val <= b.val) {
      tail.next = a;
      a = a.next;
    } else {
      tail.next = b;
      b = b.next;
    }
    tail = tail.next;
  }
  tail.next = a ?? b;
  return dummy.next;
}

const fromArray = (values: number[]): ListNode | null =>
  values.reduceRight<ListNode | null>((next, val) => ({ val, next }), null);

function toArray(list: ListNode | null): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let node = list; node; node = node.next) out.push(node.val);
  return out;
}

console.log(toArray(mergeTwoLists(fromArray([1, 2, 4]), fromArray([1, 3, 4])))); // [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]
```

Rust:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct ListNode {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
}

fn merge_two_lists(mut a: Option<Box<ListNode>>, mut b: Option<Box<ListNode>>) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    let mut head = None;
    // `tail` points at the empty slot the next node goes into
    let mut tail = &mut head;
    while let (Some(x), Some(y)) = (&a, &b) {
        let source = if x.val <= y.val { &mut a } else { &mut b };
        let mut node = source.take().unwrap();
        *source = node.next.take(); // detach: the node now has no successor
        tail = &mut tail.insert(node).next; // move the Box in, then step to its `next`
    }
    *tail = a.or(b); // attach whichever list still has nodes
    head
}

fn from_slice(values: &[i32]) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    values.iter().rev().fold(None, |next, &val| Some(Box::new(ListNode { val, next })))
}

fn to_vec(mut list: &Option<Box<ListNode>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while let Some(node) = list {
        out.push(node.val);
        list = &node.next;
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let merged = merge_two_lists(from_slice(&[1, 2, 4]), from_slice(&[1, 3, 4]));
    println!("merged = {:?}", to_vec(&merged));
    println!("empty + [0] = {:?}", to_vec(&merge_two_lists(None, from_slice(&[0]))));

    // null is the None niche, so the link is one pointer; each node is its own heap allocation
    println!(
        "Option<Box<ListNode>> = {}B, ListNode = {}B",
        size_of::<Option<Box<ListNode>>>(),
        size_of::<ListNode>()
    );
}
```

- **Pro tip:** The cursor pattern `tail = &mut tail.insert(node).next;` (with `Option::insert`, Rust 1.53+) avoids `unwrap()` and keeps the borrow checker happy. Finish with `*tail = a.or(b);` to attach whatever is left in a single assignment.
- **Footgun:** Dropping a long `Option<Box<ListNode>>` chain is recursive: each Box's destructor drops the next one. A 100,000-node list overflows the 8 MiB main-thread stack in a debug build (about 1 million in release). For your own list types, implement `Drop` with a loop that uses `take()`.
- **Architecture note:** Linked lists trade cache locality for O(1) splicing. Unless you really need to splice in the middle, a `Vec` plus `sort` or a k-way merge over slices wins, because sequential memory is what CPU caches and prefetchers are built for.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC121: Best Time to Buy & Sell Stock (#121)

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_buy_sell_stock

Find the maximum profit from buying once and selling once later. A single greedy pass that tracks the lowest price seen so far solves it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**Why Rust does it this way:** The loop state is two `i32`s (`min_price` and `best`), which the compiler keeps in registers; the only memory traffic is the sequential 4-byte reads of `prices` from one contiguous buffer, which the hardware prefetcher streams in ahead of time. No heap allocation happens beyond the input. LeetCode's signature takes `Vec<i32>` by value, so the function owns the buffer and frees it when it returns; for your own code take `&[i32]` and the caller keeps it. `i32::MAX` is a safe sentinel because `price - min_price` is only computed once `price >= min_price`, and prices are non-negative, so it can't overflow. In V8 the `number[]` holds small integers in tagged slots (`PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS`), and since `minPrice` starts as `Infinity`, a double, optimized code works on that variable as a 64-bit float. JS integers don't wrap: they lose precision past 2^53 and overflow to `Infinity` only near 1.8e308.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
function maxProfit(prices: number[]): number {
  let minPrice = Infinity; // a double, so optimized code keeps this in a float register
  let best = 0;
  for (const price of prices) {
    if (price < minPrice) minPrice = price;
    else if (price - minPrice > best) best = price - minPrice;
  }
  return best;
}

console.log(maxProfit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4])); // 5
console.log(maxProfit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1])); // 0
```

Rust:

```rust
// LeetCode's signature: the Vec is moved in and freed when the function returns
fn max_profit(prices: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
    let mut min_price = i32::MAX;
    let mut best = 0;
    for price in prices {
        if price < min_price {
            min_price = price;
        } else if price - min_price > best {
            // only reached when price >= min_price, so the subtraction can't overflow
            best = price - min_price;
        }
    }
    best
}

// Same greedy pass as a fold over a borrowed slice; state is just (min, best)
fn max_profit_fold(prices: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let (_, best) = prices.iter().fold((i32::MAX, 0), |(min, best), &price| {
        let min = min.min(price);
        (min, best.max(price - min))
    });
    best
}

fn main() {
    println!("[7,1,5,3,6,4] -> {}", max_profit(vec![7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]));
    println!("[7,6,4,3,1]   -> {}", max_profit(vec![7, 6, 4, 3, 1]));
    println!("fold          -> {}", max_profit_fold(&[2, 4, 1, 7]));
    println!("empty         -> {}", max_profit_fold(&[]));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** The same pass as a fold: `prices.iter().fold((i32::MAX, 0), |(min, best), &p| { let min = min.min(p); (min, best.max(p - min)) })`. It borrows a slice, so the caller keeps ownership of the data.
- **Footgun:** Strictly decreasing prices give a profit of 0, not a negative number: you are allowed not to trade. And a sentinel like `i32::MAX` is only safe if you never subtract from it before it has been replaced; with negative inputs `p - min` could overflow.
- **Architecture note:** This is the simplest dynamic program: the best profit up to day i depends only on the minimum before day i, so the DP table collapses into two variables. Each element costs a load, a compare and a subtract.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC125: Valid Palindrome (#125) — Two Pointers

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_valid_palindrome

Check whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards after lowercasing and removing everything except letters and digits. Two indices moving inward over the raw bytes solve LeetCode's ASCII version in O(n) time with zero allocations.

**Why Rust does it this way:** A Rust `&str` is UTF-8 bytes. `s.as_bytes()[i]` is an O(1) byte read, but there is no O(1) "i-th character", because a `char` takes 1 to 4 bytes. LeetCode counts only ASCII letters and digits, so the byte version is exactly right: `is_ascii_alphanumeric` and `eq_ignore_ascii_case` compare bytes without allocating, and every byte of a non-ASCII character is 0x80 or above, so it is skipped as non-alphanumeric instead of being split into false matches. Keeping `right` one past the end means an empty string can't underflow `usize`. For a Unicode-aware check, `Chars` is a `DoubleEndedIterator` that decodes UTF-8 from both ends, and `filter` plus `flat_map(char::to_lowercase)` keep that property, so `next()` and `next_back()` still compare from both ends with zero allocations. The two definitions really differ: "ñaña" is a palindrome under the ASCII rule (only "aa" counts) and not under the Unicode one. Neither handles grapheme clusters such as `e` plus a combining accent (unicode-segmentation crate) or NFC vs NFD forms of `é` (unicode-normalization crate). In JavaScript, strings are UTF-16: `charCodeAt` returns one 16-bit code unit in O(1) on a flat string, `length` counts code units (`'😀'.length` is 2), and the usual `toLowerCase().replace(...).split('').reverse().join('')` one-liner allocates several new strings and an array.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
const isAsciiAlnum = (code: number) =>
  (code >= 48 && code <= 57) || (code >= 65 && code <= 90) || (code >= 97 && code <= 122);

const asciiLower = (code: number) => (code >= 65 && code <= 90 ? code + 32 : code);

// Two pointers over UTF-16 code units: no copies, unlike the
// toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '') + split/reverse/join one-liner (three new strings and an array)
function isPalindrome(s: string): boolean {
  let left = 0;
  let right = s.length - 1;
  while (left < right) {
    const a = s.charCodeAt(left);
    const b = s.charCodeAt(right);
    if (!isAsciiAlnum(a)) left++;
    else if (!isAsciiAlnum(b)) right--;
    else if (asciiLower(a) !== asciiLower(b)) return false;
    else {
      left++;
      right--;
    }
  }
  return true;
}

console.log(isPalindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama')); // true
console.log(isPalindrome('race a car')); // false
console.log('ñaña'.length, [...'😀'].length, '😀'.length); // 4 1 2: length counts UTF-16 units
```

Rust:

```rust
// LeetCode's rules: only ASCII letters and digits count. Two indices over bytes,
// zero allocations. Bytes of non-ASCII characters are all >= 0x80, so they are
// skipped as non-alphanumeric and never split into false matches.
fn is_palindrome(s: &str) -> bool {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    // `right` is one past the end, so an empty string never underflows usize
    let (mut left, mut right) = (0, bytes.len());
    while left < right {
        if !bytes[left].is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            left += 1;
        } else if !bytes[right - 1].is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            right -= 1;
        } else if !bytes[left].eq_ignore_ascii_case(&bytes[right - 1]) {
            return false;
        } else {
            left += 1;
            right -= 1;
        }
    }
    true
}

// Unicode-aware: Chars decodes UTF-8 from both ends, still without allocating
fn is_palindrome_unicode(s: &str) -> bool {
    let mut chars = s.chars().filter(|c| c.is_alphanumeric()).flat_map(char::to_lowercase);
    loop {
        match (chars.next(), chars.next_back()) {
            (Some(front), Some(back)) if front != back => return false,
            (Some(_), Some(_)) => continue,
            _ => return true, // met in the middle
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    for input in ["A man, a plan, a canal: Panama", "race a car", " ", "ñaña"] {
        println!("{input:?}: ascii={} unicode={}", is_palindrome(input), is_palindrome_unicode(input));
    }
    // 'ñ' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so byte length and char count differ
    println!("\"ñaña\" is {} bytes, {} chars", "ñaña".len(), "ñaña".chars().count());
}
```

- **Pro tip:** `u8::is_ascii_alphanumeric` and `u8::eq_ignore_ascii_case` are the allocation-free tools for ASCII rules. For Unicode, `chars().next_back()` lets you walk from the end without collecting into a `Vec<char>`.
- **Footgun:** Don't mix Unicode classification with ASCII case folding: `'É'.is_alphanumeric()` is true, but `to_ascii_lowercase()` leaves it unchanged, so "Éé" fails a check that is meant to ignore case. `char::to_lowercase` returns an iterator, not a char, because one character can lowercase to several ('İ' becomes "i̇"), hence `flat_map`.
- **Architecture note:** UTF-8 continuation bytes always look like `10xxxxxx`, so `next_back()` finds the start of the last character by skipping at most three of them. That self-synchronizing property is why byte-level scanning for ASCII is always safe on a valid `&str`.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC206: Reverse Linked List (#206) — Ownership Transfer

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_reverse_linked_list

Reverse a singly linked list. In Rust every node has exactly one owner, so reversal means moving each `Box` from `head` to `current` to `prev` with `Option::take`, which never copies, clones or reallocates a node.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Each iteration does three moves: `head = current.next.take()` detaches the rest of the list (`take` is `mem::replace` with `None`), `current.next = prev` points the node backwards, and `prev = Some(current)` gives `prev` ownership. At every step each node has exactly one owner, so the compiler rules out both cycles and dangling links. The demo shows that the old head ends up as the last node at the same address: reversal rewrites 8-byte `next` fields and nothing else. The JavaScript version performs the same three assignments on GC references, but nothing stops you from creating a cycle by getting the order wrong (then printing the list never terminates), and the old `list` variable still points at a node that is now the tail. Two live aliases into one structure are normal in JS and impossible in safe Rust. Pointer stores into heap objects also go through V8's write barrier (TurboFan elides it where it can prove it unnecessary), so the generational GC can record old-to-new references and incremental marking can see the change.

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
interface ListNode {
  val: number;
  next: ListNode | null;
}

function reverseList(head: ListNode | null): ListNode | null {
  let prev: ListNode | null = null;
  let curr = head;
  while (curr) {
    const next = curr.next;
    curr.next = prev; // each pointer store into a heap object passes V8's GC write barrier
    prev = curr;
    curr = next;
  }
  return prev;
}

const fromArray = (values: number[]): ListNode | null =>
  values.reduceRight<ListNode | null>((next, val) => ({ val, next }), null);

function toArray(list: ListNode | null): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let node = list; node; node = node.next) out.push(node.val);
  return out;
}

const list = fromArray([1, 2, 3, 4]);
const reversed = reverseList(list);
console.log(toArray(reversed)); // [4, 3, 2, 1]
// `list` still points at the old head, which is now the tail: two live aliases, no error
console.log(list?.val, list?.next); // 1 null
```

Rust:

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct ListNode {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
}

fn reverse_list(mut head: Option<Box<ListNode>>) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    let mut prev = None;
    // Each loop moves one Box: head -> current -> prev. Every node always has exactly one owner.
    while let Some(mut current) = head {
        head = current.next.take(); // detach the rest; current.next is now None
        current.next = prev;
        prev = Some(current);
    }
    prev
}

fn from_slice(values: &[i32]) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    values.iter().rev().fold(None, |next, &val| Some(Box::new(ListNode { val, next })))
}

fn to_vec(mut list: &Option<Box<ListNode>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while let Some(node) = list {
        out.push(node.val);
        list = &node.next;
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let list = from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
    let first_node: *const ListNode = list.as_deref().unwrap();

    let reversed = reverse_list(list);
    println!("reversed = {:?}", to_vec(&reversed));

    // No node was copied or reallocated: the old head is now the last node, same address
    let mut last = reversed.as_deref().unwrap();
    while let Some(next) = last.next.as_deref() {
        last = next;
    }
    println!("old head reused in place: {}", std::ptr::eq(first_node, last));
    println!("reverse(None) = {:?}", reverse_list(None));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** `Option::take()` (shorthand for `mem::replace(&mut opt, None)`) moves a value out of a field you only have `&mut` access to. `Option::replace(new)` does the same while putting a new value in.
- **Footgun:** Getting past borrow errors with `current.next.clone()` compiles, but it deep-copies the whole rest of the list at every step: O(n²) time and n² allocations for what should be pointer moves.
- **Architecture note:** The reversal reuses every allocation, so node addresses never change and the allocator is never called. That is the payoff of modelling ownership: Rust can move whole structures by moving 8-byte pointers, with no GC write barriers or reference counts.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

### Chapter LC53: Maximum Subarray (#53) — Kadane's Algorithm

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_max_subarray

Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. Kadane's algorithm, a dynamic program that only needs the previous step, does it in one O(n) pass with O(1) space.

**Why Rust does it this way:** Kadane's recurrence is `best_ending_here[i] = max(nums[i], best_ending_here[i-1] + nums[i])`. Each step only needs the previous value, so the DP table collapses into one variable, and a second one tracks the overall best. `&nums[1..]` creates a new slice (a pointer and a length, 16 bytes) over the same buffer, while JS `nums.slice(1)` copies the array. `num.max(...)` is `Ord::max`, which LLVM usually lowers to a compare plus conditional select (`cmov` on x86-64, `csel` on AArch64) instead of a branch, but that is the optimizer's choice, not a guarantee. Overflow is bounded by LeetCode's limits (at most 10^5 values of magnitude 10^4, so |sum| <= 10^9 < i32::MAX); with arbitrary input use `i64` or `checked_add`, since debug builds panic on overflow and release builds wrap. The span version shows the idiomatic signature: `split_first()` returns `None` for an empty slice, so "no answer" is part of the type. The TypeScript version declares `number` and returns `undefined` for `[]`. JS integers don't wrap (they lose precision past 2^53), and V8 represents small integers as Smis, switching to float64 once a value leaves the Smi range (unboxed in registers and double arrays, a heap-allocated HeapNumber in tagged slots).

Node.js / TypeScript:

```ts
function maxSubArray(nums: number[]): number {
  let best = nums[0];
  let current = nums[0];
  for (let i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const n = nums[i];
    current = Math.max(n, current + n); // extend the run or restart at n
    best = Math.max(best, current);
  }
  return best;
}

console.log(maxSubArray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])); // 6
console.log(maxSubArray([-3, -1, -2])); // -1
console.log(maxSubArray([])); // undefined at runtime, despite the `number` return type
```

Rust:

```rust
// LeetCode's signature; the constraints guarantee at least one element
fn max_sub_array(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
    let mut best = nums[0];
    let mut current = nums[0];
    // &nums[1..] is a new (pointer, length) pair over the same buffer, not a copy
    for &num in &nums[1..] {
        // Either extend the running subarray or start a fresh one at `num`
        current = num.max(current + num);
        best = best.max(current);
    }
    best
}

// Idiomatic: an empty slice has no answer, so return Option, and report where the run is
fn max_sub_array_span(nums: &[i32]) -> Option<(i32, usize, usize)> {
    let (&first, _) = nums.split_first()?;
    let (mut best, mut best_start, mut best_end) = (first, 0, 0);
    let (mut current, mut start) = (first, 0);
    for (i, &num) in nums.iter().enumerate().skip(1) {
        if current < 0 {
            current = num; // a negative prefix only drags the sum down: restart here
            start = i;
        } else {
            current += num;
        }
        if current > best {
            (best, best_start, best_end) = (current, start, i);
        }
    }
    Some((best, best_start, best_end))
}

fn main() {
    println!("max = {}", max_sub_array(vec![-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]));
    println!("(sum, start, end) = {:?}", max_sub_array_span(&[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]));
    println!("all negative = {:?}", max_sub_array_span(&[-3, -1, -2]));
    println!("empty = {:?}", max_sub_array_span(&[]));
}
```

- **Pro tip:** `slice.split_first()` gives you the first element and the rest as `Option<(&T, &[T])>`, a panic-free replacement for `nums[0]` plus `&nums[1..]`. Reslicing is O(1) because it only creates a new pointer and length.
- **Footgun:** Initializing `best` to 0 gives the wrong answer when every number is negative (it should return the largest single element, -1 for `[-3, -1, -2]`). Start from the first element. And `nums[0]` panics on an empty Vec, which is fine under LeetCode's constraints and a bug anywhere else.
- **Architecture note:** Each element costs a load, an add and two max operations, and the loop-carried dependency on `current` is what bounds its speed. Reading 4-byte values sequentially from a contiguous slice keeps the loop fed straight from the hardware prefetcher.

Go deeper: [Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode)

# Part B: Architecture Appendices (14 guides)

## Appendix 1: Borrow Checker Mastery

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/borrow-checker

Appendix 01 • Core Mental Model

### Mastering the Rust Borrow Checker

Aliasing XOR Mutability, Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL), and how the borrow checker rules out data races in safe Rust at compile time.

#### Key takeaways

- Rust's borrow checker allows either any number of shared references (`&T`) or exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`) to a value at a time, never both.

- Since Rust 1.31 (December 2018), Non-Lexical Lifetimes (RFC 2094) end a borrow at its last use instead of at the closing brace of its scope.

- Polonius is the next borrow checker; it accepts some correct programs that NLL rejects, but it is still nightly-only (`-Zpolonius`) and its stabilization is a 2026 Rust project goal.

- Shared references implement `Copy` and mutable references do not, so `let r2 = r1;` moves an `&mut T` while passing it to a function parameter typed `&mut T` reborrows it.

- When ownership rules are too strict for a design, `Rc<RefCell<T>>` (single thread) and `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (multi-thread) move the aliasing check from compile time to run time.

#### 1. The Golden Rule: Aliasing XOR Mutability

In JavaScript, object references are shared without restrictions. If three functions hold a reference to the same object, any of them can mutate it at any time. In single-threaded Node.js this shows up as hard-to-trace state mutation bugs. With shared memory across threads (for example `SharedArrayBuffer` in worker threads), unsynchronized access becomes a data race. Safe Rust rules data races out at compile time.

At any given time, for any value of type T, you can have:

• Any number of shared references (`&T`) OR

• Exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`),

**NEVER BOTH AT THE SAME TIME.**

#### 2. Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL) & Polonius

Before NLL, borrows were **lexical**: a borrow stayed active until the closing curly brace `}` of its enclosing scope. NLL (RFC 2094) shipped in Rust 1.31 for the 2018 edition and in Rust 1.36 for the 2015 edition. It computes borrows over the MIR control-flow graph, so a borrow ends at its *last use*.

```
let mut data = vec![1, 2, 3];

let first = &data[0];               // Shared borrow begins
println!("First item: {}", first);  // Last use of `first`: under NLL the borrow ends here

data.push(4);                       // Accepted under NLL; the old lexical checker rejected it
```

###### The Next Frontier: Polonius (Origin-Based Analysis)

NLL still rejects some correct code, most famously a conditional return of a borrow (listed as "problem case #3" in RFC 2094). **Polonius** is a reformulation of the borrow checker that tracks where each loan can flow (its "origins") statically, per program point. It is available on nightly with `-Zpolonius` and is not yet on stable; stabilizing "Polonius Alpha" is a 2026 Rust project goal.

```
use std::collections::HashMap;

// Rejected by NLL (E0502), accepted under Polonius:
fn get_or_insert<'a>(map: &'a mut HashMap<String, String>, key: &str) -> &'a String {
    if let Some(v) = map.get(key) {
        return v; // Returning `v` forces this borrow to last for all of 'a, even on the path below
    }
    map.insert(key.to_string(), String::from("default")); // NLL: cannot borrow `*map` as mutable
    &map[key]
}
```

On stable today, work around it with the entry API: `map.entry(key.to_string()).or_insert_with(|| String::from("default"))`.

#### 3. Reborrowing vs. Move Semantics

Shared references (`&T`) implement `Copy`; mutable references (`&mut T`) **do not**. Moving an `&mut T` makes the source variable unusable. However, when the target type is already known to be `&mut T` (a function parameter, or a `let` with an explicit type), the compiler inserts an implicit **reborrow** instead of a move.

**Move of a Mutable Reference**
An untyped `let` moves the reference itself:

```
let mut s = String::from("hi");
let r1 = &mut s;
let r2 = r1; // MOVES r1 into r2

// println!("{}", r1);
// ERROR: borrow of moved value: `r1`
println!("{}", r2); // OK
```

**Reborrowing (`&mut *r`)**
Creates a shorter child borrow that suspends the parent:

```
let mut s = String::from("hi");
let r1 = &mut s;

// Explicit reborrow:
let r2 = &mut *r1; // r1 suspended while r2 is in use
r2.push_str(" world");

println!("{}", r1); // OK: r2 is no longer used
```

#### 4. Escape Hatches & Smart Pointers

| Pattern | Rust Primitive | JavaScript Analogy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared Read-Only (Multi-threaded) | `Arc<T>` | `Object.freeze(obj)` reference |
| Shared Mutable (Single-Threaded) | `Rc<RefCell<T>>` | Plain shared JS object, plus a runtime check that panics on a conflicting borrow |
| Shared Mutable (Multi-Threaded) | `Arc<Mutex<T>>` | Shared object guarded by a lock (like `Atomics` on a `SharedArrayBuffer`) |
| Read-Heavy Shared State | `Arc<RwLock<T>>` | In-memory cache with concurrent reads |

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why does Rust say "cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable"?**

A: Error E0502 means a shared reference is still used later in the code while you try to take a mutable one. Rust allows many shared references or one mutable reference to a value, never both at once. Move the last use of the shared reference before the mutation, or clone the data you need from it.

**Q: Does Rust have a garbage collector like Node.js?**

A: No, Rust has no tracing garbage collector. Each value has one owner and is dropped when that owner goes out of scope, and the borrow checker proves at compile time that no reference outlives the value. Reference counting with `Rc` or `Arc` is available when you need shared ownership.

**Q: What are non-lexical lifetimes in Rust?**

A: Non-lexical lifetimes (NLL, RFC 2094) end a borrow at its last use instead of at the end of its enclosing block. NLL became the default in Rust 1.31 for the 2018 edition and in Rust 1.36 for the 2015 edition. It removed many false borrow errors that the older lexical checker reported.

**Q: Is Polonius available on stable Rust?**

A: Not yet. Polonius can be enabled on nightly with `-Zpolonius`, and stabilizing its "alpha" form is a 2026 Rust project goal. On stable, rewrite code that needs it, for example using the `HashMap` entry API for get-or-insert.

**Q: How do I share mutable state between functions in Rust like a JavaScript object?**

A: Use `Rc<RefCell<T>>` on one thread or `Arc<Mutex<T>>` across threads. Both let several owners mutate the same value, with the exclusive-access rule checked at run time instead of compile time. `RefCell` panics on a conflicting borrow, while `Mutex` blocks until the lock is free.

#### Sources and further reading

- [The Rust Book: References and Borrowing](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-02-references-and-borrowing.html): the shared-or-mutable borrowing rules.

- [RFC 2094: Non-lexical lifetimes](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2094-nll.html): NLL design and the conditional-return problem case.

- [The Polonius book](https://rust-lang.github.io/polonius/): how origin-based borrow checking works.

- [Rust Project Goals 2026](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/goals.html): lists "Stabilize and model Polonius Alpha".

- [std::cell module docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/index.html): interior mutability with `Cell` and `RefCell`.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter B2: Ownership & Move Semantics](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_ownership), [Chapter B3: Borrowing & References (&T vs &mut T)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_borrowing), [Chapter B10: Lifetimes Explained for JS Devs](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_lifetimes), [Chapter 2: Shared State with Arc<T> vs Global Singletons](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/state_singleton), [Chapter 10: Smart Pointers: Box, Rc, Arc & RefCell](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/smart_pointers), [Chapter 11: Interior Mutability: Cell, RefCell, Mutex & RwLock](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/interior_mutability), [Chapter 32: Atomics & Hardware Memory Ordering](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/atomics_memory_ordering)

## Appendix 2: Async Rust & Tokio Runtime

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio

Appendix 02 • Concurrency Deep Dive

### Node.js libuv vs Tokio Multi-Threaded Runtime

Understanding poll-based futures, work-stealing executors, cooperative scheduling, and cancellation safety in async Rust.

#### Key takeaways

- Node.js runs all JavaScript on one thread, while Tokio's default multi-thread runtime runs async tasks on one worker thread per CPU core and moves tasks between workers by work-stealing.

- Rust futures are lazy: nothing runs until the future is awaited or spawned, unlike a JavaScript Promise whose executor runs immediately.

- Blocking calls such as `std::thread::sleep` inside an async task stall every other task on that worker thread; use `tokio::time::sleep`, `tokio::fs`, or `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` instead.

- Tokio gives each task a budget of 128 operations per scheduling tick on its own sockets, timers and channels, but a CPU loop with no `.await` never yields.

- `tokio::select!` drops the branches that lose, so only cancellation-safe operations such as `mpsc::Receiver::recv` are safe to race in a loop.

##### 🟢 Node.js (libuv + V8)

- **Single-threaded JS Engine:** User JavaScript executes on one V8 thread (per isolate; worker threads get their own).

- **libuv Threadpool:** File I/O, `dns.lookup`, and some async crypto (e.g. `pbkdf2`, `scrypt`) run on a pool that defaults to 4 threads (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`).

- **Callback Queues:** Resolved Promises queue microtasks; timers and I/O callbacks run in the event loop phases.

- **Event loop starvation:** CPU-heavy work on the main thread blocks all HTTP routing and I/O handlers until it finishes.

- **Eager Promises:** A Promise's executor runs synchronously the moment the Promise is created.

##### 🦀 Rust (Tokio)

- **Work-Stealing Multi-Threading:** By default one worker thread per CPU core; idle workers steal queued tasks from busy ones (see Tokio's 2019 post "Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster").

- **OS I/O Multiplexing:** Non-blocking network I/O driven by `mio` (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows).

- **Pull-based Futures:** Futures are lazy state machines; the executor polls them, and a `Waker` tells it when a pending future is ready to be polled again.

- **Separate Blocking Pool:** `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` runs blocking work on a separate pool (default cap 512 threads). `tokio::fs` uses this pool internally.

- **Task Budgets:** Tokio's own resources make a task yield after 128 operations per tick so one busy task cannot hog a worker.

#### The Cardinal Rule of Tokio

Do not call synchronous blocking code inside an async function.

`std::thread::sleep` or synchronous file I/O blocks the OS thread running the Tokio worker, so every other task queued on that worker waits until the call returns.

Use non-blocking equivalents (`tokio::time::sleep`, `tokio::fs`) or offload with `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. Runtime shape is set on the entry point:

```
// Multi-thread runtime pinned to 4 workers (the default is one worker per CPU core)
#[tokio::main(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 4)]
async fn main() {
    let hash = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| expensive_hash(b"password"))
        .await
        .expect("blocking task panicked");
    println!("{hash}");
}

// Single-threaded alternative, closest to Node's model:
// #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
```

#### Cooperative Multitasking & tokio::task::yield_now()

Node.js developers use `setImmediate()` to break up long-running loops so the event loop can service I/O. Tokio tasks are also cooperative: there is no preemption, and a task only gives up its worker thread at an `.await` that returns `Pending`. A tight CPU loop without such a point starves other tasks on the same worker.

**The Solution:** Call `tokio::task::yield_now().await` inside long-running async loops. This returns control to the scheduler, which re-queues the current task behind other pending tasks.

```
use tokio::task;

async fn process_large_dataset(chunks: Vec<Chunk>) {
    for (i, chunk) in chunks.into_iter().enumerate() {
        process_chunk(chunk);

        // Cooperatively yield every 100 iterations:
        if i % 100 == 99 {
            task::yield_now().await;
        }
    }
}
```

*Note:* Tokio's automatic co-op budget (128 operations per tick, introduced in Tokio 0.2.14) only applies to Tokio resources such as sockets, timers and channels. Plain CPU loops need manual yields, or better, `spawn_blocking` or a dedicated thread pool such as rayon for heavy compute.

#### tokio::select! & Cancellation Safety

In JavaScript, `Promise.race([a, b])` lets the losing promise keep running in the background. In Tokio, `tokio::select!` uses **drop-based cancellation**: when one branch completes, the other branch futures are dropped, running their `Drop` code. Their work stops at whatever `.await` point they had reached.

Tokio's docs define a method as **cancellation-safe** if, when it is used as a branch of `select!` in a loop and another branch completes first, no data is lost.

| Safety Category | Methods & Operations | Why / Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ✅ Cancellation Safe | `AsyncReadExt::read`; `mpsc::Receiver::recv`; `tokio::time::sleep`; `tokio::net::TcpListener::accept` | Either the operation completed and returned its data, or it consumed nothing. Calling it again on the next loop iteration loses nothing. |
| ❌ Cancellation Unsafe | `AsyncReadExt::read_exact`; `AsyncWriteExt::write_all`; `AsyncBufReadExt::read_line`; `tokio::sync::Mutex::lock` | **Data loss hazard:** If cancelled midway, bytes already read are lost, or you cannot tell how many bytes were written. `Mutex::lock` loses no data but loses its place in the fair wait queue. |

###### Idiomatic Handling for Non-Cancellation-Safe Operations:

For operations like `write_all`, dropping the future midway leaves the stream partly written. Move the write into its own spawned task and race a channel against a `CancellationToken` (from `tokio-util`); the spawned task finishes the write even if you stop waiting:

```
use tokio::io::AsyncWriteExt;
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;

let (tx, rx) = tokio::sync::oneshot::channel();
tokio::spawn(async move {
    let res = writer.write_all(&payload).await;
    let _ = tx.send(res);
});

tokio::select! {
    res = rx => { /* write finished: res is Result<io::Result<()>, RecvError> */ }
    _ = cancel_token.cancelled() => { /* stop waiting; the write is not torn midway */ }
}
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Tokio the Rust equivalent of the Node.js event loop?**

A: Yes, Tokio plays the role of libuv: it drives I/O readiness from the OS and schedules async tasks. The difference is that Tokio's default runtime runs tasks on several worker threads at once, while Node runs all JavaScript on one thread. `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]` gives a single-threaded runtime closer to Node's model.

**Q: Why does my Rust async function not run when I call it?**

A: Rust futures are lazy, so calling an async function only builds a future and does nothing until it is awaited or passed to `tokio::spawn`. This differs from JavaScript, where a Promise starts work as soon as it is created. The compiler warns about unused futures with "futures do nothing unless you .await or poll them".

**Q: What happens if I call blocking code in a Tokio async function?**

A: The blocking call occupies the worker thread, so every other task scheduled on that worker waits until it returns. Use async versions such as `tokio::time::sleep` and `tokio::fs`, or move the work to `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, which runs it on a separate thread pool capped at 512 threads by default.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of Promise.race?**

A: `tokio::select!` waits on several futures and runs the branch of the first one to finish. Unlike `Promise.race`, the losing futures are dropped and stop running. Only race cancellation-safe operations, such as `mpsc::Receiver::recv`, inside a loop.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of setImmediate for long loops?**

A: `tokio::task::yield_now().await` hands control back to the Tokio scheduler so other tasks can run, then resumes the current task later. For heavy CPU work, `spawn_blocking` or a rayon thread pool is usually a better fit than sprinkling yields.

#### Sources and further reading

- [Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster (Tokio blog, 2019)](https://tokio.rs/blog/2019-10-scheduler): design of the work-stealing scheduler.

- [Reducing tail latencies with automatic cooperative task yielding (Tokio blog, 2020)](https://tokio.rs/blog/2020-04-preemption): the 128-operation task budget.

- [tokio::select! docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/macro.select.html): the official list of cancellation-safe and unsafe methods.

- [tokio::task::spawn_blocking docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html): blocking pool behaviour and the default thread cap.

- [The Node.js Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick): event loop phases, `setImmediate` and `process.nextTick`.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 4: HTTP Client: fetch / axios vs reqwest](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/reqwest_client), [Chapter 19: BullMQ vs Redis Streams in Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/redis_queues), [Chapter 21: Promise.all vs tokio::join! & tokio::spawn](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/tokio_spawn), [Chapter 22: Promise.race vs tokio::select!](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/select_race), [Chapter 23: AbortController vs CancellationToken](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/cancellation_tokens), [Chapter 25: Channels: mpsc, broadcast, watch & oneshot](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/channels_sync), [Chapter P1: Fearless Concurrency & Send / Sync](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_fearless_concurrency)

## Appendix 3: Cargo vs npm Architecture Guide

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cargo-vs-npm

Appendix 03 • Package Management

### Cargo vs npm / pnpm

Additive feature flags, duplicate dependency handling without node_modules, workspace inheritance, pre-1.0 SemVer rules, and release profiles.

#### Key takeaways

- Cargo is the Rust build tool and package manager in one: `cargo add`, `cargo check`, `cargo build --release`, `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` cover what npm scripts, tsc, a bundler, a test runner and ESLint do in a Node.js project.

- Cargo resolves all SemVer-compatible requirements for a crate to one version, and builds two copies of a crate only when the requirements are SemVer-incompatible, such as `0.9` and `1.0`.

- Cargo features are additive: when several crates in the dependency graph enable different features of the same dependency, Cargo compiles that dependency once with the union of those features.

- In Cargo.toml a bare version such as `"0.2.3"` means the caret range `^0.2.3`, which allows `0.2.x` updates but not `0.3.0`, while the same string in package.json pins an exact version.

- Release builds already use `opt-level = 3`; `lto`, `codegen-units = 1`, `strip` and `panic = "abort"` trade longer compile times or different panic behaviour for smaller or faster binaries.

#### 1. Rosetta Stone: Core CLI Workflow

| Node.js / npm | Rust / Cargo | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `npm init -y` | `cargo init` / `cargo new <name>` | Initialize new project |
| `npm install <pkg>` | `cargo add <crate>` | Add dependency to Cargo.toml |
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | `cargo check` | Type & borrow check without generating machine code |
| `npm run build` | `cargo build --release` | Compile optimized machine code |
| `npm test` | `cargo test` | Run unit & integration tests |
| `npx eslint .` | `cargo clippy` | Run the official linter |

#### 2. How Cargo Solves the node_modules Problem

In Node.js, conflicting version ranges are resolved by nesting extra copies of a package inside `node_modules`, so the same package can be installed and loaded several times. Cargo has no `node_modules`: crate sources live in the shared `~/.cargo/registry` cache and compiled artifacts go to the project's `target/` directory. The resolver picks a single version for all SemVer-compatible requirements (for example `^1.0.100` and `^1.0.190` resolve to one `1.0.x`). Only SemVer-incompatible requirements (e.g. `serde 1.0` and `serde 0.9`) produce two copies, which are linked side by side with distinct mangled symbols.

The catch: types from the two copies are different types. Passing a value built with `serde 0.9` where `serde 1.0` traits are expected fails to compile with a confusing "expected X, found X" error. `cargo tree --duplicates` (`cargo tree -d`) lists every crate built more than once, similar to `npm ls <pkg>`.

#### 3. Additive Feature Flags & Opt-Out (default-features = false)

In Rust, crate capabilities are gated behind compile-time feature flags. Features are **additive**: if crate A depends on `serde` with `features = ["derive"]` and crate B depends on it without, Cargo compiles `serde` once with the union of both feature sets. With resolver version 2 or later (the default since edition 2021), features enabled only by build-dependencies, proc-macros, dev-dependencies or other target platforms are not merged into your normal build. To drop features you don't need, declare `default-features = false` and list the ones you want:

```
[dependencies]
# reqwest 0.13 defaults: default-tls (rustls), charset, http2, system-proxy.
# Keep only rustls TLS and the JSON helpers:
reqwest = { version = "0.13", default-features = false, features = ["rustls", "json"] }
# no_std use: drop the default "std" feature, keep heap types:
serde = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

#### 4. Cargo Workspaces & Dependency Inheritance

Similar to pnpm workspaces, Cargo workspaces manage multiple crates with one shared `Cargo.lock` and one `target/` directory. Versions declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]` are inherited with `workspace = true`:

```
# Root Cargo.toml
[workspace]
members = ["crates/api", "crates/auth", "crates/db"]
resolver = "3"   # edition 2024 default (Rust 1.84+); a virtual workspace without it falls back to "1"

[workspace.dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
tracing = "0.1"

# crates/api/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
tokio = { workspace = true }
serde = { workspace = true }
```

#### 5. SemVer Quirks: Pre-1.0 Versions in Cargo vs npm

Cargo's caret rules for `0.x` match npm's `^` rules. The difference for Node.js engineers is the default: in `Cargo.toml` a bare `"0.2.3"` means `^0.2.3`, while a bare `"0.2.3"` in `package.json` is an exact pin. Write `"=0.2.3"` for an exact pin in Cargo. Ranges per The Cargo Book, "Specifying Dependencies":

| Declared Version | Cargo Permitted Range | Breaking Change Point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"1.2.3"` (or `"^1.2.3"`) | `>= 1.2.3, < 2.0.0` | Bump to `2.0.0` |
| `"0.2.3"` | `>= 0.2.3, < 0.3.0` | Bump to `0.3.0`: **minor bumps are breaking in 0.x** |
| `"0.0.3"` | `>= 0.0.3, < 0.0.4` | Bump to `0.0.4`: **every patch bump is breaking in 0.0.x** |

#### 6. Production Build Profiles & LTO Optimization

In Node.js, minification with esbuild/terser trims bundle size. In Rust, `[profile.release]` in `Cargo.toml` controls optimization level, cross-crate inlining (LTO) and symbol stripping. `cargo build --release` already uses `opt-level = 3`, and since Rust 1.77 it strips debuginfo by default when `debug` is off. The settings below can shrink the binary further at the cost of compile time; measure the effect on your own crate with `ls -lh target/release/<bin>`:

```
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3        # Already the release default; "s" or "z" optimize for size
lto = "thin"         # Link-Time Optimization across crates ("fat" / true: slower, more thorough)
codegen-units = 1    # One codegen unit: slower compile, more inlining opportunities
panic = "abort"      # No unwinding tables; a panic in any thread or Tokio task ends the process
strip = true         # Strip symbols as well as debuginfo (same as "symbols")
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Cargo equivalent of npm install?**

A: `cargo add <crate>` adds a dependency to Cargo.toml, like `npm install <pkg>`. A fresh clone needs no separate install step: `cargo build` or `cargo check` downloads and compiles everything listed in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock. `cargo install <crate>` is for command-line tools, similar to `npm install -g`.

**Q: Does Rust have a node_modules folder?**

A: No. Cargo downloads crate sources into a shared cache under `~/.cargo/registry` and writes compiled output to the project's `target/` directory. Rust dependencies are statically linked into the final binary by default, so the binary is the only build artifact that needs to ship.

**Q: Should I commit Cargo.lock like package-lock.json?**

A: Yes. The Cargo Book recommends committing Cargo.lock for applications and, since 2023, for libraries as well. Cargo ignores a library's lockfile when that library is used as a dependency, the same way npm ignores a dependency's package-lock.json.

**Q: Why doesn't cargo update move my 0.x dependency to the next minor version?**
