A: Cargo treats `0.2` to `0.3` as a breaking change. A requirement of `"0.2.3"` means `>=0.2.3, <0.3.0`, so `cargo update` stays within `0.2.x`. Change the version in Cargo.toml, or run `cargo add <crate>@0.3`, to move to the next minor release.

**Q: What are Cargo features compared to optional npm packages?**

A: Cargo features are compile-time switches declared by a crate that turn on optional code and optional dependencies. They are additive: Cargo compiles each dependency once with the union of features requested anywhere in the graph. npm has no direct equivalent; the closest patterns are optional peer dependencies and separate entry points.

#### Sources and further reading

- [The Cargo Book: Specifying Dependencies](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html): caret requirements and the 0.x / 0.0.x ranges.

- [The Cargo Book: Features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html): feature unification and `default-features = false`.

- [The Cargo Book: Dependency Resolution](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/resolver.html): unification of SemVer-compatible versions and resolver versions 2 and 3.

- [The Cargo Book: Workspaces](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html): shared Cargo.lock and `[workspace.dependencies]` inheritance.

- [The Cargo Book: Profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html): release defaults for `opt-level`, `lto`, `codegen-units`, `panic` and `strip`.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 27: SIMD Vectorization & Zero-Cost Abstractions](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/simd_optimization), [Chapter 33: Macros: Declarative vs Procedural Macros](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/procedural_macros)

## Appendix 4: Production Axum Microservice

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice

Appendix 04 • Microservice Blueprint

### Production Axum 0.8 Microservice Architecture

From Express & Mongoose to Axum, Tower Middleware, Sub-State Extractors, SQLx Pooling, and Graceful SIGTERM/SIGINT Shutdown.

#### Key takeaways

- Axum 0.8 route paths use `/{id}` for parameters and `/{*rest}` for wildcards; the 0.7 syntax `/:id` panics when the route is registered.

- An Axum 0.8 server binds a `tokio::net::TcpListener` and runs `axum::serve(listener, app)`; `.with_graceful_shutdown(signal)` stops accepting connections and waits for in-flight requests.

- Axum shares dependencies through the `State<T>` extractor and `Router::with_state`; implementing `FromRef` lets a handler extract only one field of the app state, such as the database pool.

- In an Axum handler, extractors that read only request metadata (`Path`, `Query`, `State`, `HeaderMap`) can appear in any order, but at most one body extractor (`Json`, `String`, `Bytes`) is allowed and it must be the last argument.

- SQLx's `Pool::close().await` rejects new acquires, closes idle connections and waits until checked-out connections are released and closed, so calling it after the HTTP server stops gives PostgreSQL a clean disconnect.

#### Canonical Project Layout

```
my-axum-service/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs            # Entry point: TCP bind, router setup, signal listener & pool draining
│   ├── state.rs           # AppState & FromRef sub-states (DB pool, config)
│   ├── error.rs           # AppError enum -> IntoResponse implementation
│   └── routes/
│       ├── mod.rs         # pub mod health; pub mod users;
│       ├── health.rs      # GET /healthz
│       └── users.rs       # POST /api/users, GET /api/users?page=&limit=, GET /api/users/{id}
└── tests/
    └── api_tests.rs       # tower::ServiceExt::oneshot or reqwest integration tests
```

```
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
axum = "0.8"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
tower-http = { version = "0.6", features = ["trace"] }
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = "0.3"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
sqlx = { version = "0.8", features = ["runtime-tokio", "postgres", "uuid"] }
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v4", "serde"] }
```

#### 1. Entrypoint & Graceful Shutdown with Pool Draining

Axum 0.7 removed `axum::Server` in favour of a `tokio::net::TcpListener` passed to `axum::serve()`, and 0.8 keeps that API. Axum 0.8 changed path syntax: parameters are written `/{id}` and wildcards `/{*rest}`. Graceful shutdown listens for both `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C) and Unix `SIGTERM`, which Kubernetes sends before a pod is killed (followed by `SIGKILL` once `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, 30 seconds by default, runs out). Once the HTTP server has finished in-flight requests, the application awaits `db.close().await` so PostgreSQL connections are closed cleanly before the process exits.

```
// src/main.rs
use axum::{routing::{get, post}, Router};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tower_http::trace::TraceLayer;

mod error;
mod routes;
mod state;

use state::AppState;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // 1. Initialize structured logging
    tracing_subscriber::fmt::init();

    // 2. Build shared application state (cheap to clone: the pool is an Arc inside)
    let state = AppState::new().await?;

    // 3. Assemble routes with State and Tower middleware (Axum 0.8 path syntax)
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/healthz", get(routes::health::check))
        .route("/api/users", post(routes::users::create_user).get(routes::users::list_users))
        .route("/api/users/{id}", get(routes::users::get_user))
        .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
        .with_state(state.clone());

    // 4. Bind a Tokio TCP listener
    let addr = "0.0.0.0:3000";
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(addr).await?;
    tracing::info!("Listening on {}", addr);

    // 5. Serve until SIGINT / SIGTERM, then wait for in-flight requests
    axum::serve(listener, app)
        .with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())
        .await?;

    // 6. Close the pool: closes idle connections, waits for checked-out ones to be released
    tracing::info!("Draining PostgreSQL connection pool...");
    state.db.close().await;
    tracing::info!("PostgreSQL pool closed. Server shutdown complete.");

    Ok(())
}

async fn shutdown_signal() {
    let ctrl_c = async {
        tokio::signal::ctrl_c()
            .await
            .expect("failed to install Ctrl+C handler");
    };

    #[cfg(unix)]
    let terminate = async {
        let mut sig = tokio::signal::unix::signal(tokio::signal::unix::SignalKind::terminate())
            .expect("failed to install SIGTERM handler");
        sig.recv().await;
    };

    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    let terminate = std::future::pending::<()>();

    tokio::select! {
        _ = ctrl_c => tracing::info!("Received SIGINT (Ctrl+C), draining HTTP connections..."),
        _ = terminate => tracing::info!("Received SIGTERM, draining HTTP connections..."),
    }
}
```

#### 2. Dependency Injection: State, FromRef & Extractor Ordering Rules

Unlike Express's untyped `req.app.locals`, Axum injects dependencies through typed extractors. Implement `FromRef` (or `#[derive(FromRef)]` with the `macros` feature) so handlers can extract only the sub-state they need.

**Extractor Ordering Rule:**

Extractors implementing `FromRequestParts` (e.g. `Path`, `Query`, `State`, `HeaderMap`) read only request metadata and may appear in any order.

An extractor implementing only `FromRequest` consumes the request body (e.g. `Json`, `String`, `Bytes`), so a handler can have at most one and it **must be the last argument**. Breaking this rule produces a compile error saying the handler function does not implement `Handler<_, _>`; add `#[axum::debug_handler]` to the function to get a message that names the offending argument.

```
// src/state.rs
use axum::extract::FromRef;
use sqlx::{Pool, Postgres, postgres::PgPoolOptions};

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct AppState {
    pub db: Pool<Postgres>,
}

impl AppState {
    pub async fn new() -> Result<Self, sqlx::Error> {
        let db_url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL").expect("DATABASE_URL must be set");
        let db = PgPoolOptions::new()
            .max_connections(20)
            .connect(&db_url)
            .await?;
        Ok(Self { db })
    }
}

// Enables handlers to extract State(db): State<Pool<Postgres>> directly
impl FromRef<AppState> for Pool<Postgres> {
    fn from_ref(app_state: &AppState) -> Self {
        app_state.db.clone()
    }
}
```

```
// src/error.rs
use axum::{http::StatusCode, response::{IntoResponse, Response}};

pub enum AppError {
    NotFound(String),
    Database(sqlx::Error),
}

// Lets handlers use `?` on SQLx calls
impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError {
    fn from(err: sqlx::Error) -> Self {
        AppError::Database(err)
    }
}

impl IntoResponse for AppError {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        match self {
            AppError::NotFound(msg) => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, msg).into_response(),
            AppError::Database(err) => {
                tracing::error!(error = %err, "database error");
                (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "internal server error").into_response()
            }
        }
    }
}

// src/routes/health.rs
pub async fn check() -> &'static str {
    "ok"
}
```

```
// src/routes/users.rs
use axum::{
    extract::{Path, Query, State},
    http::StatusCode,
    Json,
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use sqlx::{Pool, Postgres};
use uuid::Uuid;
use crate::error::AppError;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
pub struct CreateUserPayload {
    pub email: String,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
pub struct PaginationQuery {
    #[serde(default = "default_page")]
    pub page: u32,
    #[serde(default = "default_limit")]
    pub limit: u32,
}

fn default_page() -> u32 { 1 }
fn default_limit() -> u32 { 20 }

#[derive(Serialize, sqlx::FromRow)]
pub struct UserResponse {
    pub id: Uuid,
    pub email: String,
}

// POST /api/users
// ORDER RULE: State (request parts) first. Json (body consumer) is LAST.
pub async fn create_user(
    State(db): State<Pool<Postgres>>,
    Json(payload): Json<CreateUserPayload>, // Consumes the request body
) -> Result<(StatusCode, Json<UserResponse>), AppError> {
    let user = sqlx::query_as::<_, UserResponse>(
        "INSERT INTO users (id, email) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id, email"
    )
    .bind(Uuid::new_v4())
    .bind(&payload.email)
    .fetch_one(&db)
    .await?;

    Ok((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(user)))
}

// GET /api/users?page=1&limit=20
// Query and State both implement FromRequestParts, so their order is free
pub async fn list_users(
    Query(pagination): Query<PaginationQuery>,
    State(db): State<Pool<Postgres>>,
) -> Result<Json<Vec<UserResponse>>, AppError> {
    let limit = pagination.limit.clamp(1, 100) as i64; // cap client-supplied page size
    let offset = (pagination.page.max(1) as i64 - 1) * limit;
    let users = sqlx::query_as::<_, UserResponse>(
        "SELECT id, email FROM users ORDER BY email LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2"
    )
    .bind(limit)
    .bind(offset)
    .fetch_all(&db)
    .await?;

    Ok(Json(users))
}

// GET /api/users/{id}
pub async fn get_user(
    Path(id): Path<Uuid>,
    State(db): State<Pool<Postgres>>,
) -> Result<Json<UserResponse>, AppError> {
    let user = sqlx::query_as::<_, UserResponse>(
        "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = $1"
    )
    .bind(id)
    .fetch_optional(&db)
    .await?
    .ok_or_else(|| AppError::NotFound("User not found".into()))?;

    Ok(Json(user))
}
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How do I write a route parameter like Express's /users/:id in Axum?**

A: In Axum 0.8, write `.route("/users/{id}", get(handler))` and read the value with `Path(id): Path<Uuid>` or another deserializable type. Catch-all segments use `/{*rest}`. The Express-style `/:id` syntax was used up to Axum 0.7 and panics at route registration in 0.8.

**Q: What replaced app.listen() and axum::Server in Axum?**

A: Bind a `tokio::net::TcpListener` and pass it with the router to `axum::serve(listener, app).await`. This API arrived in Axum 0.7 and is unchanged in 0.8. Chain `.with_graceful_shutdown(future)` to stop on a signal and let in-flight requests finish.

**Q: How do I share a database pool between Axum handlers?**

A: Put the pool in a `Clone` state struct, attach it with `Router::with_state(state)`, and extract it with `State<AppState>`. Implement `FromRef<AppState>` for the pool type if a handler should receive only the pool. SQLx's `Pool` is reference-counted internally, so cloning it is cheap.

**Q: Why does my Axum handler fail with "the trait Handler is not implemented"?**

A: The most common cause is a body extractor such as `Json` that is not the last argument, or two body extractors in one handler. Other causes are an argument type that is not an extractor or a return type that does not implement `IntoResponse`. Adding `#[axum::debug_handler]` to the function makes the compiler point at the exact argument.

**Q: Do I still need #[async_trait] for custom Axum extractors?**

A: No. Since Axum 0.8, `FromRequestParts` and `FromRequest` use native async functions in traits, so implementations are written without the `#[async_trait]` macro. Code migrated from 0.7 should remove the attribute.

#### Sources and further reading

- [Announcing axum 0.8.0 (Tokio blog)](https://tokio.rs/blog/2025-01-01-announcing-axum-0-8-0): the `/{param}` path syntax and removal of `#[async_trait]`.

- [Announcing axum 0.7.0 (Tokio blog)](https://tokio.rs/blog/2023-11-27-announcing-axum-0-7-0): `axum::serve` with `TcpListener` replacing `axum::Server`.

- [axum::extract documentation](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/extract/index.html): extractor ordering, `State` and `FromRef`.

- [sqlx::Pool documentation](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/struct.Pool.html): `Pool::close` semantics and cheap cloning.

- [tokio::signal documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/signal/index.html): `ctrl_c` and Unix `SIGTERM` handling.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 1: Express.js vs Axum Routing & Handlers](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/axum_api), [Chapter 2: Shared State with Arc<T> vs Global Singletons](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/state_singleton), [Chapter 3: Tower Middleware vs Express Middleware](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/tower_middleware), [Chapter 6: Environment Variables & Configuration](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/env_config), [Chapter 13: Prisma / TypeORM vs SQLx Compile-Time SQL](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/sqlx_compile_time), [Chapter 14: Connection Pools: pg.Pool vs sqlx::Pool](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/db_pool), [Chapter 18: MongoDB: Mongoose vs official mongodb crate](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/mongodb_driver), [Chapter 23: AbortController vs CancellationToken](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/cancellation_tokens), [Chapter 24: Error Architecture: anyhow vs thiserror](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/error_anyhow_thiserror), [Chapter 26: Graceful Shutdown & OS Signal Handling](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/graceful_shutdown)

## Appendix 5: Production Distroless Rust Dockerfile

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/docker

Appendix 05 • Containerization

### Production Multi-Stage Dockerfile & Binary Optimization

Build static binaries with cargo-chef caching, symbol stripping, MUSL cross-compilation, and distroless/scratch runtime containers.

#### Key takeaways

- A multi-stage Dockerfile compiles a Rust service in a full `rust` image and copies only the finished binary into a small runtime image, so the compiler and build cache never ship to production.

- cargo-chef caches dependency compilation in its own Docker layer: `cargo chef prepare` writes a recipe of the dependency graph and `cargo chef cook` builds only the dependencies, so source-only changes skip that layer.

- A Rust binary built against glibc on Debian 13 (trixie) runs on `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian13`, which provides glibc, libgcc, CA certificates and a `nonroot` user but no shell or package manager.

- Building for `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` produces a statically linked binary that can run in an empty `scratch` image, provided you also copy in CA certificates if the service makes TLS calls.

- For comparison, the official `node:22-slim` image is about 80 MB compressed on Docker Hub (amd64, October 2026) before any application code or node_modules are added.

#### 1. Multi-Stage Dockerfile with cargo-chef (glibc + Distroless)

This follows the pattern from the cargo-chef README: dependencies are compiled in a cached layer, then the binary is stripped and copied into Google Distroless. The builder and the runtime (`cc-debian13`) are both Debian 13 (trixie), so they share the same glibc version, which avoids "GLIBC_x.y not found" errors at startup. `latest-rust-1-trixie` tracks the newest stable Rust; pin a specific tag such as `latest-rust-1.NN-trixie` for reproducible builds.

```
# Stage 1: base image with Rust and cargo-chef preinstalled
FROM lukemathwalker/cargo-chef:latest-rust-1-trixie AS chef
WORKDIR /app

# Stage 2: compute the dependency recipe
FROM chef AS planner
COPY . .
RUN cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json

# Stage 3: build dependencies (cached layer), then the app
FROM chef AS builder
COPY --from=planner /app/recipe.json recipe.json
RUN cargo chef cook --release --recipe-path recipe.json
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release --bin server
# Remove the symbol table (same effect as strip = true in Cargo.toml)
RUN strip /app/target/release/server

# Stage 4: minimal runtime: glibc + libgcc + CA certs, no shell
FROM gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian13:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/target/release/server /app/server
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 3000
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"]
```

#### 2. Declarative Stripping in Cargo.toml

Instead of invoking the external `strip` utility in Docker, you can have Cargo strip symbols and enable link-time optimization through `[profile.release]`. Since Rust 1.77, release builds already strip debuginfo by default; `strip = true` also removes the symbol table. Check the result with `ls -lh target/release/server` rather than relying on a fixed percentage:

```
# Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3          # Release default; use "s" or "z" to optimize for size
lto = true             # Full ("fat") Link-Time Optimization across crates
codegen-units = 1      # Larger optimization scope at the cost of compile time
strip = true           # Strip symbols and debuginfo from the output binary
panic = "abort"        # No unwinding tables; any panic ends the whole process
```

#### 3. Static Binaries with MUSL (FROM scratch)

Rust's `*-linux-gnu` targets dynamically link to GNU libc (`glibc`). The `*-linux-musl` targets link **musl libc** statically by default, producing an executable with no shared-library dependencies that can run in an empty `scratch` image. `scratch` also has no CA certificates, timezone data or user database, so copy in what your service needs.

##### Common Target Triplets:

- `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`: 64-bit Linux (Intel/AMD)

- `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`: 64-bit Linux (ARM64 / AWS Graviton / Docker on Apple Silicon)

MUSL multi-stage Dockerfile:

```
# Build a statically linked binary for the musl target on Debian
FROM rust:1-trixie AS builder
# musl-tools provides musl-gcc for crates that compile C code
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends musl-tools musl-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app

RUN rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
COPY src ./src
RUN cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --bin server

# Empty base image: only the binary and the CA bundle
FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
COPY --from=builder /app/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/server /server
# Numeric UID: scratch has no /etc/passwd, and the default would be root
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 3000
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
```

**Note on OpenSSL & TLS:** Linking OpenSSL statically against musl is awkward, so prefer a `rustls`-based TLS stack (the default in reqwest 0.13) over `native-tls` / `openssl`. Either way the binary still needs trusted root certificates: copy the CA bundle as shown above, or compile them in with the `webpki-roots` crate.

**Note on allocator performance:** musl's built-in `malloc` is simpler than glibc's and can be slower under multi-threaded allocation load. Services built for musl often set a global allocator such as `mimalloc` or `tikv-jemallocator`; benchmark your own workload before and after.

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why are Rust Docker builds so slow compared to npm ci?**

A: Rust compiles every dependency from source, and a plain `COPY . .` followed by `cargo build` invalidates that work on every source change. cargo-chef fixes this by building dependencies from a recipe file in a separate layer that Docker reuses until Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock change. BuildKit cache mounts for `~/.cargo/registry` and `target/` are an alternative.

**Q: Which base image should I use to run a Rust binary?**

A: For a glibc build from a Debian 13 (trixie) builder, use `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian13:nonroot`, which includes glibc, libgcc and CA certificates and runs as a non-root user. For a static musl build, `scratch` works if you copy in CA certificates yourself. Use `debian:trixie-slim` instead if you need a shell for debugging.

**Q: Do I need node_modules or a runtime in the final Rust image?**

A: No. Rust crates are compiled into the executable, so the runtime image needs only the binary plus any system libraries it links dynamically (glibc for `-gnu` targets, nothing for static musl builds). There is no interpreter or package directory to copy.

**Q: Why does my Rust binary fail with "GLIBC_2.xx not found" in Docker?**

A: The binary was built against a newer glibc than the runtime image provides. Build and run on the same Debian release, for example a `-trixie` builder with `distroless/cc-debian13`, or build for a musl target to remove the glibc dependency entirely.

**Q: Should I use musl or glibc for a Rust container?**

A: glibc on a distroless image is the simpler default and avoids musl's slower allocator under multi-threaded load. Choose musl when you want a fully static binary for `scratch` or for running on any Linux distribution, and pair it with rustls and a faster allocator such as mimalloc.

#### Sources and further reading

- [cargo-chef README](https://github.com/LukeMathWalker/cargo-chef): the planner / cook pattern and the `latest-rust-<alias>` image tags.

- [GoogleContainerTools/distroless](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless): contents of the `cc` image and the `nonroot` tags.

- [The Cargo Book: Profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html): `strip`, `lto`, `codegen-units` and `panic` settings and their defaults.

- [rustc Platform Support](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/platform-support.html): the `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` and `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` targets.

- [Docker Docs: Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/): how `COPY --from` keeps build tools out of the final image.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 1: Express.js vs Axum Routing & Handlers](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/axum_api), [Chapter 6: Environment Variables & Configuration](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/env_config), [Chapter 30: FFI: Calling C Libraries from Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/foreign_function_interface), [Chapter 31: Custom Allocators: jemalloc & mimalloc](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/custom_allocators)

## Appendix 6: Testing & Mocking in Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/testing

Appendix 06 • Quality & Testing

### Testing & Mocking: Jest / Vitest vs Rust

Unit tests, external integration tests, serial database testing, and trait mocking with mockall.

#### Key takeaways

- Rust's test runner is built into Cargo: `cargo test` compiles and runs `#[test]` functions with no extra framework like Jest or Vitest.

- Unit tests live in a `#[cfg(test)]` module inside the source file and can call private functions; integration tests live in `tests/` and only see the crate's public API.

- Each file directly under `tests/` is compiled as its own crate, so shared helpers go in `tests/common/mod.rs` to avoid being run as a test file.

- Tests within one test binary run in parallel threads by default; `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` runs them one at a time, similar to `jest --runInBand`.

- Rust has no runtime module patching like `jest.mock()`; you put dependencies behind a trait and let `mockall` generate a mock type at compile time.

#### 1. Built-in Synchronous & Async Unit Tests

Unit tests live right inside your source files in a `#[cfg(test)]` module. They can access private functions and run in parallel threads by default. Async tests use `#[tokio::test]`, which builds a fresh single-threaded (`current_thread`) runtime per test; use `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]` when the code under test needs multiple workers.

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn test_sync_math() {
        assert_eq!(2 + 2, 4);
    }

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn test_async_fetch() {
        let result = async_query_user(1).await;
        assert!(result.is_ok());
    }
}
```

#### 2. External Integration Tests & Directory Convention

In Node.js, test runners search for `*.test.ts` anywhere. In Rust, Cargo compiles each file directly under `tests/` as an **independent external crate** that links your library crate (`src/lib.rs`). A binary-only crate with just `src/main.rs` cannot be imported this way. To share fixtures without Cargo treating them as standalone tests, use the `tests/common/mod.rs` convention from The Rust Book:

```
my_project/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs
│   └── main.rs
└── tests/
    ├── common/
    │   └── mod.rs          # Shared fixture module (NOT compiled as a test binary)
    └── integration_test.rs # Root test crate (tests only public APIs)
```

Shared helper in `tests/common/mod.rs`:

```
// tests/common/mod.rs
pub fn setup_test_db() -> String {
    // Spin up test db or create temporary schema
    "postgres://localhost:5432/test_db".to_string()
}
```

Integration test in `tests/integration_test.rs`:

```
// tests/integration_test.rs
use my_project::app; // Imported as an external crate
mod common;

#[tokio::test]
async fn test_create_user_flow() {
    let db_url = common::setup_test_db();
    let response = app::run_migration(&db_url).await;
    assert!(response.is_ok());
}
```

#### 3. Isolated Database Tests: --test-threads=1

Rust's built-in test harness runs the tests inside each test binary on multiple threads at once (by default one per available CPU). Cargo runs the separate test binaries (the lib, each `tests/*.rs` file) one after another. When tests share a database and truncate tables or depend on row counts, parallel tests inside one binary can clash and cause flaky failures.

To run tests serially in a single thread:

```
# Pass --test-threads to the test binary via Cargo
cargo test -- --test-threads=1

# Or run only integration tests serially:
cargo test --test integration_test -- --test-threads=1

# Alternatively, set the environment variable:
RUST_TEST_THREADS=1 cargo test
```

**Node.js Comparison:** In Jest, this is the equivalent of `jest --runInBand`; in Vitest, `vitest --no-file-parallelism`. In Rust, you can also use the `serial_test` crate (`#[serial]` attribute) to force only DB tests into serial execution while keeping pure unit tests parallel.

#### 4. Mocking Traits with mockall

JavaScript allows runtime module replacement (`jest.mock('./api')`, `vi.mock()`). In Rust, dependencies are abstracted behind traits, and `mockall` generates a mock implementation of the trait at compile time. In real code, write `#[cfg_attr(test, mockall::automock)]` so the mock only exists in test builds.

```
#[mockall::automock]
pub trait UserRepository {
    fn get_user(&self, id: u32) -> Result<String, &'static str>;
}

#[test]
fn test_service_with_mock() {
    let mut mock = MockUserRepository::new();
    mock.expect_get_user()
        .with(mockall::predicate::eq(42))
        .returning(|_| Ok("Alice".to_string()));

    assert_eq!(mock.get_user(42).unwrap(), "Alice");
}
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of Jest or Vitest?**

A: Rust's test harness is built into the compiler and Cargo, so `cargo test` replaces Jest or Vitest for most projects. Mark functions with `#[test]` and use `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` for assertions. Crates such as `mockall`, `serial_test` and the separate runner `cargo-nextest` add features on top.

**Q: Where do I put tests in a Rust project?**

A: Put unit tests in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block at the bottom of the source file they test, where they can reach private functions. Put integration tests in a top-level `tests/` directory, where each file is compiled as a separate crate that can only use your library's public API.

**Q: How do I test async functions in Rust?**

A: Annotate an `async fn` test with `#[tokio::test]`, which creates a Tokio runtime for that test and awaits the body. The default runtime is single-threaded; use `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]` if the code needs several worker threads.

**Q: How do I run Rust tests one at a time like jest --runInBand?**

A: Run `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`, or set `RUST_TEST_THREADS=1`. The flag goes after `--` because it is passed to the test binary, not to Cargo. To serialize only some tests, mark them with `#[serial]` from the `serial_test` crate.

**Q: How do I mock a dependency in Rust like jest.mock?**

A: Define the dependency as a trait, make your code accept any type implementing it, and add `#[cfg_attr(test, mockall::automock)]` to the trait. mockall then generates a `MockYourTrait` type where you set expectations with `expect_method().returning(...)`. Rust cannot swap modules at run time the way `jest.mock()` does.

#### Sources and further reading

- [The Rust Book: Test Organization](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch11-03-test-organization.html): unit vs integration tests and the `tests/common/mod.rs` convention.

- [The Cargo Book: cargo test](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html): test targets, `--test`, and passing flags to the harness.

- [tokio::test docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/attr.test.html): default `current_thread` runtime and the `flavor` option.

- [mockall docs](https://docs.rs/mockall/latest/mockall/): `automock`, expectations and predicates.

- [serial_test docs](https://docs.rs/serial_test/latest/serial_test/): the `#[serial]` attribute.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter B7: Result<T, E> & the '?' Operator](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_result), [Chapter B8: Traits & Explicit Contracts](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_traits), [Chapter 13: Prisma / TypeORM vs SQLx Compile-Time SQL](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/sqlx_compile_time), [Chapter 15: Transactions & RAII Rollback](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/db_transactions), [Chapter 33: Macros: Declarative vs Procedural Macros](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/procedural_macros)

## Appendix 7: AI & Autonomous Agents in Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/ai-agents

Appendix 07 • Artificial Intelligence

### Building AI Agents in Rust

Token streaming with Server-Sent Events (SSE) in Axum 0.8, typed tool definitions with rig-core, and local inference with Hugging Face Candle.

#### Key takeaways

- Axum streams LLM tokens to a browser with `axum::response::sse::Sse`, fed by a bounded `tokio::sync::mpsc` channel so a slow client applies backpressure to the producer.

- When an SSE client disconnects, Axum drops the response stream, the channel receiver is dropped, and the producer's next `send` returns an error it can use to stop generating.

- rig-core is an LLM client library for Rust; its 0.x releases change the API between minor versions, so pin the exact version and check docs.rs for that version before copying examples.

- In rig-core 0.44 a tool is a type implementing `PortableTool` (name, description, JSON Schema, async `call`), and the multi-turn agent loop that executes tool calls lives in the companion `rig-agent` crate.

- Candle is Hugging Face's Rust ML framework: it runs models on CPU without Python, and its optional `cuda` and `metal` features add GPU backends.

#### 1. Token Streaming Gateway (Axum 0.8 SSE)

Each open SSE connection in Axum is one Tokio task plus its socket buffers. The Tokio tutorial states that a task needs a single allocation and 64 bytes of memory on top of the size of its future, so the number of concurrent streams is usually limited by file descriptors, buffer memory and the upstream model API's rate limits rather than by the runtime. Node.js can also hold many idle SSE connections; the difference is that Tokio's multi-threaded scheduler spreads token parsing and fan-out across all CPU cores without `worker_threads`.

```
use axum::{
    response::sse::{Event, KeepAlive, Sse},
    routing::post,
    Json, Router,
};
use futures_util::stream::{Stream, StreamExt};
use serde::Deserialize;
use std::{convert::Infallible, time::Duration};
use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio_stream::wrappers::ReceiverStream;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
pub struct ChatRequest {
    pub prompt: String,
}

pub fn router() -> Router {
    Router::new().route("/chat", post(chat_stream_handler))
}

pub async fn chat_stream_handler(
    Json(req): Json<ChatRequest>,
) -> Sse<impl Stream<Item = Result<Event, Infallible>>> {
    // Bounded channel: the producer waits once 16 tokens are queued and unsent
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel::<String>(16);

    // Stand-in for a model call that yields tokens
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let _prompt = req.prompt;
        let tokens = ["Rust", " provides", " fearless", " concurrency", " for", " AI."];
        for token in tokens {
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
            // send fails once the client disconnects and Axum drops the stream
            if tx.send(token.to_string()).await.is_err() {
                break;
            }
        }
    });

    // Adapt the mpsc receiver into an SSE event stream
    let stream = ReceiverStream::new(rx).map(|token| Ok(Event::default().data(token)));

    Sse::new(stream).keep_alive(
        KeepAlive::new()
            .interval(Duration::from_secs(15))
            .text("keep-alive-ping"),
    )
}
```

The browser's `EventSource` API only sends GET requests. For a POST endpoint like this one, read the stream on the client with `fetch()` and `response.body.getReader()`, or switch the route to GET with query parameters.

#### 2. Typed Tool Definitions with rig-core

`rig-core` fills the role the Vercel AI SDK or LangChain.js fill in Node: one interface over many model providers. Tool arguments deserialize into a Rust struct with Serde, so a malformed tool call from the model becomes a typed error instead of an `undefined` field at runtime. The snippet below targets **rig-core 0.44** (library name `rig_core`) and uses only calls from that version's docs.rs pages. Older tutorials that use `impl Tool` with `definition()` and `client.agent(...).build()` describe earlier 0.x releases.

```
// Cargo.toml: rig-core = { version = "=0.44.0", features = ["reqwest"] }
use rig_core::{
    completion::CompletionRequest,
    providers::openai::{self, OpenAI},
    tool::{tool_definition, PortableTool},
};
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_json::json;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct SumArgs {
    a: f64,
    b: f64,
}

struct SumTool;

impl PortableTool for SumTool {
    const NAME: &'static str = "calculate_sum";
    type Args = SumArgs;
    type Output = f64;
    type Error = std::convert::Infallible;

    fn description(&self) -> String {
        "Calculates the sum of two numbers".to_string()
    }

    fn parameters(&self) -> serde_json::Value {
        json!({
            "type": "object",
            "properties": { "a": { "type": "number" }, "b": { "type": "number" } },
            "required": ["a", "b"]
        })
    }

    async fn call(&self, args: Self::Args) -> Result<Self::Output, Self::Error> {
        Ok(args.a + args.b)
    }
}

pub async fn ask_with_tool() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Reads OPENAI_API_KEY (and optional OPENAI_BASE_URL)
    let model = OpenAI::from_env()?.completion(openai::GPT_5_2);

    let request = CompletionRequest::new("What is 142.50 plus 391.25?")
        .tool(tool_definition(&SumTool));
    let response = model.call(request).await?;

    for call in response.tool_calls() {
        println!("tool {:?} args {:?}", call.function.name, call.function.arguments);
    }
    println!("{}", response.text());
    Ok(())
}
```

One request returns the model's tool calls; it does not run them. To execute the tool, append the result and call the model again, or use the `rig-agent` crate, which runs that loop for you.

#### 3. Local Inference without Python using Hugging Face Candle

Candle loads safetensors and quantized GGUF models inside your Rust process, with no Python runtime or ONNX export step. The CPU backend is pure Rust; the optional `cuda` and `metal` Cargo features add GPU backends, which call the vendor GPU libraries through FFI. The snippet targets **candle-core and candle-transformers 0.11**.

```
use candle_core::{Device, IndexOp, Tensor};
use candle_transformers::generation::LogitsProcessor;

// Falls back to the CPU only when the cuda/metal features are not compiled in; with the feature on but no GPU, this returns an error
pub fn select_device() -> candle_core::Result<Device> {
    let cuda = Device::cuda_if_available(0)?;
    if cuda.is_cuda() {
        return Ok(cuda);
    }
    Device::metal_if_available(0)
}

pub fn sample_next_token(
    logits: &Tensor,
    logits_processor: &mut LogitsProcessor,
) -> candle_core::Result<u32> {
    // Reduce to the last position's 1D [vocab_size] logits
    let next_token_logits = match logits.dims() {
        [_, seq_len, _] => logits.i((0, seq_len - 1))?, // [batch, seq, vocab]
        [_, _] => logits.i(0)?,                         // [batch, vocab]
        [_] => logits.clone(),                          // [vocab]
        dims => candle_core::bail!("unexpected logits shape: {dims:?}"),
    };

    // LogitsProcessor::new(seed, temperature, top_p) applies temperature and top-p
    logits_processor.sample(&next_token_logits)
}
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How do I stream OpenAI-style tokens to the browser from a Rust server?**

A: Return `Sse::new(stream)` from an Axum handler, where the stream yields `Result<Event, Infallible>`. A common pattern is to spawn the model call into a Tokio task that writes tokens into a bounded `mpsc` channel and wrap the receiver with `tokio_stream::wrappers::ReceiverStream`. Add `KeepAlive` so proxies do not close idle connections.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of the Vercel AI SDK or LangChain.js?**

A: rig-core is the closest match: it wraps many providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama and others) behind one completion interface and supports typed tool definitions. Its agent loop is in the separate `rig-agent` crate. The API is still 0.x and changes between minor versions, so pin the version you build against.

**Q: How do I stop generating tokens when the user closes the browser tab?**

A: Check the result of `tx.send(...).await` in the producer task and break when it returns an error. When the client disconnects, Axum drops the SSE response stream, which drops the channel receiver, so the next send fails. This is the Rust counterpart of listening for the request's `close` event in Node.js.

**Q: Can I run a local LLM in Rust without Python?**

A: Yes. Hugging Face Candle loads safetensors and GGUF weights and runs inference inside a Rust binary, and `candle-transformers` ships implementations of common model families. GPU support comes from the optional `cuda` or `metal` features; without them Candle runs on the CPU.

**Q: Why does EventSource not work with my POST streaming endpoint?**

A: The browser `EventSource` API only issues GET requests and cannot send a request body. For a POST chat endpoint, read the SSE stream with `fetch()` and `response.body.getReader()`, then parse the `data:` lines yourself.

#### Sources and further reading

- [axum::response::sse (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/response/sse/index.html): the `Sse`, `Event` and `KeepAlive` APIs used in section 1.

- [Tokio tutorial: Spawning](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/spawning): source for the single allocation and 64 bytes per task figure.

- [rig-core crate documentation (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/rig-core/latest/rig_core/): `PortableTool`, `CompletionRequest` and provider clients.

- [Rig repository (GitHub)](https://github.com/0xPlaygrounds/rig): examples, changelog and the companion `rig-agent` crate.

- [Candle repository (GitHub)](https://github.com/huggingface/candle): supported models, backends and feature flags.

- [MDN: Using server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events): the SSE wire format and `EventSource` behavior.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 4: HTTP Client: fetch / axios vs reqwest](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/reqwest_client), [Chapter 5: JSON Parsing: JSON.parse() vs Serde](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/serde_json)

## Appendix 8: Senior Rust Interview Q&A

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/interviews

Appendix 08 • Career Preparation

### Senior Systems Interview Q&A

Memory layout, async, locking and unsafe questions that come up in senior Rust systems interviews, with answers grounded in the Rust docs.

#### Key takeaways

- On a 64-bit target, `String` is 24 bytes on the stack (pointer, capacity, length) and `&str` is 16 bytes (pointer, length).

- `std::sync::MutexGuard` is `!Send`, so a future that holds it across `.await` cannot be passed to `tokio::spawn`.

- Local variables are dropped in reverse declaration order, while struct fields are dropped in declaration order.

- `unsafe` does not disable the borrow checker; it only allows five extra operations, such as dereferencing raw pointers and calling unsafe functions.

- Tokio's docs recommend `std::sync::Mutex` in async code for short critical sections, and `tokio::sync::Mutex` only when the guard must be held across `.await`.

##### Q1: What is the exact difference between String and &str in memory?

`String` is an owned, growable buffer of UTF-8 bytes stored on the heap. On a 64-bit target its stack footprint is 24 bytes: a pointer to the heap buffer, the capacity, and the current length. `&str` is a borrowed string slice of 16 bytes: a pointer to existing bytes and a length. A `&str` can point into a `String`'s heap buffer, a stack array, or static data compiled into the binary (string literals are `&'static str`).

##### Q2: Why does holding std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await point fail to compile with tokio::spawn?

`std::sync::MutexGuard` does **not** implement `Send`, because on some platforms (for example pthread mutexes) the lock must be released by the thread that acquired it. A future that holds the guard across `.await` stores it in its state, which makes the future `!Send`. `tokio::spawn` requires `Send` futures because the multi-threaded scheduler may resume a task on a different worker thread, so the compiler rejects it. The code compiles if the future is never required to be `Send`, but it can then deadlock. The idiomatic fix is to drop the guard before the `.await` by scoping it in a block, or to use `tokio::sync::Mutex` or message passing.

##### Q3: What is Pin<&mut T> and why is it essential for async Rust?

Async functions compile into state machines. When a local reference lives across an `.await` point, the state machine stores both the value and a reference to it, making it a **self-referential struct**. If it moved in memory after that, the stored reference would dangle. `Pin` wraps a pointer and guarantees that a value whose type is not `Unpin` will not move again until it is dropped, which is why `Future::poll` takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`.

##### Q4: When should you choose std::sync::Mutex vs tokio::sync::Mutex vs RwLock?

Use **`std::sync::Mutex`** for short in-memory critical sections that do not cross an `.await`; Tokio's shared-state tutorial says it is fine and often preferred in async code. Use **`tokio::sync::Mutex`** when the guard must be held across an `.await`, for example around an I/O resource; it is slower because locking is itself an async operation with a fair queue. Choose **`RwLock`** when reads clearly dominate and critical sections are long enough for parallel readers to matter. It does more bookkeeping than a `Mutex`, so measure before switching.

Additionally, `std::sync::Mutex` and `std::sync::RwLock` implement **Lock Poisoning**: if a thread panics while holding the lock, later calls return a `PoisonError` to warn about possibly corrupt state. `tokio::sync::Mutex` and `parking_lot::Mutex` do not poison on panic.

##### Q5: What is Rust's precise RAII drop order for variables and struct fields?

1. **Local variables** in a scope are dropped in *reverse declaration order* (last declared is dropped first).

2. **Struct fields** and tuple elements are dropped in *declaration order* (first field is dropped first).

3. Array and owned slice elements are dropped from the first element to the last.

4. A temporary is dropped at the end of its enclosing statement, and `let _ = value;` does not bind, so a temporary on the right side is dropped immediately.

##### Q6: What is a Fat Pointer in Rust and what are its memory dimensions?

A reference to a sized type (e.g. `&i32` or `&MyStruct`) is 1 word (8 bytes on a 64-bit target) pointing directly to the data. A **Fat Pointer** to a dynamically sized type is 2 words (16 bytes): a data pointer plus metadata:

• **Slices (`&[T]` or `&str`)**: the data pointer and the element count.

• **Trait Objects (`&dyn Trait`)**: the data pointer and a vtable pointer. The vtable holds the concrete type's size, alignment, drop glue, and the trait's method pointers. Its exact layout is not a stable, documented ABI.

##### Q7: What is undefined behavior (UB) in Rust and does unsafe turn off the borrow checker?

**No.** An `unsafe` block does NOT turn off type checking or the borrow checker for references. The Rust Book lists five extra abilities it grants: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions (including FFI), accessing or modifying mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and accessing fields of a union. Undefined behavior is any operation the language rules forbid, such as creating two live `&mut` references to the same data. The compiler optimizes on the assumption that UB never happens, so code containing UB can be miscompiled in ways that are hard to predict.

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between String and &str in Rust?**

A: `String` owns a growable heap buffer of UTF-8 bytes and is 24 bytes on the stack on 64-bit targets. `&str` is a borrowed view into UTF-8 bytes owned by something else and is 16 bytes. Take `&str` as a function parameter when you only need to read text.

**Q: Should I use std::sync::Mutex or tokio::sync::Mutex in async Rust?**

A: Use `std::sync::Mutex` unless you must hold the lock across an `.await`. Tokio's own tutorial recommends the standard mutex for short critical sections because it is cheaper. Use `tokio::sync::Mutex` only when the guard has to live across an `.await`.

**Q: Does unsafe Rust disable the borrow checker?**

A: No. The borrow checker still checks all references inside an `unsafe` block. `unsafe` only allows five extra operations, including dereferencing raw pointers and calling unsafe functions, and you become responsible for upholding the rules the compiler cannot check for those operations.

**Q: In what order does Rust drop variables and struct fields?**

A: Local variables are dropped in reverse order of declaration when their scope ends. Struct fields, tuple elements and array elements are dropped in forward order. The Rust Reference chapter on destructors defines these rules.

**Q: Why do Rust futures need Pin?**

A: An async function's state machine can hold references to its own fields across `.await` points, so moving it after polling starts would leave those references dangling. `Pin` guarantees a non-`Unpin` value stays at one address until it is dropped, which is why `Future::poll` takes `Pin<&mut Self>`.

#### Sources and further reading

- [std::sync::MutexGuard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.MutexGuard.html): the `!Send` implementation discussed in Q2.

- [Tokio tutorial: Shared state](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/shared-state): guidance on `std::sync::Mutex` versus `tokio::sync::Mutex`.

- [tokio::sync::Mutex (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html): no poisoning and when the async mutex is appropriate.

- [The Rust Reference: Destructors](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html): drop order for variables, fields, elements and temporaries.

- [std::pin module docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html): the pinning guarantee used by futures.

- [The Rust Book: Unsafe Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch20-01-unsafe-rust.html): the five unsafe superpowers.

## Appendix 9: Diagnostics, Profiling & Valgrind

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting

Appendix 09 • Diagnostics

### Diagnostics, Flamegraphs & Profiling

Compilation flags, profiler setup, and step-by-step workflows for finding CPU hot spots, async stalls, heap churn and undefined behavior in Rust services.

#### Key takeaways

- `cargo flamegraph` (install with `cargo install flamegraph`) records CPU stacks with perf on Linux and DTrace on macOS and writes an interactive `flamegraph.svg`.

- Release builds need `debug = true` under `[profile.release]`, or `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=true`, so flamegraphs show function names instead of raw addresses.

- Miri runs tests in an interpreter that detects many kinds of undefined behavior in `unsafe` code; install it with `rustup +nightly component add miri` and run `cargo +nightly miri test`.

- `tokio-console` shows live per-task poll times and wakeups, but the service must be built with `RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"` and must call `console_subscriber::init()`.

- The `dhat` crate swaps in a profiling global allocator and writes `dhat-heap.json` when its `Profiler` is dropped, which DHAT's online viewer can open.

#### Diagnostics & Profiling Rosetta Stone

How core Node.js diagnostic tooling maps directly to Rust systems profiling equivalents:

| Diagnostic Goal | Node.js Tooling | Rust Equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU Profiling / Flamegraphs | `0x`, `clinic flame`, `node --prof` | `cargo flamegraph` (perf / DTrace) |
| Event Loop / Async Starvation | `clinic bubbleprof`, `event-loop-lag` | `tokio-console` (Task tracing subscriber) |
| Heap Allocations & Churn | Chrome DevTools Heap Snapshot, `clinic heapprofiler` | `dhat-rs`, Valgrind `massif` |
| Memory Safety & UB | N/A (Managed VM) / ASan for C++ Addons | `cargo +nightly miri` (MIR interpreter) |

#### 1. CPU Flamegraph Profiling (cargo-flamegraph)

Generates interactive SVG call graphs (like `0x` or `clinic flame` in Node). Profile a release build with debug info enabled, otherwise inlined frames show as addresses. You can also set `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=true` for a single run instead of editing `Cargo.toml`.

Cargo.toml configuration:

```
[profile.release]
debug = true       # Retain DWARF symbols for function names (line numbers & symbols)
strip = false      # Do not strip symbol tables
```

Execution commands (use `--root` instead of running `sudo cargo` to avoid target/ permission corruption):

```
# Installation
cargo install flamegraph

# macOS (uses DTrace under the hood; --root elevates DTrace safely):
cargo flamegraph --root --bin my-service -- --port 8080

# Linux (uses perf; ensure perf events are unlocked or pass --root):
sudo sysctl -w kernel.perf_event_paranoid=-1
cargo flamegraph --bin my-service -- --port 8080

# Profile specific benchmark or integration test:
cargo flamegraph --test integration_tests -- test_throughput
```

#### 2. Undefined Behavior Detection (cargo miri)

Miri interprets Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) and reports undefined behavior it observes while running your tests: out-of-bounds and use-after-free accesses, invalid values, aliasing violations, data races, and memory leaks. It only checks code paths your tests execute, runs much slower than native code, and cannot execute most FFI calls, so keep Miri test cases small.

```
# Install nightly toolchain & Miri component
rustup +nightly component add miri

# Run test suite under Miri using toolchain override without polluting global default:
cargo +nightly miri test

# Run a specific binary:
cargo +nightly miri run --bin my-service

# Extra checks: Tree Borrows aliasing model, strict provenance, symbolic alignment:
MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-tree-borrows -Zmiri-strict-provenance -Zmiri-symbolic-alignment-check" cargo +nightly miri test

# Allow tests that read env vars, files or the clock (Miri isolates them by default):
MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-disable-isolation" cargo +nightly miri test
```

#### 3. Real-Time Async Task Tracing (tokio-console)

Inspect task scheduling starvation, blocked async worker threads, and channel backpressure live (equivalent to Node.js event-loop lag inspection and `clinic bubbleprof`).

```
// 1. Cargo.toml dependency:
// [dependencies]
// console-subscriber = "0.5"
// tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full", "tracing"] }

// 2. In src/main.rs: initialize before spawning the tasks you want to inspect.
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Sets the global tracing subscriber and serves gRPC on 127.0.0.1:6669
    // (override with TOKIO_CONSOLE_BIND) from its own background thread
    console_subscriber::init();

    tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
        .enable_all()
        .build()?
        .block_on(async {
            // ... rest of async service
            Ok(())
        })
}
```

```
# 3. Compile service with Tokio unstable flags enabled:
RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable" cargo run

# 4. In a separate terminal, launch the console TUI:
cargo install --locked tokio-console
tokio-console http://127.0.0.1:6669
```

#### 4. Memory Allocation & Heap Profiling (DHAT & Valgrind)

Track heap churn, short-lived allocations, and memory leaks down to the allocating stack frame. DHAT works on every platform because it lives inside your binary; Valgrind Massif needs Linux (or another Valgrind-supported OS) but requires no code changes.

```
// 1. Cargo.toml:
// [dependencies]
// dhat = { version = "0.3", optional = true }
// [features]
// dhat-heap = ["dep:dhat"]

// 2. In src/main.rs:
#[cfg(feature = "dhat-heap")]
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: dhat::Alloc = dhat::Alloc;

fn main() {
    #[cfg(feature = "dhat-heap")]
    let _profiler = dhat::Profiler::new_heap();

    // Application logic...
    // Writes `dhat-heap.json` when `_profiler` is dropped at the end of main
    // (not on std::process::exit or an aborting panic)
}
```

DHAT Profiling execution & inspection:

```
# Run binary with dhat-heap feature and release debug symbols:
cargo run --release --features dhat-heap

# Visualize results in the interactive DHAT web viewer:
# Open https://nnethercote.github.io/dh_view/dh_view.html and load `dhat-heap.json`
```

```
# Linux Valgrind Massif (Full Process Heap Profiler):
valgrind --tool=massif --pages-as-heap=yes --massif-out-file=massif.out target/release/my-service
ms_print massif.out
```

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of clinic flame or 0x?**

A: `cargo flamegraph` from the flamegraph-rs project is the closest equivalent. Install it with `cargo install flamegraph` and run `cargo flamegraph --bin <name>`; it uses perf on Linux and DTrace on macOS and writes `flamegraph.svg`. Enable `debug = true` in `[profile.release]` so frames have names.

**Q: Why does my Rust flamegraph show hex addresses instead of function names?**

A: The release profile does not include debug info by default, so the profiler has no symbol data for many frames. Add `debug = true` under `[profile.release]` or run with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=true`, and do not set `strip = true` for profiling builds.

**Q: How do I find what is blocking the Tokio runtime, like event loop lag in Node.js?**

A: Use tokio-console. Add the `console-subscriber` crate, call `console_subscriber::init()`, build with `RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"`, then run the `tokio-console` TUI. Tasks with long poll times are usually doing blocking or CPU-heavy work that belongs in `spawn_blocking`.

**Q: How do I check unsafe Rust code for undefined behavior?**

A: Run your tests under Miri with `cargo +nightly miri test` after installing it with `rustup +nightly component add miri`. Miri reports undefined behavior on the code paths the tests execute, such as use-after-free, out-of-bounds access and aliasing violations. Pass extra options through the `MIRIFLAGS` environment variable.

**Q: How do I take a heap profile of a Rust program, like a Chrome heap snapshot?**

A: Use the `dhat` crate: install `dhat::Alloc` as the global allocator behind a Cargo feature, create `dhat::Profiler::new_heap()` at the start of `main`, and open the resulting `dhat-heap.json` in DHAT's viewer. On Linux, Valgrind's Massif tool profiles the heap without code changes.

#### Sources and further reading

- [flamegraph-rs/flamegraph (GitHub)](https://github.com/flamegraph-rs/flamegraph): install, `--root`, perf and DTrace usage.

- [The Cargo Book: Profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html): `debug`, `strip` and the `CARGO_PROFILE_*` environment overrides.

- [rust-lang/miri (GitHub)](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri): installation, what Miri detects, and the `-Zmiri-*` flags.

- [tokio-rs/console (GitHub)](https://github.com/tokio-rs/console): console-subscriber setup and the `tokio_unstable` requirement.

- [dhat crate documentation (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/dhat/latest/dhat/): heap profiling setup and the viewer link.

- [Valgrind Massif manual](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/ms-manual.html): Massif options including `--pages-as-heap`.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter 12: Struct Memory Layout, Alignment & Padding](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/memory_alignment), [Chapter 27: SIMD Vectorization & Zero-Cost Abstractions](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/simd_optimization), [Chapter 28: NAPI-RS: Accelerating Node.js with Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/napi_rs), [Chapter 29: Unsafe Rust: When & How to Use It](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/unsafe_rust), [Chapter 30: FFI: Calling C Libraries from Rust](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/foreign_function_interface), [Chapter 31: Custom Allocators: jemalloc & mimalloc](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/custom_allocators), [Chapter P3: The Zero-Cost Abstraction Principle](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_zero_cost)

## Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy

Appendix 10 • Philosophy

### The Core Philosophy of Rust

Memory safety without a garbage collector, zero-cost abstractions, and data-race-free concurrency, with the conditions that make each one true.

#### Key takeaways

- Rust has no tracing garbage collector: each value has one owner, and its memory is freed at a point the compiler decides statically, when that owner goes out of scope.

- In safe Rust, the borrow checker rejects use-after-free, double free, dangling references and data races at compile time; memory leaks and deadlocks are not prevented.

- Rust iterator chains are lazy and allocate nothing until a method like `collect()` runs, while each JavaScript `map()` or `filter()` call builds a new array.

- The `Send` and `Sync` auto traits let the compiler refuse to move or share non-thread-safe values, such as `Rc<T>`, across threads.

- The typestate pattern encodes states like "authenticated" in the type, so calling a method in the wrong state is a compile error instead of a runtime check.

PILLAR 1

#### Safety: Compile-Time Ownership Over Tracing GC

Node.js relies on V8's generational garbage collector: a parallel Scavenger for the young generation and a Mark-Compact collector for the old generation, with concurrent marking from V8's Orinoco project. Orinoco shortens main-thread pauses but does not remove them, and a tracing collector needs heap headroom above the live data to run efficiently. When an object is actually freed is up to the collector, not your code.

Rust has no tracing GC. Ownership works like an **affine type system** (a value can be moved at most once), and RAII runs a value's `Drop` at a known point: when its owner goes out of scope. Freeing still costs time, but you can see where it happens. Borrow rules enforce `aliasing XOR mutability`: at any moment you hold either any number of shared references `&T` or exactly one exclusive reference `&mut T`, never both. In safe Rust this rejects use-after-free, double free, dangling references and iterator invalidation at compile time. It does not prevent leaks: an `Rc` cycle or `std::mem::forget` is safe code that never frees memory.

PILLAR 2

#### Speed: The Zero-Cost Abstraction Principle

Rust adopts Bjarne Stroustrup's zero-overhead principle as a design goal: *"What you don't use, you don't pay for. And further: What you do use, you couldn't hand code any better."* It is a goal the compiler usually meets for iterators and generics, not a guarantee for every program.

In TypeScript, `arr.map(f).filter(g)` builds a new intermediate array at each step. In Rust, `iter().map(f).filter(g)` is lazy: no collection is allocated until `collect()`, and closures are plain values, not heap objects. Through **monomorphization** and inlining, LLVM typically compiles such a chain to the same machine code as a hand-written loop, and can auto-vectorize it when bounds checks are proven unnecessary. The Rust Book's "Comparing Performance: Loops vs. Iterators" section shows this with a benchmark.

PILLAR 3

#### Fearless Concurrency: The Send & Sync Auto Traits

In Node.js, your JavaScript runs on one event loop thread per isolate. Some blocking work (file system, DNS lookup, crypto, zlib) goes to libuv's thread pool, which has 4 threads by default and can be resized with `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`. `worker_threads` give you more JS threads, but objects are copied between them by structured clone; shared mutable memory is limited to `SharedArrayBuffer` with manual `Atomics` synchronization.

Rust lets threads share typed memory, and safe Rust cannot express a data race. Two auto traits do the work; the compiler implements them for a type automatically when all its fields implement them:

- `Send`: ownership of the value can be transferred to another thread.

- `Sync`: the value can be shared by reference across threads. Formally, `T` is `Sync` exactly when `&T` is `Send`.

Passing non-thread-safe state such as `Rc<RefCell<T>>` to `std::thread::spawn` fails to compile with error E0277, which says the type cannot be sent between threads safely. The thread-safe version is `Arc<Mutex<T>>`. These guarantees cover data races only: deadlocks and higher-level race conditions (for example, check-then-act bugs) are still possible.

PILLAR 4

#### Correctness: The Typestate Pattern & Parse, Don't Validate

In JavaScript, invalid states are usually caught by runtime checks (e.g. `if (!req.isAuthenticated) throw new Error(...)`), and every call site has to remember to make that check.

Rust code often follows *"Parse, Don't Validate"* (Alexis King, 2019): check input once and return a type that proves the check passed. The **typestate pattern** applies the same idea to state machines using zero-sized marker types. A `Connection<Unauthenticated>` is consumed by value by `authenticate()`, which returns a `Connection<Authenticated>`. If `send_query()` exists only on `Connection<Authenticated>` and the struct's fields are private, calling it on an unauthenticated connection is a compile error. The marker is stored as `PhantomData<State>`, which takes zero bytes at runtime.

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does Rust have a garbage collector like Node.js?**

A: No. Rust frees each value when its single owner goes out of scope, and the compiler decides where that happens. For shared ownership you opt into reference counting with Rc or Arc, which frees the value when the last reference is dropped.

**Q: Is Rust 100% memory safe?**

A: Safe Rust is memory safe: the compiler rejects use-after-free, double free, dangling references and data races. Code inside unsafe blocks can break these rules, and the standard library relies on carefully reviewed unsafe code internally. Memory leaks are considered safe, so an Rc reference cycle can still leak.

**Q: What does zero-cost abstraction mean in Rust?**

A: It means a high-level feature should compile to code as fast as what you would write by hand without it. Generics are monomorphized into specialized copies, and iterator chains are usually inlined into a plain loop. The cost moves elsewhere: longer compile times and larger binaries.

**Q: What are Send and Sync in Rust?**

A: Send marks a type whose values can be moved to another thread, and Sync marks a type that can be shared between threads by reference. The compiler implements both automatically when every field of a type implements them. Rc is neither, so trying to use it across threads is a compile error.

**Q: Can Rust prevent deadlocks?**

A: No. Safe Rust prevents data races, meaning unsynchronized access to the same memory from two threads where at least one writes. Two threads can still deadlock by locking two mutexes in opposite order, and logic-level race conditions are still possible.

#### Sources and further reading

- [The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 4: Understanding Ownership](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership.html): ownership, borrowing and drop rules.

- [The Rust Programming Language: Comparing Performance, Loops vs. Iterators](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-04-performance.html): iterators as a zero-cost abstraction.

- [The Rustonomicon: Send and Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/send-and-sync.html): exact definitions of both auto traits.

- [V8 blog: Trash talk, the Orinoco garbage collector](https://v8.dev/blog/trash-talk): how V8's Scavenger and Mark-Compact collectors work.

- [libuv docs: Thread pool work scheduling](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html): default pool size of 4 and UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.

- [Alexis King: Parse, don't validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/): the original essay behind the pattern.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter B2: Ownership & Move Semantics](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_ownership), [Chapter B5: Algebraic Enums & Pattern Matching](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_enums), [Chapter B8: Traits & Explicit Contracts](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_traits), [Chapter B9: Generics & Monomorphization](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_generics), [Chapter 25: Channels: mpsc, broadcast, watch & oneshot](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/channels_sync), [Chapter 32: Atomics & Hardware Memory Ordering](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/atomics_memory_ordering), [Chapter 34: Compile-Time Computation with const fn](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/const_eval), [Chapter P1: Fearless Concurrency & Send / Sync](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_fearless_concurrency), [Chapter P2: RAII & Deterministic Resource Management](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_raii_drop), [Chapter P3: The Zero-Cost Abstraction Principle](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_zero_cost), [Chapter P4: Make Illegal States Unrepresentable](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_type_driven), [Chapter P5: Explicit Over Implicit](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/philo_explicit_over_implicit)

## Appendix 11: Top 10 Rust Pitfalls & Footguns

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/pitfalls

Appendix 11 • Footguns

### Top 10 Rust Footguns for Node Developers

Common misconceptions, memory traps, and async hazards when transitioning from dynamic JavaScript to systems Rust.

#### Key takeaways

- Blocking calls such as `std::thread::sleep` or `std::fs` inside async Rust stall every task scheduled on that Tokio worker thread; move them to `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` or use the async equivalents.

- In Rust release builds, integer overflow wraps silently by default (`overflow-checks` is off in the release profile), while debug builds panic.

- `tokio::select!` drops the branches that did not finish, so futures that are not cancellation safe, such as `read_exact` and `write_all`, can lose data.

- Reference cycles of `Rc` or `Arc` leak memory because Rust has no tracing garbage collector; break them with `Weak`.

- Running destructors is not guaranteed in Rust: `std::mem::forget` is a safe function, and `panic = "abort"` or `std::process::exit` skip `Drop`.

##### Footgun 1: Calling .clone() to appease the compiler

Calling `.clone()` on a `String`, `Vec` or similar type allocates and copies the whole heap buffer. Cloning a large buffer on every HTTP request adds an allocation and a memory copy proportional to its size, which can erase the performance you moved to Rust for. Pass borrowed references (`&T`) where you can, or share the data with `Arc<T>`, whose `clone()` only increments an atomic reference count and does not copy the data.

##### Footgun 2: Blocking the Tokio worker thread pool

Calling synchronous file I/O or `std::thread::sleep` inside an async function blocks the OS worker thread it runs on, so every other task queued on that worker waits until it returns. Use `tokio::time::sleep` and `tokio::fs`, move blocking calls into `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, and send long CPU-bound work to a dedicated thread pool such as `rayon`, as the `spawn_blocking` docs recommend.

##### Footgun 3: Unbuffered File and Socket I/O

Node.js streams buffer for you. In Rust, each `read()` or `write()` on a `File` or `TcpStream` is a separate system call. When you do many small reads or writes (line-by-line parsing, writing small records), wrap the handle in `BufReader` or `BufWriter`, which batch them through an in-memory buffer (8 KiB by default on most platforms). Call `flush()` on a `BufWriter` before you rely on the data being written, because errors during the implicit flush on drop are ignored.

##### Footgun 4: Production .unwrap() & .expect() Panics

Calling `.unwrap()` on `None` or `Err` panics. A panic on the main thread ends the process. A panic inside a `tokio::spawn` task ends only that task, and its `JoinHandle` returns a `JoinError`, so a request can fail silently if nobody awaits the handle. With `panic = "abort"` in the profile, any panic ends the process. Propagate errors with `?`, using `anyhow` in applications and `thiserror` for library error types.

##### Footgun 5: Cancellation Hazards in tokio::select!

When one branch of `tokio::select!` completes, the futures in the other branches are dropped. Tokio documents `AsyncReadExt::read_exact`, `read_to_end`, `read_to_string` and `AsyncWriteExt::write_all` as not cancellation safe: bytes already read or written are lost. In a `select!` loop, use cancellation-safe operations such as `AsyncReadExt::read`, `mpsc::Receiver::recv`, or `StreamExt::next` on a framed stream, or create the future once outside the loop and poll it by `&mut` reference.

##### Footgun 6: Holding std::sync::MutexGuard Across .await

`std::sync::MutexGuard` is `!Send`, because on some platforms the lock must be released by the thread that acquired it. Holding the guard across an `.await` makes the whole future `!Send`, so `tokio::spawn` rejects it at compile time. In futures that do not need `Send`, holding the guard across an `.await` can deadlock: another task on the same thread may try to take the lock while the holder is suspended. Copy what you need out in a tight scope, `let val = { let guard = m.lock().unwrap(); guard.clone() };`, or use `tokio::sync::Mutex` when the lock must span an `.await`. Clippy's `await_holding_lock` lint flags this pattern.

##### Footgun 7: Memory Leaks via Reference Cycles

Rust has no cycle-detecting garbage collector. Two values holding `Rc` or `Arc` pointers to each other never reach a strong count of 0, so neither is freed until the process exits. Break cycles by making one direction a `Weak<T>` (created with `Rc::downgrade` or `Arc::downgrade`), for example child-to-parent links in a tree.

##### Footgun 8: Silent Integer Overflow in --release Mode

In the default debug profile, integer overflow panics. In `--release`, overflow checks are off by default and arithmetic wraps using two's complement. When overflow matters (money, counters, index math), use `checked_add()`, `saturating_add()` or `wrapping_add()` to make the behavior explicit, or set `overflow-checks = true` under `[profile.release]`.

##### Footgun 9: Self-Referential Structs & Pin Mechanics

JavaScript objects can freely reference their own fields. In safe Rust, a struct cannot hold a reference to one of its own fields, because moving the struct (returning it or passing it by value) changes its address and would leave that reference dangling. Async state machines need exactly this pattern, so Rust uses `Pin<P>`: once a value whose type is not `Unpin` is pinned, it is guaranteed not to move until it is dropped.

##### Footgun 10: Destructor Leaks via std::mem::forget & Aborts

Rust's memory safety guarantee does NOT include running destructors. `std::mem::forget()` is a safe function, and `panic = "abort"`, `std::process::exit()` and signals such as `SIGKILL` all end the process without running `Drop`. The OS still reclaims memory and closes file descriptors, but state outside the process, such as temporary files, lock files and unflushed `BufWriter` data, is left behind.

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is it bad to use .clone() everywhere in Rust?**

A: Not always, but it costs an allocation and a copy for heap types like `String` and `Vec`. Cloning small values or `Arc` handles is cheap; cloning large buffers in a hot path is not. Prefer borrowing with `&T` and share large data with `Arc<T>`.

**Q: Why is my async Rust server slow when I call std::thread::sleep or read a file?**

A: Those calls block the Tokio worker thread, so every other task on that worker stops making progress until they return. Use `tokio::time::sleep` and `tokio::fs`, or wrap blocking code in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. This is the Rust version of blocking the Node.js event loop with synchronous calls.

**Q: Does integer overflow crash a Rust program in production?**

A: Not by default. Release builds disable overflow checks, so arithmetic wraps around silently, while debug builds panic. Use `checked_*`, `saturating_*` or `wrapping_*` methods, or enable `overflow-checks = true` in the release profile.

**Q: Can Rust leak memory?**

A: Yes. Leaking memory is considered safe in Rust, so `std::mem::forget`, `Box::leak` and `Rc` or `Arc` reference cycles all leak without any `unsafe` code. Use `Weak` pointers to break cycles.

**Q: What happens when a spawned Tokio task panics?**

A: With the default `panic = "unwind"`, only that task stops, and awaiting its `JoinHandle` returns a `JoinError` whose `is_panic()` is true. The runtime and other tasks keep running. With `panic = "abort"`, the whole process exits.

#### Sources and further reading

- [tokio::task::spawn_blocking (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html): when to use the blocking pool versus a dedicated CPU pool.

- [tokio::select! (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/macro.select.html): the cancellation safety lists cited in footgun 5.

- [The Rust Reference: Operator expressions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html): integer overflow behavior in debug and release.

- [The Rust Book: Reference Cycles Can Leak Memory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-06-reference-cycles.html): `Rc` cycles and `Weak`.

- [std::mem::forget](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/fn.forget.html): why skipping destructors is safe Rust.
