## Appendix 12: LeetCode Easy in Rust

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/leetcode

Appendix 12 • Problem Solving

### LeetCode in Rust (JS vs Rust)

Seven classic LeetCode problems solved in Rust, each compared with the JavaScript solution you already know.

#### Key takeaways

- LeetCode linked lists in Rust use `Option<Box<ListNode>>`, where `None` plays the role of JavaScript's `null` next pointer.

- `Option::take()` moves a value out and leaves `None` behind, which is how you rewire linked list nodes without fighting the borrow checker.

- A Rust `String` is UTF-8 and cannot be indexed with `s[i]`; for ASCII-only problems, iterate over `s.bytes()` or index `s.as_bytes()`.

- `HashMap::with_capacity(n)` allocates once up front, so inserting n elements never triggers a resize.

- A `Vec` works as a stack: `push()` adds to the end and `pop()` returns an `Option`, so popping an empty stack is `None` instead of `undefined`.

[LC #1 Two Sum Single pass with a pre-sized HashMap, O(n) time.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_two_sum)
[LC #20 Valid Parentheses LIFO stack of expected closing bytes in a Vec<u8>.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_valid_parentheses)
[LC #21 Merge Two Sorted Lists Moving Box nodes between Option<Box<ListNode>> lists with take().](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_merge_lists)
[LC #121 Best Time to Buy/Sell Single-pass greedy algorithm in O(1) space.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_buy_sell_stock)
[LC #125 Valid Palindrome Two pointers over bytes with ASCII case-insensitive comparison.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_valid_palindrome)
[LC #206 Reverse Linked List Ownership transfer with Option::take.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_reverse_linked_list)
[LC #53 Maximum Subarray Kadane's algorithm in O(n) time.](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/lc_max_subarray)

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can I solve LeetCode problems in Rust?**

A: Yes. Rust is one of the languages LeetCode accepts, and it provides Rust function signatures for most problems. The signatures often take owned types such as Vec<i32> and String, and linked list problems give you a ListNode struct with an Option<Box<ListNode>> next field.

**Q: Why are linked lists so hard in Rust?**

A: Each Box node has exactly one owner, so you cannot keep two mutable pointers into the same list the way you would in JavaScript. The usual fix is Option::take(), which moves the next node out and leaves None, so ownership passes along one node at a time. Doubly linked lists need Rc and RefCell or unsafe code.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of a JavaScript Map or object for LeetCode?**

A: Use std::collections::HashMap for key lookups and HashSet for membership checks. Unlike a JavaScript Map, a Rust HashMap does not keep insertion order; use BTreeMap if you need keys in sorted order. The entry() API lets you insert or update a key in one lookup, which is handy for frequency counts.

**Q: How do I index characters of a string in Rust?**

A: You cannot write s[i] on a Rust String, because it is UTF-8 and one character can take several bytes. For ASCII-only inputs, which covers most LeetCode problems, use s.as_bytes()[i] or iterate with s.bytes(). For full Unicode, iterate with s.chars() or collect into a Vec<char>.

**Q: How do I use a stack in Rust like a JavaScript array?**

A: Use a Vec: push() adds to the end and pop() removes from the end. pop() returns an Option, so an empty stack gives None, which you handle with match or if let instead of checking for undefined. For a queue, use std::collections::VecDeque.

#### Sources and further reading

- [Rust std docs: Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html): take(), as_ref() and the combinators used in the linked list solutions.

- [Rust std docs: HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html): with_capacity(), entry() and lookup methods.

- [The Rust Programming Language: Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch08-02-strings.html): why strings cannot be indexed by position.

- [Learning Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists](https://rust-unofficial.github.io/too-many-lists/): a full walk-through of linked lists and ownership.

- [LeetCode #1: Two Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/): the original problem statement and Rust signature.

## Appendix 13: Rosetta Stone Cheatsheet

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cheatsheet

Appendix 13 • Reference

### Rosetta Stone Syntax Cheatsheet

Side-by-side TypeScript and Rust idioms, from variables to shared state across threads.

#### Key takeaways

- Rust bindings are immutable by default; `let mut` is the opt-in, and Rust's `let` is closer to TypeScript's `const` than to its `let`.

- TypeScript's `number` is a 64-bit float, while Rust makes you pick an exact integer or float type such as `i32`, `u64` or `f64`.

- The `?` operator returns early with the error, converting it with `From`, which replaces most try/catch-and-rethrow code.

- `tokio::try_join!` is the closest match to `Promise.all`: it waits for all futures and returns the first error.

- A Rust `HashMap` does not preserve insertion order the way a JavaScript `Map` does.

| Domain | TypeScript / Node.js | Rust Equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Variables | `const x = 5;; let y = 10;` | `let x = 5;; let mut y = 10;; const MAX: u32 = 100; // compile-time constant` |
| Numeric Types | `number` (IEEE 754 64-bit float); `bigint` (arbitrary precision) | `i8, i16, i32, i64, i128, isize; u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, usize, f32, f64`; No built-in bigint; use a crate such as `num-bigint`. |
| Strings | `string` (a sequence of UTF-16 code units; V8 stores strings that fit in Latin-1 as one byte per character internally) | `String` (owned, growable, UTF-8, heap); `&str` (borrowed UTF-8 string slice) |
| Pattern Matching | `switch (status.kind) {; case "ok": return status.val > 0 ? 1 : 0;; default: return -1;; }` | `match status {; Status::Ok(val) if val > 0 => 1,; Status::Ok(_) => 0,; _ => -1,; }; // must be exhaustive, or it fails to compile` |
| Guard / Destructure | `if (user !== null) { ... }` | `if let Some(user) = maybe_user { ... }` |
| Option / Nullable | `user?.profile?.avatar ?? "default.png"` | `// user: Option<User>, profile and avatar are Options; user.and_then(\|u\| u.profile); .and_then(\|p\| p.avatar); .unwrap_or_else(\|\| "default.png".to_string())` |
| Error Propagation | `const res = await fetch(url);; // a rejection propagates to the caller` | `let res = client.get(url).send().await?;; // ? returns Err early, converting it with From` |
| Custom Errors | `class ApiError extends Error { ... }` | `#[derive(thiserror::Error, Debug)]; pub enum AppError {; #[error("Not found: {0}")]; NotFound(String),; #[error(transparent)]; Db(#[from] sqlx::Error),; }` |
| Closures & Captures | `const add = (x: number) => x + n;; // implicit lexical capture by reference` | `\|x\| x + n // captures n by the least it needs (&, &mut, or value); move \|x\| x + n // forces capture by value; Traits: Fn, FnMut, FnOnce` |
| Interfaces vs Traits | `interface Printable {; print(): void;; }; // structural: any matching shape fits` | `pub trait Printable {; fn print(&self);; }; impl Printable for MyStruct { ... }; // nominal: needs an explicit impl` |
| Generics & Bounds | `function log<T extends Printable>(x: T)` | `fn log<T: Printable + Send>(x: T); // or with where clause: where T: Printable` |
| Arrays & Vectors | `const arr = [1, 2, 3];; arr.push(4);` | `let mut vec = vec![1, 2, 3];; vec.push(4);; let fixed: [i32; 3] = [1, 2, 3]; // fixed-size array` |
| Hash Maps / Records | `const map = new Map<string, number>();; map.set("key", 42);; // iterates in insertion order` | `use std::collections::HashMap;; let mut map = HashMap::new();; map.insert("key".to_string(), 42);; // iteration order is unspecified; BTreeMap is sorted` |
| Concurrent Async Work | `const p = doWork(); // starts without awaiting; await Promise.all([fut1, fut2]);` | `let handle = tokio::spawn(async move { ... });; let (a, b) = tokio::try_join!(fut1, fut2)?;; // futures are lazy: nothing runs until awaited or spawned` |
| Shared State | `const shared = { count: 0 };; // accessible everywhere on single thread` | `Arc<Mutex<T>> // shared mutable state across threads; Arc<RwLock<T>> // many readers or one writer; // hold a lock across .await? use tokio::sync::Mutex` |

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between String and &str in Rust?**

A: String is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer on the heap, and &str is a borrowed view into UTF-8 text owned by something else. Functions usually take &str as a parameter so they accept both, and return String when they build new text. String literals like "hello" have type &'static str.

**Q: What replaces null and undefined in Rust?**

A: Option<T>, which is either Some(value) or None. The compiler will not let you use the inner value until you handle the None case, for example with match, if let, unwrap_or or the ? operator. Safe Rust has no null references.

**Q: Is there a try/catch in Rust?**

A: No. Recoverable errors are values of type Result<T, E>, and the ? operator returns the error to the caller early. Panics exist for bugs and unrecoverable states, and they are not meant for normal error handling.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of Promise.all?**

A: tokio::try_join! is the closest match: it runs futures concurrently and returns the first error, like Promise.all rejecting. tokio::join! waits for every future and returns all results, closer to Promise.allSettled. For a dynamic number of tasks, use tokio::task::JoinSet.

**Q: Are Rust traits the same as TypeScript interfaces?**

A: They are similar contracts but work differently. TypeScript interfaces are structural, so any object with the right shape fits, and they are erased at runtime. Rust traits are nominal, so a type must have an explicit impl block, and traits can also provide default methods and be implemented for types you did not write.

#### Sources and further reading

- [The Rust Programming Language: Strings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch08-02-strings.html): String vs &str and UTF-8 encoding.

- [The Rust Programming Language: Closures](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-01-closures.html): capture modes, move, and Fn, FnMut, FnOnce.

- [Rust std docs: HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html): API and the note that iteration order is arbitrary.

- [Tokio docs: try_join!](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/macro.try_join.html): concurrent futures that stop at the first error.

- [thiserror docs](https://docs.rs/thiserror/latest/thiserror/): the #[error] and #[from] attributes used above.

- [Rust by Example](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/): runnable examples for every row in this table.

Foundational chapters: [Chapter B1: Variables, Immutability & let mut](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_vars), [Chapter B4: Structs, impl Blocks & Methods](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_structs), [Chapter B5: Algebraic Enums & Pattern Matching](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_enums), [Chapter B6: Option<T> — Banishing null & undefined](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_option), [Chapter B9: Generics & Monomorphization](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_generics), [Chapter 5: JSON Parsing: JSON.parse() vs Serde](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/serde_json), [Chapter 7: Array.map / filter / reduce vs Vec Iterators](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/vec_transform), [Chapter 8: Map & Set vs HashMap & HashSet](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/hashmap_set)

## Appendix 14: Rust Developer Roadmap (roadmap.sh)

URL: https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/roadmap

🧭 Appendix 14 • Official Roadmap Track

### Rust Developer Roadmap

A step-by-step curriculum that follows the topics of [roadmap.sh/rust](https://roadmap.sh/rust), mapped to chapters written for JavaScript & TypeScript engineers.

#### Key takeaways

- A practical Rust learning order for Node.js developers is: toolchain, ownership and borrowing, enums and error handling, traits and generics, async with Tokio, then web services.

- `rustup` replaces `nvm` for managing toolchains, and `cargo` replaces both `npm` and your build scripts.

- Ownership and borrowing come second because every later stage depends on them: Rust frees memory at points the compiler knows, instead of using a garbage collector.

- Rust replaces `null` and exceptions with `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>`, so missing values and errors show up in function signatures.

- A common Rust web stack is Axum 0.8 on Tokio, SQLx or SeaORM for the database, Serde for JSON, and a multi-stage Docker build.

##### 🗺️ roadmap.sh/rust Milestone Path

From Node.js mental models to production Rust services, in six stages.

[View on roadmap.sh ↗](https://roadmap.sh/rust)

**Stage 1** Basics & Syntax

**Stage 2** Ownership & Memory

**Stage 3** Types, Enums & Errors

**Stage 4** Traits & Generics

**Stage 5** Async & Tokio

**Stage 6** Microservices & Prod

#### 01
Toolchain, Installation & Cargo Essentials

Stage 1 of 6

In the Node.js universe, version managers like `nvm` or `fnm` manage Node runtimes while `npm`/`pnpm` handle package dependencies. In Rust, `rustup` manages toolchains (stable, beta, nightly), components and cross-compilation targets, and `cargo` is both the build tool and the package manager. The default rustup profile installs `rustc`, `cargo`, `rust-std`, `rust-docs`, `rustfmt` and `clippy`; add the language server with `rustup component add rust-analyzer`.

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- `rustup`: Toolchain channels (stable, beta, nightly)

- `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo check`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`

- `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` (the Prettier and ESLint equivalents)

- `rust-analyzer` language server (`rustup component add rust-analyzer`)

- Playground vs Native compilation

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter B1: Variables, Mutability & Types](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_vars)

- [Appendix 03: Cargo vs npm Deep Dive](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cargo-vs-npm)

- [Appendix 09: Diagnostics & Compiler Flags](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/troubleshooting)

#### 02
Memory Management, Ownership & Borrowing

Stage 2 of 6

Node.js developers rely on V8's generational garbage collector (a Scavenger for young objects and Mark-Compact for old ones, both part of V8's Orinoco project) to reclaim unreachable objects. Rust has no tracing garbage collector: ownership rules checked at compile time, plus RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization), drop each value at a known point, when its single owner goes out of scope.

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- Stack vs Heap allocations & cache locality

- Single ownership rule & Move semantics

- Shared (`&T`) vs exclusive (`&mut T`) references

- Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL, RFC 2094) & lifetime annotations (`'a`)

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter B2: Ownership & Move Semantics](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_ownership)

- [Chapter B10: Lifetimes in 5 Minutes](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_lifetimes)

- [Appendix 01: The Interactive Borrow Checker](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/borrow-checker)

- [Appendix 10: The Rust Philosophy (Affine Types)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/philosophy)

#### 03
Algebraic Types, Enums & Errors as Values

Stage 3 of 6

In TypeScript, union types and nullable types (`null | undefined`) are checked at compile time but erased at runtime, leaving programs vulnerable to `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Safe Rust has no null references. Instead, it uses Algebraic Data Types (ADTs) such as `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>`, and the compiler requires every `match` to handle all cases.

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- Structs (tuple, named, unit) & `impl` methods

- Enums with data payloads (tagged unions)

- `match` expressions & `if let` destructuring

- The `?` (try) operator for early error return

- `thiserror` for domain errors & `anyhow` for applications

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter B6: Option instead of null/undefined](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_option)

- [Chapter B7: Result<T, E> instead of try/catch](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_result)

- [Chapter 24: thiserror vs anyhow Patterns](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/error_anyhow_thiserror)

- [Appendix 13: TypeScript vs Rust Rosetta Cheatsheet](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/cheatsheet)

#### 04
Traits, Monomorphization & Smart Pointers

Stage 4 of 6

TypeScript interfaces are structural: any object with the right shape fits. Rust traits are nominal: a type implements a trait only through an explicit `impl`. Generic code is monomorphized into a specialized copy per concrete type (static dispatch with no runtime lookup, paid for in compile time and binary size). When you need dynamic dispatch, `dyn Trait` calls methods through a vtable. Smart pointers (`Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`) make ownership explicit, and `RefCell`, `Mutex` and `RwLock` provide interior mutability.

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- Traits: definition, derive macros (`#[derive(Debug, Clone)]`)

- Static dispatch (Generics + Trait bounds) vs Dynamic dispatch (`Box<dyn Trait>`)

- `Box<T>` for heap allocation & recursive structures

- `Rc<T>` vs `Arc<T>`: Single-threaded vs Thread-safe reference counting

- `RefCell<T>` vs `Mutex<T>` / `RwLock<T>` interior mutability

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter B8: Traits vs TypeScript Interfaces](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_traits)

- [Chapter B9: Generics & Monomorphization (Static Dispatch)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/basic_generics)

- [Chapter 10: Smart Pointers (Box, Rc, Arc)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/smart_pointers)

- [Chapter 11: Arc<Mutex<T>> for Shared Mutability](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/interior_mutability)

#### 05
Concurrency, Fearless Multi-Threading & Tokio

Stage 5 of 6

In Node.js, your JavaScript runs on a single event loop thread, so a long CPU-bound function delays every other request until it finishes. In Rust, the `Send` and `Sync` marker traits let the compiler reject safe code that could cause a data race. An `async fn` compiles to a state machine that does nothing until an executor polls it; Tokio's multi-threaded runtime spreads tasks across worker threads with work stealing, as described in Tokio's 2019 post "Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster".

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- OS threads (`std::thread::spawn`) vs lightweight async tasks (`tokio::spawn`)

- CPU-bound work off the async workers with `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`

- Message passing with `tokio::sync` channels (`mpsc`, `broadcast`, `watch`, `oneshot`)

- `Future` trait, `Pin<P>`, and cooperative polling loops

- `tokio::select!`, `JoinSet`, cooperative yield (`tokio::task::yield_now`) and `CancellationToken` from `tokio-util`

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter 21: Promise.all vs tokio::join! & spawn](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/tokio_spawn)

- [Chapter 25: Tokio Channels (mpsc, broadcast, oneshot)](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/channels_sync)

- [Chapter 23: Cancellation Tokens & AbortHandles](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/cancellation_tokens)

- [Appendix 02: Async Rust & Tokio Architecture](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/async-tokio)

#### 06
Web Services, Databases & Production Deployment

Stage 6 of 6

Moving from Express, Fastify or NestJS to Rust web services. A common production stack is **Axum** (built on Tower and Hyper), **SQLx** for SQL checked at compile time, **SeaORM** as an async ORM, **Serde** for serialization, and multi-stage Docker builds that cache dependencies with **cargo-chef** and ship on a distroless base image.

###### Key Roadmap Concepts

- Web frameworks: Axum 0.8 (path params as `/{id}`), Actix-web, Tower middleware

- Databases: SQLx (`query!` macros check SQL against a live database or data cached by `cargo sqlx prepare`), SeaORM

- Serialization: `serde`, `serde_json`, with optional borrowed (zero-copy) `&str` fields

- Production containers: `cargo-chef` dependency caching & `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian13` runtime images

###### Corresponding Book Chapters & Guides

- [Chapter 1: Express.js vs Axum HTTP Server](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/axum_api)

- [Chapter 13: pg/Prisma vs SQLx with Postgres](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/chapter/sqlx_compile_time)

- [Appendix 04: Production Axum Microservice Architecture](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/microservice)

- [Appendix 05: Distroless Docker & cargo-chef](https://rust-for-node-devs.vercel.app/docker)

#### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What should a Node.js developer learn first in Rust?**

A: Start with cargo and basic syntax, then spend real time on ownership and borrowing before touching async. Many errors in async and web code, such as use of a moved value or a future that is not Send, are ownership errors, so learning the rules first makes later stages easier.

**Q: Do I need to learn async Rust to build a web server?**

A: Yes, for the mainstream frameworks. Axum and Actix-web are async, and Axum runs on the Tokio runtime, so you need async fn, .await and the basics of Send and 'static bounds on spawned tasks.

**Q: What is the Rust equivalent of Express.js?**

A: Axum is the closest match for most Express users: you build a Router, attach async handler functions to routes, and add middleware as Tower layers. Actix-web is a mature alternative with a similar handler-and-extractor style.

**Q: What replaces nvm and npm in Rust?**

A: rustup replaces nvm: it installs and switches between stable, beta and nightly toolchains. cargo replaces npm and most build scripts: it creates projects, downloads crates from crates.io, builds, runs tests and formats code with cargo fmt.

**Q: Is this roadmap the same as roadmap.sh/rust?**

A: No. It groups the same core topics into six stages and links each stage to chapters in this book. Use roadmap.sh/rust for the full topic map, which covers more areas than this book.

#### Sources and further reading

- [roadmap.sh: Rust Developer Roadmap](https://roadmap.sh/rust): the community topic map this page follows.

- [The rustup book: Profiles](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/profiles.html): which components the default profile installs.

- [RFC 2094: Non-lexical lifetimes](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2094-nll.html): how the borrow checker reasons about reference lifetimes.

- [Tokio blog: Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster](https://tokio.rs/blog/2019-10-scheduler): the work-stealing design of Tokio's multi-threaded runtime.

- [Axum documentation on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/): routing, extractors and state for the web stage.

- [cargo-chef README](https://github.com/LukeMathWalker/cargo-chef): caching Rust dependencies in Docker builds.
